- Reading reference AVX-512 kernels for Dilithium (16-way NTT in ntt512.c/inv_ntt512.c, 8-way SHAKE sampling in fips202x8.c and keccak8x.c) when writing your own ML-DSA backend
- Checking the paper's component benchmarks: dilithium2_avx512/test/test_speed.c times PQClean ('clean') against the authors' ('xurq') Keccak permutation, matrix expansion, uniform_eta and uniform_gamma1 side by side
- Research on Rocket Lake / Ice Lake-class CPUs with full AVX-512 (F/VL/CD/BW/DQ/VBMI/VBMI2), where the paper's i7-11700F numbers apply

**Skip it when:**
- Any production or FIPS 204 use: the repo is Round 3 Dilithium only (Dilithium2 sk = 2528 bytes) and does not include the ML-DSA code behind the headline Table XI numbers
- Anywhere you need a license: there is no LICENSE file, so legally the code is reference-only even though parts derive from permissively licensed PQClean/NIST code
- Code you would trust without re-testing. By reading (not running) it: only dilithium5_avx512 signing actually calls pspm_tee_r0/pspm_tee_z, and those functions store |value| (after _mm512_abs_epi32) into z and r0 before z is packed into the signature. The last 64-coefficient block is also loaded at offset N+182-j, versus 192 in pspm()
- CPUs without AVX-512 (many client Intel parts, older AMD): the _avx512 trees are compiled with -mavx512f/vl/cd/bw/dq/vbmi/vbmi2, and the AVX2 trees gain only about 3-8% in signing from PSPM-TEE (paper Tables VII/X)
- Side-channel-sensitive deployments: the paper says constant-time was 'not the focus', and PSPM-TEE branches on challenge coefficients and returns early from rejection checks

**Vs siblings:** Dilithium-AVX512 (github.com/Dilithium-AVX512/Dilithium-AVX512) is catalogued from the same paper with the same numbers. It is a single pq-crystals-style tree with KAT files and a DILITHIUM_MODE switch, but it has no PSPM code. Pick this repo only when you want the PSPM-TEE source and the AVX2 variants; for a usable ML-DSA, neither sibling qualifies, and the Plantard-NTT codegen entry is the more rigorous (formally verified) option if you need portable speedups.

**Gotchas:**
- PSPM is not used in most trees: dilithium2_avx512 compiles PSPMTEE.c but signs with NTT, and dilithium3_avx512 plus all three _avx2 trees contain no PSPM code, although the paper describes PSPM-TEE for AVX2 and AVX-512
- The test_speed harnesses never check verify's return value (the D5 AVX-512 harness even signs in place over its message buffer). They run NTESTS = 10000, not the paper's 100000 repetitions, so a passing speed run proves nothing about correctness
- Build artifacts are committed (common/keccak/*.o and a roughly 20 MB 'our_3_avx512_test_speed' binary in dilithium3_avx512); rebuild from source rather than trusting them
- The paper's text and tables disagree on where PSPM-TEE helps most: the text says 7.7% for Dilithium3, while Table VII shows 7.7% for Dilithium2 and 3.1% for Dilithium3

**Status:** Stale research dump (10 commits, last 2025-07-16, 3 stars, no issues) with no license, so it is reference-only; treat it as a companion to the TDSC paper, not a library.

[repo](https://github.com/xurq5953/Optimizing-Dilithium-Implementation-with-AVX2-512) · [benchmark](https://arxiv.org/abs/2306.01989)

### interpreters-and-vms

#### bytecode-vms-and-wasm

##### Wasmer (LLVM backend)  `Rust`  `MIT (repository); BUSL-1.1 for the LLVM and Singlepass compiler crates from Wasmer 6.0`  `active`  `Tier B`

Rust WebAssembly runtime whose optional LLVM backend runs WASI code about 1.15x faster than Wasmtime and 1.34x faster than V8.

**Beats:** Wasmtime (Cranelift) and V8 (Node.js) — Frank Denis's December 2022 run of libsodium's built-in benchmark suite compiled once to WASI (about 70 crypto primitives, the same wasm for every runtime, compile time excluded; per a snippet of his post, a Zen 2 CPU pinned to one core, with runtime versions and flags unstated) gives wasmer-llvm 0.872x Wasmtime's per-test time and 0.747x Node/V8's. These are geomeans over 69 shared tests, faster on 54 and 60 respectively (derived from page data). I reproduced both figures exactly from the CSVs; dropping the tiny rows gives 0.841x and 0.753x, and WAMR's iwasm and wasm2c stay faster than wasmer-llvm.

**Known shortcoming:** In the Frank Denis libsodium CSVs behind the 0.872x-of-wasmtime and 0.747x-of-node figures, WAMR iwasm (a listed baseline) is faster (wasmer-llvm takes 1.277x its time and wins 1 of 69 tests) and wasm2c is faster too; no CPU model or versions. The LLVM and Singlepass backends are BUSL-1.1 from Wasmer 6.0 (usability mixed) while the measured numbers come from the old MIT-era backend; the 2026 Denis post snippets put Wasmer ahead of Wasmtime.

**Known shortcoming:** Enricher: about 18 of the 70 libsodium rows are tiny (under 5000 units, onetimeauth2 at 0 or 1) with the 2022 units and timer undocumented (today's cmptest.h uses ITERATIONS=200 on a microsecond clock, so values are multiples of 5000); the wins over wasmtime and node survive on rows at or above 5000 (0.841x and 0.753x), but the apparent win over WasmEdge (0.819x, faster on 31 of 69) comes only from the tiny rows and WasmEdge is faster on rows at or above 5000 (1.031x, 1.104x above 100000). The README's 'LLVM about 50% faster than Cranelift' is not reproduced (0.858x of wasmer-cranelift time, 0.902x on rows at or above 5000). Per-function LLVM modules with no inlining, volatile memory ops by default (#3987), requires exactly LLVM 22 (other versions silently disable the backend), BUSL-1.1 from 6.0.0 with the last MIT crate 5.0.6 (2025-05-02); open LLVM performance issues #6535, #6529, #6521, #6491, #6489.

**How:** Each Wasm function is lowered to its own LLVM IR module (via inkwell) and the functions are compiled in parallel on a rayon pool. Ordinary-size functions get a hand-picked function-level pass list (SCCP, early-CSE, SROA, aggressive-instcombine, jump threading, GVN, DSE, loop-rotate, indvars, memcpyopt), and code generation runs at OptimizationLevel::Aggressive with the host CPU's feature flags. Statically reserved linear memories rely on guard pages instead of explicit bounds compares (dynamic memories get a check marked likely-in-bounds with llvm.expect). Memory 0's base pointer is passed as a hidden first argument (the 'm0' or pass-params optimization, on by default since 7.1), and memory accesses carry per-memory TBAA tags. There is no cross-function inlining because each function is its own module, and functions above a size threshold drop to an O1-style pipeline; both cap how close it gets to whole-module LLVM AOT runtimes such as WAMR's wamrc, wasm2c or WAVM.

**Use it when:**
- Long-running, CPU-bound WASI modules (crypto, codecs, numeric kernels) where steady-state throughput matters more than compile latency, and compiled modules can be cached or serialized.
- You already embed Wasmer (Rust or C API, WASIX) on its default Cranelift backend: swapping in LLVM gave a 0.858x geomean time (about 1.17x) on the 2022-12 libsodium suite, or about 1.08-1.10x on the non-trivial rows (derived from page data).
- Ahead-of-time pipelines: compile with LLVM on a build machine (cross-compilation is supported), ship the serialized artifact and run it headless without LLVM on the target.
- x86-64 or aarch64 hosts on Linux, macOS or Windows where an LLVM 22 toolchain can be installed for the build.

**Skip it when:**
- Startup- or compile-latency-sensitive work (cold starts, untrusted uploads, blockchains): LLVM compiles far slower than Cranelift or Singlepass. Wasmer's own Singlepass README recommends Singlepass where JIT bombs are a risk, and the 7.1 changelog says huge functions had to drop optimization (Python compile time from about 90 s to about 10 s). A Wasmer 2.2 blog snippet (page blocked) describes a module where Cranelift took about 10 minutes and the LLVM compile was stopped after 3 hours.
- When peak steady-state speed is the only goal: in the same 2022-12 data WAMR's iwasm (wasmer-llvm takes 1.277x its time, faster on 1 of 69 tests) and wasm2c (1.171x) are faster. WasmEdge is also faster on every row large enough to measure well (see gotchas).
- Production use of Wasmer 6.0 or later with the LLVM backend when you are not a paying Wasmer sponsor: the crate is BUSL-1.1. The last MIT release of wasmer-compiler-llvm is 5.0.6 (2025-05-02).
- SIMD-heavy or unusual store patterns: open issues report large LLVM-backend slowdowns for v128.bitselect feeding extends (#6535), i64x2 shifts by 32..63 (#6529), dynamic i8x16 shifts (#6521), store16 and rem_u-addressed stores (#6491, #6489), f64.convert_i64_u (#6083) and memory.size (#6147).
- Code written against the Wasmtime embedding API or Node's WASI: this is a different runtime and API, not a drop-in replacement.

**Vs siblings:** Pick it over Wasmtime and V8 (and over Wasmer's own Cranelift default) when you are already on Wasmer and want steady-state throughput on long-running modules. If peak throughput is the only goal, the WAMR (iwasm) and wasm2c siblings were faster on the same libsodium data. For startup-bound work, interpreters such as Wasmi, wasm3 or Fizzy are the right choice.

**Gotchas:**
- Licence split: the repository and its badge say MIT, but wasmer-compiler-llvm and wasmer-compiler-singlepass from 6.0.0 (2025-04-24) are under the Business Source License 1.1 (crates.io lists them as 'non-standard'). Production use is allowed only for Wasmer sponsors; each version becomes MPL 2.0 four years after publication. The last MIT LLVM crate is 5.0.6 (2025-05-02). The benchmarked 2022 build was MIT-era (release dates suggest 3.0.x to 3.1.0; the version is not stated).
- The build needs LLVM 22 exactly: BUILD.md says any other version silently disables the backend, so check the 'Enabled Compilers:' banner.
- Semantics knobs: by default, user memory loads and stores on static memories are marked volatile so LLVM cannot delete them, which costs speed (issue #3987 shows a dead load emitted before each store). Non-volatile memops are faster but the code calls them 'not 100% SPEC compliant'; they are switched on automatically for WASIX modules (PR #6212), with --disable-non-volatile-memops to opt out. NaN canonicalization is off by default.
- Harness flaw in the benchmark: about 18 of the 70 libsodium rows are tiny (values under 5000 for every runtime; onetimeauth2 is recorded as 0 or 1). The 2022 run's units and timer are undocumented: today's cmptest.h, with ITERATIONS=200 and a microsecond clock, could only print multiples of 5000. The wins over Wasmtime and V8 survive dropping those rows (0.841x and 0.753x on 51 rows at 5000 or above). The apparent geomean win over WasmEdge (0.819x on 69 rows, but faster on only 31) comes from the tiny rows: on rows at 5000 or above, wasmer-llvm takes 1.031x WasmEdge's time (faster on 15 of 51), and 1.104x on rows at 100000 or above. The first-party README claim of 'about 50% faster' than Cranelift is not reproduced: 0.858x wasmer-cranelift's time (about 1.17x faster) on 70 rows, 0.902x on rows at 5000 or above (all derived from page data).

**Status:** Actively maintained (7.5.0 released 2026-10-01, commits on 2026-10-06, 21.1k stars) and usable as a crate or CLI, but the LLVM backend's BUSL-1.1 licence since 6.0 limits production use to Wasmer sponsors unless you pin the MIT 5.0.6 release; the speedup was measured on a 2022 MIT-era build with undocumented units for the tiny rows.

[repo](https://github.com/wasmerio/wasmer) · [benchmark](https://github.com/jedisct1/webassembly-benchmarks/tree/master/2022-12/res)

#### embedded-scripting

##### yklua (Yk JIT retrofitted into PUC Lua)  `C (Lua interpreter) with the Rust Yk JIT`  `MIT (PUC-Rio Lua notice in src/lua.h and doc/readme.html); no repository-level LICENSE file covering the Yk additions`  `active`  `Tier A`

PUC-Rio Lua 5.5.0 with the yk meta-tracing JIT bolted on; about 1.96x faster than stock Lua 5.5 on a 22-benchmark geomean.

**Beats:** PUC-Rio Lua 5.5.0 (stock lua.org tarball, the version yklua is based on) built with -flto as an LTO baseline — yk's public ReBench harness (ykjit/yk-benchmarks) runs 22 benchmarks (14 AWFY, 4 CLBG, 3 real-world, BigLoop) for 5 invocations of 10 iterations each, on an AMD EPYC 7F52 (Debian, kernel 6.12.57). It compares yklua against stock PUC Lua 5.5.0 built with gcc -O2 -flto. I recomputed the 2026-10-06 14:23 run from its data file: a geomean time ratio of 0.511 (1.96x), with per-benchmark speedups from 1.09x (DeltaBlue) to 5.77x (Mandelbrot). The last 10 nightly runs range from 0.504 to 0.519.

**Known shortcoming:** Upgraded C to A on the ykjit/yk-benchmarks gh-pages data (geomean time ratio 0.513, about 1.95x, over 22 benchmarks against stock Lua 5.5.0 -flto on an AMD EPYC 7F52, harness and flags public); the record's Mandelbrot 3.2 s to 0.8 s claim was not found (data shows 5.84x). Experimental, needs the yk toolchain (ykllvm versus gcc), uneven 1.09x-5.84x. No repository LICENSE file (Lua core MIT), so usability is mixed.

**Known shortcoming:** Enricher: recomputed 20261006_142333.data gives geomean 0.511 (1.96x), from 1.09x DeltaBlue to 5.77x Mandelbrot, but the timing is wall clock while yk compiles on YK_JOBS (num_cpus minus 1) background threads against a single-threaded baseline with CPU time unreported; there is no JIT-off executor, the baseline is gcc computed-goto against ykllvm switch dispatch, the location leak #113 is confirmed in code (luaF_freeproto never calls yk_location_drop), LuLPeg slows over its run (787 vs 911 ms), Linux x86-64 only, and the yk docs rate it pre-alpha.

**How:** yk is a meta-tracing system. ykllvm embeds the interpreter's own LLVM IR (fat LTO, .llvmbc section) and stackmaps in the binary. A yk_mt_control_point call at the top of luaV_execute counts executions of per-pc YkLocations, which are placed at backward-jump and for-loop heads at parse time and at the entry of functions found to be recursive. Once a location passes YK_HOT_THRESHOLD (131 by default), yk records the interpreter's path through its own IR and compiles that trace. The interpreter is annotated so that traces specialise well: yk_promote on constants, prototype sizes and the pc, yk_idempotent on loads, and yk_unroll on helper loops. Constant-folded traces then remove dispatch, type checks and table lookups, in the same way PyPy's meta-tracing does.

**Use it when:**
- Loop-heavy numeric Lua on Linux x86-64, where gains are largest: Mandelbrot 5.8x, BigLoop 3.9x, spectralnorm 3.4x, Heightmap 3.1x, Sieve 3.0x and NBody 2.9x against stock Lua 5.5.0.
- You want a JIT while keeping current PUC Lua 5.5 semantics (integers, 5.4/5.5 features) rather than moving to LuaJIT's Lua 5.1 dialect.
- Research or prototyping on meta-tracing: the yk changes are a small set of USE_YK hooks in lvm.c, ldo.c, lparser.c, lfunc.c and lstate.c, so it is a readable worked example of retrofitting a JIT into a C interpreter.
- Long-running scripts where a 1.5-2x average speedup is worth carrying an experimental toolchain (Rust nightly, ykllvm).

**Skip it when:**
- Production or shipped embeddings. The README says experimental, yk's docs rate it pre-alpha, all.lua is 'currently failing for non-serialised compilation', and 25 issues are open, including per-file test failures since 2023 and a lua_assert failure in luac (#110).
- Any platform other than Linux on x86-64 (a yk requirement), or builds that cannot use Rust nightly and the ykllvm LLVM fork.
- Object-heavy or allocation-heavy code gains little: DeltaBlue 1.09x, Storage 1.23x, Havlak 1.24x, CD 1.35x and binarytrees 1.36x.
- Hosts that load Lua C modules or other code with dlopen at run time. yk's gotchas say it assumes no code is loaded or unloaded at run time, and code without embedded IR cannot be inlined into traces.
- When peak speed matters more than Lua 5.5 compatibility: the author's 2026 blog post says it does not reach LuaJIT's peak performance (search snippet only; tratt.net is blocked here).

**Vs siblings:** LuaJIT Remake (Deegen) and Luau target Lua 5.1 or a 5.1-derived dialect, and Pallene compiles a typed subset. yklua is the only catalogued option that JIT-compiles unmodified Lua 5.5, so pick it when you need 5.5 semantics and can accept pre-alpha status. For production embedding, Luau's interpreter or LuaJIT are the mature choices.

**Gotchas:**
- Harness caveat on the timing: AWFY's harness.lua measures wall-clock time (os.monotonic), and yk compiles traces on up to num_cpus - 1 background threads (YK_JOBS default) on the 16-core EPYC 7F52. Stock Lua is single-threaded. CPU time is not reported, so the 1.96x is a wall-clock figure that does not charge JIT compilation. The suite also has no yklua executor with the JIT off (YK_JITC=none), so the cost of the yk instrumentation in interpreter mode is not shown.
- The two binaries are built differently. The baseline is gcc -O2 -flto with Lua's computed-goto jump-table dispatch, which lvm.c enables by default under GCC. yklua is ykllvm clang -O2 with -DLUA_USE_JUMPTABLE=0, because yk cannot trace threaded dispatch. Results are correctness-checked: harness.lua asserts each benchmark's verification result. The cbgame inputs are scaled down from the standard sizes (fannkuchredux 10, binarytrees 15), and ReBench runs with --no-denoise.
- Yk locations leak (issue #113, open since 2025-04): luaF_freeproto frees the yklocs array but never calls yk_location_drop. Programs that create functions repeatedly (load, string.dump and undump) therefore accumulate yk location state. The yklocs array is also not counted in luaF_protosize, so the GC does not account for it.
- Warm-up is cheap but steady state is not always better. In the 2026-10-06 14:23 run, no benchmark's first iteration was more than 10% slower than its steady-state mean (iterations 6-10), and most were under 5% slower (DeltaBlue is the worst case, 793 ms against 720 ms). LuLPeg got slower as it ran (787 ms in iteration 1 against 911 ms over iterations 6-10, coefficient of variation 0.18; derived from page data).

**Status:** Very active (a run of ltratt PRs merged 2026-10-05) but experimental and pre-alpha with 7 stars. The Lua core carries PUC-Rio's MIT notice and yk is Apache-2.0 or MIT, but the yklua repo has no LICENSE file covering its own changes, so treat it as a research artefact rather than something to vendor.

[repo](https://github.com/ykjit/yklua) · [benchmark](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/ykjit/yk-benchmarks/gh-pages/index.html)

### media-and-graphics

#### color-and-resampling

##### ImageSharp (SixLabors)  `C#`  `Six Labors Split License 1.0 (not an SPDX id, non-OSI): Apache-2.0 for open-source or source-available use, transitive dependency use, for-profit under 1M USD annual gross revenue and non-profits; paid Six Labors Commercial License otherwise`  `active`  `Tier A`

Fully managed C# image library; 4.4x faster than Magick.NET and 3.2x faster than System.Drawing on a load-resize-sharpen-save JPEG pipeline.

**Beats:** Magick.NET (ImageMagick) and System.Drawing — Third-party BenchmarkDotNet suite by the NetVips author (.NET 10.0.1 NativeAOT, x86-64-v4, AMD Ryzen 9 7900 with 24 threads, Windows 11): load a 5000x5000 JPEG or tiled TIFF, crop 100 px, shrink to 90% with a Triangle filter, 3x3 sharpen, save at quality 75. ImageSharp 3.1.12 took 366.95 ms against Magick.NET-Q8-AnyCPU 14.10.1 at 1,626.85 ms (about 4.4x, derived from page data) and System.Drawing at 1,185.58 ms (about 3.2x, no sharpen); on TIFF 186.51 ms against 1,533.49 ms (8.2x) and 985.05 ms (5.3x). Magick.NET ran single-threaded (non-OpenMP package) while ImageSharp's sharpen step used up to 24 threads.

**Known shortcoming:** Six Labors Split License 1.0 (not OSI approved), so reference only. In the NetVips Benchmark.cs run (Triangle filter and quality 75 on both sides, Magick.NET-Q8, OpenCL off, .NET 10.0.1 NativeAOT, Ryzen 9 7900, library-default thread counts) NetVips beats ImageSharp in the same table; ImageSharp's own LoadResizeSave bench against Magick.NET is different work (decode-to-target-size versus Q16 full decode).

**Known shortcoming:** Threading asymmetry: Magick.NET-Q8-AnyCPU is built without OpenMP (docs/Readme.md), so the ImageMagick side is single-threaded, while ImageSharp's convolution runs ParallelRowIterator on 24 threads (resize's single ResizeWorker and the JPEG code are single-threaded). 3.1.12 is affected by GHSA-jj3q-cwqj-842r (3.0.0 and later, fixed only in 4.1.1); v4 needs a build-time licence key per a search snippet; the internal ConvolutionProcessor is reached via reflection.

**How:** Hot codec paths use .NET hardware intrinsics picked at run time: the JPEG float DCT has an AVX Vector256 path (FloatingPointDCT.Intrinsic.cs) and colour conversion has AVX, Arm and Vector<T> converters (JpegColorConverterBase). Resize is a separable two-pass filter with precomputed ResizeKernelMap weights run by a sliding-window ResizeWorker over a transposed Vector4 first-pass buffer sized to Configuration.WorkingBufferSizeHintInBytes, which keeps the working set in cache; in 3.1.12 and on main it is one sequential worker per image. Convolution-type processors are row-parallel through ParallelRowIterator with MaxDegreeOfParallelism defaulting to Environment.ProcessorCount. Much of the gap to Magick.NET also reflects the baseline: the Magick.NET-Q8-AnyCPU package is built without OpenMP, so ImageMagick runs every step on one thread.

**Use it when:**
- A .NET service or app that needs in-process decode, resize and encode with no native dependency (containers, ARM64, trimmed builds; the benchmark itself ran under NativeAOT) and currently uses Magick.NET or System.Drawing: 4.4x faster than Magick.NET-Q8-AnyCPU on the JPEG pipeline and 8.2x on TIFF in the NetVips table.
- Replacing System.Drawing for thumbnail-style work: 3.2x faster on JPEG and 5.3x on TIFF even though the System.Drawing path skipped the sharpen step.
- Your use qualifies for the Apache-2.0 side of the Six Labors Split License: transitive dependency, open-source or source-available use, a for-profit under 1M USD annual gross revenue, or a non-profit.
- Pipelines dominated by convolution-type filters on large images, which ImageSharp spreads over every core by default.

**Skip it when:**
- You want the fastest option in .NET: NetVips (libvips) is 4.93x faster on JPEG and 3.75x on TIFF in the same table, and NetVips (806.8 ms) and MagicScaler (888.0 ms) beat ImageSharp (1,098.4 ms) in Six Labors' own LoadResizeSave stress benchmark.
- A for-profit direct dependency above 1M USD revenue without a paid Six Labors Commercial License; version 4 enforces a build-time licence key (a third-party issue seen as a search snippet says it is an error in Release builds), and the net-vips project pins 3.1.12 for that reason.
- Staying on 3.1.12 to avoid the key while decoding untrusted files: GHSA-jj3q-cwqj-842r (heap out-of-bounds write in TIFF CCITT T4/Modified Huffman decompression, CVSS 7.5) affects >= 3.0.0 and is patched only in 4.1.1, and eight more advisories followed in August-September 2026 (TIFF, ICC, EXR, HistogramEqualization).
- One very large resize where you expect all cores to help: the resampling pass runs as a single worker (the source comments that parallelism would need multiple workers), so parallelise across images instead.
- JPEG decode-bound workloads where Huffman decoding dominates: issue #1607 'JpegDecoder: Optimize HuffmanScanDecoder' has been open since 2021.

**Vs siblings:** Among .NET options, pick ImageSharp over NetVips/libvips or MagicScaler when a fully managed library with no native binaries matters more than raw speed, since both are faster in the same benchmarks; against Magick.NET and System.Drawing it is the faster managed choice, provided the Six Labors licence terms fit.

**Gotchas:**
- MaxDegreeOfParallelism defaults to the processor count; a server that already processes many images concurrently should lower it (Six Labors' own Resize benchmark sets it to 1) to avoid oversubscription.
- In 3.1.12 the general 2D ConvolutionProcessor<TPixel> is internal; the NetVips benchmark reaches it through reflection (Type.GetType plus MakeGenericType), which is fragile under trimming, NativeAOT and version upgrades.
- Convolution kernels are applied exactly as given, with no divisor parameter: the benchmark's sharpen kernel sums to 8, so ImageSharp's output is brighter and clipped compared with libvips and ImageMagick, which divide by 8.
- Processors work on rows converted to Vector4 floats (ToVector4 and FromVector4Destructive per row), so 8-bit pipelines pay a conversion each step; chaining many cheap operations costs more than the per-operation numbers suggest.

**Status:** Actively maintained (v4.1.2 released 2026-09-14, 8.0k stars, 14,518 commits); usability stays reference because of the non-OSI Six Labors Split License and v4's build-time key, and the benchmarked 3.1.12 is the latest 3.x release on the releases page, so it does not carry the fix for GHSA-jj3q-cwqj-842r (patched only in 4.1.1).

[repo](https://github.com/SixLabors/ImageSharp) · [benchmark](https://github.com/kleisauke/net-vips/tree/master/tests/NetVips.Benchmarks)

#### image-codecs

##### HALIC (High Availability Lossless Image Compression)  `unknown (binaries only; README says built with GCC and Clang)`  `MIT`  `stale`  `Tier B`

Closed-source lossless RGB/gray image codec (CLI binaries) that encodes about 15-32x faster than Pillow PNG and WebP lossless at smaller size.

**Beats:** libwebp lossless (Pillow 10.1.0, method 1) and PNG (Pillow 10.1.0, optimize=False) — In WangXuan95's Image-Compression-Benchmark (Intel Core i7-12700H, Windows 10, every codec single-threaded, timed with time.time() over the whole set), HALIC 0.7.2 .exe compressed CLIC2021 (585 RGB images, 4.1 GB) to 1,473,481,803 bytes in 22.187 s and decompressed it in 28.447 s, versus Pillow 10.1.0 WebP lossless method 1 at 1,496,478,650 bytes, 720.160 s and 37.044 s, and Pillow PNG optimize=False (zlib default level; Pillow 10.1.0's Windows build script pins libwebp 1.3.2 and zlib 1.3) at 2,003,016,524 bytes, 334.791 s and 33.677 s; on GDCC2020 it took 4.780 s and 5.426 s versus PNG at 152.321 s and 11.545 s. The WebP baseline ran at quality=100, which in libwebp lossless mode means maximum compression effort, so the 32x encode gap is against a slow WebP setting, while HALIC's times include one process launch per image and the Pillow codecs ran in-process.

**Known shortcoming:** Reference only: binaries, no source in any author repo; last release 2024-05-24 (stale). Tier B on WangXuan95's Image-Compression-Benchmark (i7-12700H, Windows 10, single thread; CLIC2021 and GDCC2020 numbers match).

**How:** Per the README: simple prediction without context modelling or error correction, so many residuals remain, followed by an ANS entropy coder (FSE) over completely independent blocks and per-channel sub-streams; the measured build runs on one thread. Skipping context mixing is what keeps it near QOI-class speed while compressing close to WebP lossless. The predictor, block size and any SIMD use are not documented: the README says no SIMD or assembly, yet the 0.7.2 assets are labelled AVX and AVX2 builds (compiler target flags, presumably).

**Use it when:**
- Batch archiving of large 24-bit photographs (multi-megapixel PPM/PNM) where encode time dominates: on CLIC2021 it encoded 4.1 GB in 22.2 s versus 334.8 s for Pillow PNG and 720.2 s for Pillow WebP lossless m1, with output 26% smaller than that PNG.
- Research or comparison work that needs a fast-symmetric reference point between QOI/QOIR-class speed and WebP-lossless-class size.
- Closed environments (offline tools, internal storage) on x86-64 Windows or Linux where running a third-party binary is acceptable and interoperability with other software is not needed.

**Skip it when:**
- Anything that must be built, audited, fuzzed or embedded: there is no source in the repo, releases or the author's HALIC-Image-Converter, despite the MIT LICENSE file.
- Interchange or long-term storage: .halic is undocumented, single-vendor, and the project has had no release since 0.7.2 (March 2024) or commit since May 2024.
- Small images: process start-up per file dominates, and on UCID (1338 small images) HALIC decoded in 27.2 s versus 15.0 s for WebP lossless m1 and 15.2 s for Pillow PNG; on Kodak Pillow PNG decoded faster too (0.484 s versus 0.615 s).
- Best ratio: JPEG XL e3 and up, fNBLI, BMF, EMMA and other context-mixing codecs are 5-17% smaller on CLIC2021.
- Alpha channels, 16-bit samples, PNG input or other non-PNM formats: not supported or not documented.

**Vs siblings:** Pick HALIC over fNBLI (GPL-3.0 source, 9% smaller and about as fast to decode on CLIC2021, but 43.2 s versus 22.2 s to encode) only when encode speed matters more than having code; pick Zpng (BSD-3-Clause) or QOIR (Apache-2.0) when you need embeddable source at similar speed and can accept 19-45% larger files than HALIC.

**Gotchas:**
- The 'FAST' variant (HALIC072fe/fd) is labelled trial in the 0.7.2 notes and failed to decompress zone_plate.pnm in the ImgInfoGray set of the benchmark.
- The benchmark's published RunBenchmark.py has CHECK_DISTORTION = False, so the run as published does not compare decoded pixels with the input; only non-zero exit codes are caught, which is how the FAST failure surfaced.
- The GitHub 'Source code' archives on each release are only the README-only tree; the codec itself is closed.
- The format has no spec or version-compatibility statement; keep the exact decoder binary that wrote your files.

**Status:** Stale since 2024-05-24 (LICENSE added; last binaries 0.7.2 from 2024-03-13, no issues filed) and reference-only: the MIT licence covers a README, not inspectable code, so treat it as a benchmark point rather than something to ship.

[repo](https://github.com/Hakan-Abbas/HALIC-High-Availability-Lossless-Image-Compression-) · [benchmark](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/WangXuan95/Image-Compression-Benchmark/HEAD/README.md)

#### rasterizers-2d

##### Anti-Grain Geometry (AGG 2.6)  `C++`  `BSD-3-Clause`  `abandoned`  `Tier B`

Classic scalar C++ template 2D rasterizer; an independent bl_bench run puts it ~1.2x Skia and ~2.3x Cairo single-threaded.

**Beats:** Skia (CPU pipeline) and Cairo 1.18.4 — LaurenzV's independent run of the Blend2D bl_bench harness on an Apple M1 Pro (2026-06-08, macOS, 512x600 PRGB32 target, SrcOver, single thread, options.repeat 15; compiler and flags unrecorded, Skia from vcpkg's unofficial-skia, Cairo 1.18.4 from pkg-config) gives AGG a 1.21x geometric-mean speedup over Skia and 2.29x over Cairo across the 522 cells they share (29 tests x Solid/Linear/Radial x 6 sizes), which I recomputed from the rcpms values; the same file puts AGG at 0.30x Blend2D ST, 0.48x Vello CPU ST, 0.70x JUCE 8.0.8, 1.10x raqote and 2.42x tiny-skia. The measured code is blend2d-apps' bundled AGG 2.4-line copy with its own modified Agg2D wrapper, whose core rasterizer headers match this repository.

**Known shortcoming:** Tier B on the Vello CPU author's vello_chart data (arm 2026-06-08, Apple M1 Pro: 1.21x Skia winning 66% of cells, 2.29x Cairo 1.18.4; x86 2026-01-22: 1.87x Cairo 1.18.2; compiler, flags and Skia version unrecorded): wins polygon and path fills and strokes, loses simple rectangle, round and triangle fills and StrokeRectA (0.52x). The measured code is blend2d-apps/3rdparty/agg plus Agg2D, whose hot-path headers match ghaerr/agg-2.6 except std:: qualifiers and cell_block_limit. AGG's radial gradient is centred while Skia's is focal two-point. ghaerr/agg-2.6 is not the canonical tree: the SourceForge SVN is ahead (r145, 2024-09-28; GPC moved to MIT), and this copy still carries the non-commercial GPC clipper, so usability is mixed.

**Known shortcoming:** Recomputed from the vello_chart data over 522 cells: 1.206x Skia and 2.286x Cairo, but 0.70x JUCE, 0.30x Blend2D single-threaded and 0.48x Vello CPU single-threaded. The measured Agg2D is the blend2d-apps modified wrapper (fillRectangleI, 3-colour gradients), not code in the ghaerr copy. CVE-2019-6245 and CVE-2019-6247 (AGG 2.4 via svgpp); the default integer clipper overflows beyond about 8.4M px; the cell limit drops cells silently; line() splitting of 16384+ px segments has no return; issues #13 (GCC 14 build failure) and #14 (pixfmt_custom_blend_rgba compile error) open; SourceForge r145 is ahead of this copy.

**How:** The core is an exact-area-coverage scanline rasterizer in the lineage of FreeType's gray rasterizer: edges are converted to 24.8 fixed point and walked into per-pixel cells holding signed area and cover, the cells are bucketed by row and sorted by x (qsort_cells), and sweep_scanline accumulates cover into 8-bit coverage spans with an optional gamma table and non-zero or even-odd fill. Every stage (vertex converters, span generators, blenders, pixel formats) is a template, so the whole pipeline inlines into one specialised loop with no virtual calls or per-pixel dispatch, and cell blocks (4096 cells each) and scanline buffers are reused between paths. It is plain scalar C++ with no SIMD and no threading; its lead over Skia in this benchmark comes from polygon, path and stroke work at 32 px and larger, while Skia wins simple rectangle and rounded-rect fills.

**Use it when:**
- Single-threaded CPU rendering of complex anti-aliased paths and strokes (charts, maps, plotting backends) where Cairo is the incumbent: 2.29x Cairo 1.18.4 by geometric mean on an M1 Pro, faster in 94% of cells.
- Stroke-heavy scenes: 1.39x Skia on strokes overall (StrokeWorld 1.92x, StrokeFish 1.82x, StrokeButterfly 1.67x).
- Portable or embedded targets where Skia's build or a SIMD- or JIT-dependent renderer is not an option: scalar C++, no dependencies for the core, renders into any custom pixel format.
- When you want a small, permissively licensed (Modified BSD or AGG Public License) renderer you can vendor and modify, or you already maintain an AGG-based stack.

**Skip it when:**
- When raw CPU throughput is the goal: in the same M1 Pro dataset Blend2D 0.12.0 is about 3.3x faster single-threaded and scales with threads, Vello CPU is about 2.1x faster single-threaded and JUCE 8.0.8's software renderer about 1.43x faster (derived from page data).
- Many small simple shapes: at 8x8 and 16x16 it is only at parity with Skia, and it loses FillRectA (0.84x except solid), FillRoundU (0.80x) and StrokeRectA (0.52x).
- Untrusted vector input without hardening: CVE-2019-6245 (unbounded recursion in the cell rasterizer) and CVE-2019-6247 (heap overflow via blend_hline) were filed against AGG 2.4 as used in svgpp, and the default integer clipper overflows on huge coordinates.
- When you need a maintained dependency: this GitHub copy last changed 2023-08-21 and has open build failures (issue #13: GCC 14.2.1 with FreeType 2.13.3 in agg_font_freetype.cpp); the SourceForge SVN fixed that and C++23 warnings in r140-r145 (2024).
- When you need modern features out of the box: no text shaping, colour management, GPU backend or multi-threading; the bench backend only supports Solid, Linear and Radial paints, with Agg2D's gradients limited to pad linear and centred radial (core AGG has gradient_radial_focus and repeat/reflect adaptors in agg_span_gradient.h).

**Vs siblings:** Pick Blend2D (about 3.3x faster single-threaded, multi-threaded) or JUCE's software renderer (about 1.43x faster) when speed is the main goal; pick AGG over them when you want a dependency-free, portable scalar renderer with a fully pluggable template pipeline (custom pixel formats, gamma, subpixel-accurate strokes) or already run on an AGG-based stack. Against tiny-skia and raqote AGG is faster in the same data (2.42x and 1.10x geomean, derived).

**Gotchas:**
- The default rasterizer_scanline_aa<> uses rasterizer_sl_clip_int, which converts coordinates with a plain iround(v * 256) to 24.8 fixed point before clipping, so coordinates beyond about +/-8.4 million px overflow; use rasterizer_sl_clip_int_sat or rasterizer_sl_clip_dbl and a clip box for untrusted input.
- Cell storage is capped (cell_block_limit, default 1024 blocks x 4096 cells = 4,194,304 cells) and add_curr_cell() simply returns once the cap is hit, so a huge or very detailed path renders incomplete with no error; raise the limit through the rasterizer constructor.
- As read in this copy, rasterizer_cells_aa::line() splits a segment spanning 16384 px or more horizontally into two recursive calls but has no return afterwards, so such a segment is also rasterized whole; keep geometry clipped to the canvas so segments never get that long.
- The benchmarked Agg2D is blend2d-apps' modified copy (fillRectangleI fast path for integer solid rectangles, three-colour gradients), which this repo's agg-src/agg2d lacks; this repo's Agg2D instantiates pixfmt_custom_blend_rgba, whose copy_pixel() does not compile when used (issue #14: pixel_type* passed to make_pix(int8u*)). Do not copy agg-src/gpc (non-commercial licence here; SourceForge r144 has it under MIT).

**Status:** This GitHub mirror (367 stars, 92 forks, 6 open issues, 2 stale PRs) has been unchanged since 2023-08-21 while the upstream SourceForge SVN reached r145 on 2024-09-28 with C++23, FreeType 2.13.3 and fallthrough fixes and MIT-licensed GPC, so vendor from SourceForge; the core is BSD-3-Clause or AGG Public License and copyable, and usability is mixed only because of agg-src/gpc here (issue #10 also flags a GPL-licensed SDL2 demo platform file).

[repo](https://github.com/ghaerr/agg-2.6) · [benchmark](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/LaurenzV/vello_chart/HEAD/data/arm/2026-06-08.json)

##### muSkia Skia optimizer (Semantics for 2D Rasterization)  `Lean (formal semantics); implementation language unknown`  `no license`  `unknown`  `Tier B`

Lean-verified peephole optimizer for Skia command streams; 1.12x geomean raster speedup over Skia Graphite on Chrome-generated pictures.

**Beats:** Skia (its most modern GPU backend) — Peer-reviewed first-party measurement (PACMPL OOPSLA2 2026, article 339), read from the camera-ready LaTeX in the first author's public skia-paper repo. On an 8-core Apple M2 (16 GB) with Skia f931a2e built by Clang 17.0.0 -O3 -flto=thin, Graphite/Metal nanobench playback of 139 SaveLayer-bearing pictures from Chrome on the top 100 sites (median of 25 runs, bootstrap 95% CI) gives a 1.12x geomean (max 3.04x). The other runs: Ganesh on the M2 1.08x; Intel i7-8700K with CoffeeLake-S GT2 (Clang 18.1.3) 1.14x Graphite and 1.07x Ganesh on 143 recaptured pictures; the next 100 sites 1.18x on 144 pictures with the passes frozen.

**Known shortcoming:** Paper-only entry (OOPSLA2 2026, ACM DOI 10.1145/3839471; arXiv 2603.23696) with no code found; arXiv, alphaXiv, the ACM DOI and Zenodo are all blocked here, so the 18.7% figure is snippet-only and the tier is D; reference only.

**Known shortcoming:** Enricher (e127, 2026-10-05): the camera-ready paper (bhargavkulk/skia-paper, OOPSLA2 2026 article 339) supersedes the arXiv v1 abstract: 1.12x geomean on 139 SaveLayer-bearing Skia pictures (Graphite/Metal, Apple M2, Clang 17.0.0 -O3 -flto=thin, Skia f931a2e, nanobench median of 25 runs), Ganesh 1.08x, i7-8700K 1.14x/1.07x, next 100 sites 1.18x, max 3.04x, optimisation at most 0.03 ms; retiered D to B (retier-37). Only 51 of 139 pictures are rewritten (38 with CI above 1x) so the geomean includes unrewritten noise; per-layer skp playback, not page frame time; 25 of 139 pixel diffs above 1%; four significant slowdowns on Intel. Code only on Zenodo 21386615 (blocked); Skia fork not on GitHub and not upstreamed.

**Independent measurement:** peer-reviewed first-party (OOPSLA2 2026)

**How:** It removes or cheapens SaveLayer/Restore pairs, each of which costs an offscreen GPU surface plus a blend. The four rewrites are: drop opaque SrcOver SaveLayers that contain only SrcOver draws; turn a DstIn mask layer into a Clip; fold a luminance or colour filter into the draws it covers; and delete opaque gradient masks used by one Russian web framework (mail.ru, dzen.ru, yandex.ru). Each rewrite is a single linear pass driven by a stack of small state machines, one per open SaveLayer (SkOptPass<MatchState>, with an inline STArray<8> frame stack). Removed commands become NoOps, and insertions are buffered and merged in one scan, a technique the paper credits to WebKit B3's InsertionSet. Optimization took at most 0.03 ms per picture on the M2.

**Use it when:**
- Skia clients that record SkPictures/SkRecords before playback (browser engines, compositors, picture-replay tools) and whose command streams nest SaveLayers for opacity, masks or filters.
- Web-content rendering where Chrome-style output uses SrcOver or DstIn layers for clipping and masking: the paper's largest gains were 3.04x on a vimeo.com layer (three rewrites chained) and 2.41x on dzen.ru (gradient-mask rewrite).
- Research or tooling that needs a machine-checked definition of Skia's layer, blend and clip semantics to prove a draw-list rewrite correct before shipping it.
- GPU backends, Graphite in particular: measured gains were higher there (1.12x on Apple M2 Metal, 1.14x on an Intel CoffeeLake-S GT2 integrated GPU) than on legacy Ganesh (1.08x and 1.07x).

**Skip it when:**
- As a faster rasterizer: it does not touch Skia's path filling, shaders or GPU pipeline, so pictures without SaveLayers gain nothing and pay the optimizer pass (the RQ3 total-time CDF shows more slowdowns for exactly those).
- Pixel-exact pipelines: the rewrites are proved over real-valued colours, so anti-aliasing and rounding may change. 25 of 139 benchmark pictures had pixels differing by more than 1% in a channel (judged anti-aliasing by eye).
- Programs that use mask filters, blurs, image filters, SkSL shaders or bitmap features: muSkia does not formalize these, the passes give up on unmodelled commands, and only 41 of 139 pictures could be converted for translation validation.
- Legacy Ganesh with complex clip paths: the DstIn-to-Clip rewrite slowed avast.com layer 0 significantly on Ganesh/Intel; Graphite/Intel showed three statistically significant slowdowns (intuit.com layer 15, two gravatar.com layers).
- Production use today: the code is a research fork of Skia (commit f931a2e, between milestones 143 and 144) shipped only as a Zenodo artifact, and per the first author Chrome and Skia had not agreed to upstream it as of June 2026.

**Vs siblings:** Pick it only when you are already on Skia and want fewer offscreen layers in recorded pictures without changing the rasterizer. Blend2D, ThorVG or Vello CPU replace the rasterizer and are the siblings to look at if raw fill speed is the problem, and the two approaches can stack.

**Gotchas:**
- The catalogued 18.7% (99 programs, 32 us) is the March 2026 arXiv v1 abstract. The camera-ready paper re-ran with 25 nanobench runs per picture and reports a 1.12x geomean on 139 pictures, at most 0.03 ms to optimize, and up to 3.04x.
- The benchmark set keeps only Chrome layer pictures that contain SaveLayer. Only 51 of the 139 are rewritten at all, and 38 of those have 95% confidence intervals entirely above 1x. The geomean includes unrewritten pictures whose ratios (0.96x-1.09x) are noise.
- The numbers are per-layer .skp playback times in Skia's nanobench, with the optimization applied offline. They are not whole-page frame times inside Chrome, and Chrome's layer split differs by hardware, so each machine got its own capture.
- The SrcOver-SaveLayer rewrite requires the layer to be opaque, a side condition the Lean model tracks but the paper's simplified rules omit; removing a layer can also defeat Graphite's own first-draw clear optimization (intuit.com regression).

**Status:** Research artifact (Zenodo record 21386615, not opened here because zenodo is blocked) accepted at OOPSLA 2026; no public GitHub repository for the Skia fork or the Lean code was found, and it is not upstreamed in Skia or Chrome, so treat it as a reference design rather than a library.

[benchmark](https://github.com/bhargavkulk/skia-paper/blob/main/evaluation.tex)

##### NV_path_rendering (NVpr)  `C (OpenGL extension in the NVIDIA driver)`  `no license`  `unknown`  `Tier B`

NVIDIA OpenGL extension for GPU path rendering; its peer-reviewed figure shows about 2-40x over Cairo and Skia's CPU rasterizer.

**Beats:** Cairo 1.9.6, Skia (circa May 2010, CPU raster backend), Qt 4.5.x, Direct2D and the OpenVG 1.1 reference implementation (the nvpr_svg comparison backends in the NVprSDK) — The paper's performance figure was read from the authors' LaTeX source and its vector EPS on github.com/markkilgard/gpupathrender; the values are derived from the chart's vector data, so they are approximate. Setup: NV_path_rendering at 16 samples per pixel on a GeForce 650 with an unnamed 'fast Core i7', 12 SVG scenes, windows from 100x100 to 1100x1100. NVPR beats Cairo by 2.7x (Spikes, 100x100) to 40x (Cougar, 200x200), Skia's CPU raster by 2.1x to 34x, Skia Ganesh (GPU) by 1.6x to 78x, Direct2D hardware by 0.95x to 29x, and Direct2D WARP by 4.4x to 31x. Most ratios fall as the window grows: Tiger versus Cairo goes from 17x at 200x200 to 6.3x at 1100x1100. The 105x clipping showcase (8.69 ms versus Cairo's 909 ms at 1000x1000) is a separate figure from a Core i7 with a GeForce 560M laptop GPU; the chart's own clipped-tiger scene shows 6.3x to 22x versus Cairo.

**Known shortcoming:** Reference only: the NV_path_rendering driver is closed source; the nvpr_svg comparison harness (Cairo, Qt, Skia, Direct2D, OpenVG backends) survives only in SDK mirrors. The TOG 31(6) 2012 paper PDF is blocked here, so the numbers (GeForce 650 + Core i7, 8.69 ms vs Cairo 909 ms on the clipping scene) are snippet-only; Skia has since dropped its NVPR backend, so the comparison is historical.

**Known shortcoming:** Retiered C to B (retier-27) on the paper's LaTeX and chart data in markkilgard/gpupathrender. The 105x clipping figure is a separate GeForce 560M showcase; the chart's clipped scene is 6.3-22x versus Cairo; the chart has no Qt row and OpenVG was compiled out of -xbenchmark. The nvpr_svg.cpp harness times CPU backends without the blit while the GPU time includes swap plus glFinish (vsync off); benchmark.bat is stale (runs gs_bezier.exe); Cairo 1.9.6 had a path-clipping bug per the SDK ReadMe; Qt 5.12 deprecated and Qt 6 removed the NvprRenderer; the renderer lives in NVIDIA's proprietary driver.

**Independent measurement:** paper tables (blocked)

**How:** The technique is 'stencil, then cover'. Each path is baked once into resolution-independent GPU geometry: triangle-fan anchor geometry, Loop-Blinn quadratic and cubic discard triangles (cubics are subdivided into convex hulls), and conservative cover geometry. The stencil step accumulates per-sample winding numbers in the stencil buffer. The cover step rasterizes the cover geometry, shades the samples whose stencil value is non-zero and resets the stencil as it goes. Strokes use a quadratic Bezier stroke discard shader. Antialiasing comes from multisampling (16 samples per pixel in the benchmarks), and each sample keeps its own colour, which avoids conflation artifacts. The paper credits three hardware features: coarse stencil culling that rejects hundreds of pixels per clock, 8-bit stencil traffic that runs near memory-bus saturation, and a GPU front-end processor that switches between stencil and cover without driver revalidation, so many small paths stay GPU-bound.

**Use it when:**
- Static or retained vector content (SVG art, maps, UI, glyph runs) redrawn many times under changing transforms (zoom, rotation, projective warps) on NVIDIA GPUs, so the one-time bake is amortised
- Compositing 2D paths with 3D: depth-tested paths, paths in perspective, stencil-clipping 3D against paths, or custom fragment shaders on fills
- Content with exactly shared edges (Flash-style art) where coverage-to-alpha renderers show background bleeding: per-sample colour avoids conflation
- Desktop Windows or Linux apps that already own a compatibility-profile OpenGL context and target NVIDIA hardware only

**Skip it when:**
- Anything that must run on AMD, Intel, Apple or mobile GPUs, or under Vulkan, Direct3D or Metal: this is an NVIDIA OpenGL extension (the 2011 SDK deck lists no Mac support)
- Immediate-mode drawing that re-specifies paths every frame (browser canvas, dynamic charts): baking time is linear in path commands and is excluded from the benchmark loops, and the paper itself notes that browsers re-specify paths on every redraw
- Simple line-segment scenes at large window sizes against Direct2D hardware: in the paper's figure the Spikes scene falls to about 0.95x at 1100x1100 (Direct2D slightly faster), and on the GeForce 650 most ratios shrink as the window grows
- Memory-tight GPUs: quality depends on a multisampled colour plus stencil framebuffer. The 2011 deck calls 4 samples the bare minimum and 16x 'extremely memory intensive', and the paper's future work targets the memory footprint.
- New projects that need ecosystem support: Qt deprecated Shape.NvprRenderer in 5.12 and Qt 6 has no NVPR backend; Skia has dropped its NVPR backend (per the verifier)

**Vs siblings:** Choose it only for an NVIDIA-only OpenGL application that needs paths composited with 3D, depth or custom shaders. For portable CPU rendering Blend2D wins nearly all configurations in the ETH thesis comparison, and Vello or Pathfinder are portable GPU options. NVPR's speedups were measured against 2010-2012 Cairo and Skia builds and a 2012 GPU, so they say little about today's Blend2D, Vello CPU or Skia Graphite.

**Gotchas:**
- The comparisons are not at identical output: NVPR runs at 16 samples per pixel while Cairo, Skia, Qt and Direct2D use coverage-to-alpha antialiasing, and the 2011 deck's numbers pit the GPU against a single CPU core
- The SDK sample code is under NVIDIA's SDK agreement (derivatives allowed with an attribution statement; NVIDIA may terminate the licence), not an OSI licence, and the renderer itself is closed
- The spec copy in the SDK (version 1, June 2011) is written against the OpenGL 3.2 compatibility profile and requires ARB_compatibility on 3.x; core-profile use relies on later spec revisions not read here
- nvpr_svg's benchmark.bat is stale (it runs gs_bezier.exe). The paper's 12-scene, 11-resolution sweep is the undocumented -xbenchmark mode in nvpr_svg.cpp, where OpenVG is compiled out as 'too slow to benchmark'.

**Status:** Shipped in NVIDIA drivers since 275.33 (June 2011); NVprSDK's last commit was February 2020. Qt deprecated its NVPR backend in 5.12 and removed it in Qt 6, and Skia dropped its backend, so treat it as a vendor-locked historical reference, not a dependency.

[benchmark](https://github.com/markkilgard/gpupathrender)

#### video-audio

##### rav1d-safe  `Rust`  `AGPL-3.0-only OR LicenseRef-Imazen-Commercial (Cargo.toml, LICENSE-AGPL3, LICENSE-COMMERCIAL); code inherited from dav1d/rav1d is BSD-2-Clause (COPYING)`  `active`  `Tier A`

Memory-safe Rust AV1 decoder (rav1d fork); faster only than upstream rav1d with its assembly disabled, slower than dav1d.

**Beats:** upstream memorysafety/rav1d commit d3d1cd6 (package 1.1.0) built with default-features=false (bitdepth_8, bitdepth_16 only), i.e. with its hand-written assembly disabled; not dav1d and not rav1d's default assembly build, both of which are faster — On an AMD Ryzen 9 7900X with Rust 1.98.1 (LLVM 22.1.8), fat LTO, one codegen unit and identical RUSTFLAGS for both arms, checked rav1d-safe (commit be5b244, staged 0.6.0 with a git-pinned archmage, not the crates.io package that depends on archmage ^0.9.29) decoded 12 single-frame 8-bit 4:2:0 IVF stills in 0.680x (1 worker), 0.821x (4) and 0.813x (8) the time of upstream rav1d d3d1cd6 built with default-features=false. The stills are photo and map at 2K/4K/8K, each with minimum and eight tiles. Figures are geometric means of medians of five paired repetitions, and every run was MD5-checked against upstream and dav1d 1.5.3. The baseline is a non-default scalar build, and compare.py's rotate-then-reverse ordering cancels out for two arms, so upstream always ran first in each pair (the page discloses the fixed order).

**Known shortcoming:** The win is only against upstream rav1d d3d1cd6 built without assembly; against dav1d or rav1d with assembly it is slower. The 1.77-8.62x figures come from a separate 2026-09-07 page with different inputs and an older revision (up to 12.8x against frame threading). Licence is AGPL-3.0-only or commercial, plus BSD-2-Clause inherited code; crates.io 0.6.0 is published. Usability mixed.

**Known shortcoming:** The timed be5b244 used a git-pinned archmage while crates.io 0.6.0 uses archmage ^0.9.29; compare.py's rotate-then-reverse cancels for two arms with upstream always first (disclosed). 0.6.0's mastering-display metadata is wrong (1000 nit reads as 25.6), fixed only on main; unchecked was renamed untracked after 0.6.0. The 2026-10-01 docs put the default build at 1.72-1.74x dav1d 1.5.3's time on 4K stills (480p inter 2.68 vs 0.83 ms), so it stays slower than dav1d with assembly.

**How:** Against upstream's no-assembly build, the speed comes from having SIMD at all. rav1d-safe ports dav1d's x86 and ARM assembly families to safe Rust SIMD: motion compensation, inverse transforms, intra prediction, CDEF, loop filter, loop restoration, film grain, palette and refmvs, plus an inlined msac entropy decoder. It uses archmage capability-token dispatch (AVX2, some AVX-512, NEON) and safe_unaligned_simd loads. Upstream rav1d with default-features=false falls back to its scalar Rust code. Runtime DisjointMut overlap tracking stays on in the default build; on 4K AVIF it costs about 3.9 of 42.4 ms per frame against dav1d 1.5.3 (docs/SAFE_VS_DAV1D.md).

**Use it when:**
- Decoding untrusted AVIF/AV1 stills in a Rust server where a forbid(unsafe_code) decoder with no assembly is a hard requirement
- As a replacement for upstream rav1d built without assembly (for example, a target or policy that rules out nasm/asm): on 2K-8K photo stills it took 0.51-0.78x the time, and on map stills 0.755-1.002x
- Tiled stills decoded with tile threading (1/4/8 workers, max_frame_delay=1), which works in the default checked build
- Verifying AV1 encoder output: the default Strictness::Strict reports desynchronised symbol streams as errors where dav1d would conceal them
- Cargo-only builds that still need SIMD on x86-64 (AVX2/AVX-512) and aarch64 (NEON)

**Skip it when:**
- When throughput is what matters: dav1d and default (assembly) rav1d are faster. The author's 2026-10-01 profile puts the default build at 1.72-1.74x dav1d 1.5.3's time on 4K stills, and the 2026-09-07 grid at 1.8-8.6x upstream's time (up to 12.8x against upstream frame threading)
- Inter-heavy video playback: on a 480p inter stream the default build took 2.68 ms/frame against dav1d's 0.83, mostly in warp motion compensation, and frame threading in 0.6.0 needs the unchecked feature
- Closed-source products without buying Imazen's commercial licence: the crate is AGPL-3.0-only OR LicenseRef-Imazen-Commercial (the code inherited from dav1d/rav1d is BSD-2-Clause)
- Pre-AVX2 x86 (no SSE tier, so it falls back to scalar) or ARM cores where dav1d's SVE2/dotprod/i8mm paths matter (only baseline NEON is ported)
- Streams that need S-frames, SVC operating-point selection or the argon vectors: 19 of 803 dav1d-test-data vectors are not exercised

**Vs siblings:** Pick dav1d (catalogued, BSD-2-Clause, beats libaom) whenever speed or permissive licensing matters. Pick rav1d-safe only when a Rust decoder with no assembly and forbid(unsafe_code) is required. rusty-av1-toolkit is catalogued for its rav1e encoder speed; its rav1d-derived decoder has no catalogued decoder benchmark.

**Gotchas:**
- Strictness::Strict is the default and rejects non-conforming streams that dav1d conceals; set Strictness::Lenient for dav1d-identical behaviour on corrupt input
- Feature names moved after 0.6.0: the published crate's unchecked feature (frame threading, no overlap tracking) is called untracked on main, which also adds frame threading to tracked builds. The README table still says unchecked
- Published 0.6.0 returns wrong mastering-display values (wrong fixed-point units; a 1000-nit maximum reads as 25.6 nits). The fix is only on main (Unreleased)
- frame_size_limit defaults to 120 megapixels and bounds only declared dimensions, not decode time; use set_stop for cancellation on untrusted input

**Status:** Very active (commits on 2026-10-01; 0.6.0 published 2026-09-08 with about 15k total downloads; 451 closed issues, none open), but AGPL-3.0-only or a paid commercial licence and a speed deficit against dav1d make it a memory-safety pick, not a speed upgrade.

[repo](https://github.com/imazen/rav1d-safe) · [benchmark](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/imazen/rav1d-safe/HEAD/benchmarks/noasm-2026-09-08/README.md)

### networking-and-servers

#### dns-quic-http3

##### quiche-DPDK (tumi8 kernel-bypass fork)  `C (DPDK kernel-bypass I/O layer added on top of upstream Rust quiche core)`  `no license`  `active`  `Tier B`

DPDK kernel-bypass client/server built on unmodified quiche; 1.83x the single-connection goodput of kernel-socket quiche on 100G NICs.

**Beats:** quiche — The test was a single-connection download of an 8 GiB file, 50 repetitions, between two Xeon Gold 6421N hosts with 100G Intel E810 NICs (Debian 12, Linux 6.1, DPDK 24.11). The quiche-DPDK client+server pair averaged 5937 Mbit/s (range 5826-6018). The kernel-socket quiche pair averaged 3241 Mbit/s (range 2554-3605) with GSO on and 32x socket buffers, for 1.83x; on an SR-IOV VF quiche-DPDK reached 6168 Mbit/s. The DPDK side builds quiche 0.23.2 on unpinned Rust stable and C at RelWithDebInfo. The kernel quiche binary comes from a private CI branch ('25.02') whose version and flags are unpublished.

**Known shortcoming:** Research kernel-bypass client/server around an unmodified quiche; no licence (reference only). Needs DPDK and dedicated NICs; baseline builds are private and compiler versions not pinned.

**Known shortcoming:** Not HTTP/3: it negotiates only hq-interop/http/0.9 and sends a bare GET. Frozen paper artifact (3 commits, no LICENSE file). Source defects: path traversal in the server (admitted in a comment), whole file loaded into one malloc, client disables certificate verification, TX mbuf allocations not NULL-checked, ARP frames for other IPs freed twice; IPv4 only, one port/queue/lcore. With a quiche-DPDK server, 13 of 100 picoquic(-DPDK) client runs produced no goodput. An unpublished XDP variant averaged 3168 Mbit/s, no gain over kernel quiche. Slowest of the four DPDK stacks; kernel MsQuic with GSO/GRO (8250 Mbit/s) beats it without bypass.

**How:** It uses a run-to-completion busy-poll loop on one NUMA-local lcore. The loop pulls up to 32 packets with rte_eth_rx_burst, hands each to quiche_conn_recv straight from the mbuf, then drains quiche_conn_send into freshly allocated mbufs and sends them in 32-packet rte_eth_tx_burst batches. This removes the syscalls and kernel/user context switches that the paper identifies as quiche's bottleneck; kernel quiche supports only GSO, which barely helps it (3055 -> 3197 Mbit/s in the paper's data). Other throughput settings are 4096 RX/TX descriptors, hardware IPv4 checksum offload with the UDP checksum zeroed, MBUF_FAST_FREE, CUBIC, and quiche pacing turned off on the server.

**Use it when:**
- Bulk single-connection transfers between dedicated bare-metal hosts on 25-100G links, when a quiche-based app is limited by packet I/O and not by crypto (measured: 3.2 -> 5.9 Gbit/s per connection).
- Controlled environments (datacenter point-to-point links, CDN-internal transfers, testbeds) where you can give DPDK a NIC port or an SR-IOV VF plus hugepages and root. The SR-IOV VF run was slightly faster (6168 Mbit/s) and lets the kernel keep the physical port.
- When the downloading side is the bottleneck: a DPDK client against a kernel quiche server alone gave 5464 Mbit/s (1.69x), while a DPDK server with a kernel client gave only 4036 Mbit/s (1.25x).
- As a template for adding DPDK to your own quiche application without patching quiche. The whole integration is about 1,600 lines of C (headers included) around the public quiche C API.
- To reproduce or extend the NOMS 2026 kernel-bypass measurements (configs, CSVs and Zenodo raw data are public).

**Skip it when:**
- Anything production-facing. It is a single-purpose hq-interop file-transfer demo: no HTTP/3, the client skips certificate verification, the server has a path-traversal hole its own source comment admits, and there is no LICENSE file.
- When you want the most goodput. It is the slowest of the four DPDK stacks in the paper: LSQUIC-DPDK reaches 10756 Mbit/s, picoquic-DPDK 8347 and MsQuic-DPDK 7983, and kernel-socket MsQuic with GSO+GRO reaches 8250 with no bypass at all.
- Shared or general-purpose hosts. One core busy-polls at 100% even when idle, and the programs need hugepages, elevated privileges and a DPDK-bound port or VF. They support IPv4 only, use port 0 with a single RX/TX queue, and do not route: the peer must be ARP-reachable on the same L2 segment.
- Many concurrent connections or multi-core scaling. All work runs on one lcore with one queue and no RSS, and only single-connection transfers were measured.
- Multi-hop or WAN paths. The server disables quiche pacing and sends 32-packet back-to-back bursts; the paper's Appendix D shows DPDK quiche traffic is burstier than kernel quiche.

**Vs siblings:** Pick it over LSQUIC-DPDK or picoquic-DPDK only when your stack already uses quiche's API and you want kernel bypass without forking the protocol library. Those siblings patch their libraries and reach about 1.8x and 1.4x higher goodput in the same paper. If you can't dedicate a NIC, a kernel-socket sibling such as ngtcp2 beats quiche without any bypass.

**Gotchas:**
- The protocol is hq-interop/HTTP/0.9, not HTTP/3: ALPN is `hq-interop`/`http/0.9` and the request is a bare `GET /path\r\n`. The server reads the whole requested file into one malloc'd buffer before sending, so an 8 GiB file costs 8 GiB of RAM.
- Possible memory bugs from reading the code: TX-path rte_pktmbuf_alloc results are never NULL-checked. An ARP frame for another IP, or a malformed one, is freed in handle_arp_request and then again by rte_pktmbuf_free_bulk, which is a double free. This is harmless on the paper's point-to-point fiber but risky on a shared L2 or SR-IOV segment that carries broadcast ARP.
- Interop is flaky in the published data. With the quiche-DPDK server, 7 of 50 runs against the picoquic client and 6 of 50 against the picoquic-DPDK client recorded no goodput (implementation-matrix processed.csv).
- The AF_XDP-style 'quiche-dpdkxdp' variant in the SR-IOV dataset averaged only 3168 Mbit/s and was bimodal (median 1596). That is no better than kernel quiche. Its xdp branch is not on GitHub; only main and an instrumented perf branch are.

**Status:** A frozen research artifact: 3 commits, last push 2026-02-12 to accompany the NOMS 2026 paper, 0 stars, no issues. There is no LICENSE file (upstream quiche is BSD-2-Clause), so read it as a reference design and don't vendor it.

[repo](https://github.com/tumi8/quiche-dpdk) · [benchmark](https://www.net.in.tum.de/fileadmin/bibtex/publications/papers/spaethj-noms2026.pdf)

#### event-loops-io

##### IX (protected dataplane OS)  `C`  `MIT`  `abandoned`  `Tier B`

Protected dataplane OS that runs TCP/IP and one app on dedicated polling cores; 2.8-3.6x memcached throughput over Linux+epoll.

**Beats:** Linux 3.16.1 kernel TCP stack via libevent + epoll: stock memcached-1.4.18 on tuned Linux (pinned threads, IRQ affinity, tuned interrupt moderation); mTCP is a second baseline in the microbenchmarks — OSDI'14 paper: memcached-1.4.18 ported to libix on 6 cores vs. stock memcached (libevent+epoll) on 8 pinned, interrupt-tuned cores of Linux 3.16.1, on a Xeon E5-2665 @ 2.4 GHz server with Intel x520 (82599) 10GbE and 23 Linux mutilate clients over 1,476 connections. Max RPS within a 500us p99 SLA rose from 550K to 1,550K (ETC, 2.8x) and from 500K to 1,800K (USR, 3.6x), and unloaded p99 latency fell from 94 to 45us and from 85 to 32us; no compiler or version is given (the 2016 release builds the dataplane with gcc -O3).

**Known shortcoming:** Research dataplane OS: needs Dune/VT-x, GPL kernel modules and dedicated NICs; not a library. Code was released in 2016, two years after the OSDI '14 paper, and is abandoned since 2017-11. libdune has no licence file. No compiler versions stated.

**Known shortcoming:** No receive flow control: one connection holding 128 unread segments makes the server exit (#12). The released benchmark differs from the paper (2,720 vs 1,476 connections; memcached maintenance threads disabled as a hack). DPDK pinned at 16.04, Python 2 scripts, Dune unlikely to build on recent kernels; IPv4 only, one instance per host, i40e transmit broken (#31).

**How:** Each elastic thread runs to completion: it polls its own NIC RX ring, pushes a bounded batch (default 64 packets) through an lwIP-derived TCP/IP stack, switches to the application to consume events, then executes the application's batched system calls, TCP timers and TX in the same loop, with no interrupts and no intermediate socket buffers. Batching is adaptive, so batches only grow under congestion and light load keeps latency low. RSS flow-consistent hashing gives each hyperthread its own RX/TX queue pair, flows and memory pools, so the common path takes no locks and causes no cache-coherence traffic. The dataplane also uses only 2MB pages, a hierarchical timing wheel, and refills RX descriptors 32 at a time to cut PCIe writes.

**Use it when:**
- Reproducing or extending the OSDI'14/SoCC'15 results: ix-project/ix-bench holds the memcached, ping-pong, short-message and connection-scaling scripts, and the ported memcached (ix branch of ix-project/memcached) and the mutilate load generator are public under ix-project.
- Small-message TCP request/response servers (e.g. key-value GETs with <20B keys and 2B values) where p99 latency under a few hundred microseconds sets capacity, on a dedicated server with Intel 82599/X520/X540 10GbE.
- High connection churn or many connections: the paper reports 3.8M TCP connections/s on 4x10GbE and runs up to 250K concurrent connections (at 250K, throughput falls to 47% of IX's peak from L3 cache misses).
- Research on kernel-bypass designs that keep the network stack isolated from application code (VT-x ring separation) while Linux remains the control plane.

**Skip it when:**
- Anything production or long-lived: no commits since 2017-11-06, DPDK pinned at 16.04, and the maintainer said in 2021 (issue #36) that Dune has not been updated and likely does not support recent kernels.
- Hardware or network setups outside its narrow support: non-Intel NICs (mlx4 was requested, never added, issue #24), machines without VT-x, non-x86, IPv6, SR-IOV, or more than one IX instance per host (issue #2).
- Untrusted or bursty peers: libix has no receive flow control, and one flooding connection can terminate the server process (issue #12).
- Applications that block in handlers or depend on POSIX sockets, TLS libraries or other socket-based code: every network path must be rewritten to ixev callbacks or the batched API.
- Lock-heavy or CPU-bound servers: IX only removes kernel network overhead; memcached gained less on ETC (2.8x) and stopped scaling past 6 cores on IX because of its own lock contention.

**Vs siblings:** Pick IX over mTCP or F-Stack only when you need the TCP stack protected from application code (separate rings under VT-x) or are reproducing the OSDI'14 comparison, where IX delivered 1.9x mTCP's short-message rate and lower 64B latency. Arrakis is the closer research analogue and adds IOMMU/SR-IOV support that IX lacks; for anything you must run today, F-Stack or Seastar are the maintained DPDK stacks.

**Gotchas:**
- No receive flow control: if one connection holds 128 unconsumed receive segments (IXEV_RECV_DEPTH), ixev prints 'ixev: ran out of receive memory' and calls exit(-1); a single `nc < /dev/zero` flood took down the echoserver (issue #12). A full syscall batch array likewise exits with 'ran out of command space'.
- Zero-copy rules: received buffers are read-only and should be released quickly; send buffers must stay unmodified until the peer ACKs, or the wire payload is silently wrong. sendv returns bytes accepted by the TCP window, not bytes buffered, so partial sends are resumed on the 'sent' event.
- The TCP stack runs on the application's threads: a slow handler stalls every flow hashed to that core, and IX flags the app non-responsive after about 10ms in user mode. Outbound connections pick ephemeral ports so RSS returns replies to the same thread, so two threads cannot share a flow.
- Released artifacts differ from the paper: ix-bench's bench_memcached.py drives 2,720 connections from 16 threads (paper: 1,476), and the ported memcached disables its assoc-maintenance and slab-rebalance threads while the scripts pre-size the hash with hashpower=20. No IOMMU is used, so the dataplane is trusted with host-physical addresses; profiling needs `perf kvm --guest` because IX runs as a VT-x guest (issue #35).

**Status:** Abandoned since 2017-11-06 (the maintainer still answered issues until 2021); IX's own code is MIT-style, but it needs the unlicensed Dune repo, kernel modules and DPDK 16.04 on old kernels, so treat it as a research artifact to study or reproduce, not a dependency.

[repo](https://github.com/ix-project/ix) · [benchmark](https://www.usenix.org/system/files/conference/osdi14/osdi14-paper-belay.pdf)

#### http-servers-frameworks

##### Bun (Bun.serve)  `Rust/C++/C`  `MIT for Bun's own code, per LICENSE.md (GitHub reports NOASSERTION). Bun statically links JavaScriptCore/WebKit (LGPL-2) and tinycc (LGPL-2.1), plus permissive libraries such as BoringSSL, a uWebSockets fork and uSockets (Apache-2.0), mimalloc (MIT) and zstd (BSD OR GPL-2.0).`  `active`  `Tier B`

Bun's built-in JavaScript HTTP server (Bun.serve); 2.0-2.2x Go net/http throughput on a 3-route hello-world API, 4 cores.

**Beats:** Go net/http — In the-benchmarker/web-frameworks run of 2026-09-24 (commit f673364; zrk closed-loop keep-alive, 15 s per level, mean of GET /, GET /user/:id and POST /user; server pinned to cpuset 0-3 and load generator to CPUs 4-15 of a 16-CPU x86-64 Linux 7.2 host, CPU model not recorded), Bun 1.4.x (oven/bun:1.4-slim, mislabelled 1.2.5 in data.json) running Bun.serve routes as one reusePort node:cluster worker per core did 144,254 / 145,871 / 145,897 req/s at c=64/256/512 vs 71,499 / 67,382 / 67,239 for Go 1.27 net/http with http.ServeMux (go build -trimpath, GOAMD64=v3), i.e. 2.02-2.17x. p99 latency was 0.90 vs 3.05 ms at c=64 and 4.38 vs 15.51 ms at c=512; an earlier 2026-09-20 snapshot of the suite, measured differently, gave only ~1.12x.

**Known shortcoming:** The older 2026-09-20 run (different method) shows only ~1.12x over Go net/http (93,972 vs 83,964 req/s); in the current run Bun beats Go fasthttp (the fastest Go option) by only ~1.16x. The image was oven/bun:1.4-slim though data.json labels Bun 1.2.5. The CPU name is hard-coded (uname reports x86_64, 16 CPUs). Bun's code is MIT but it statically links LGPL-2 JavaScriptCore/WebKit.

**Known shortcoming:** Bun 1.4 (2026-08-20, the benchmarked image) is a Rust rewrite; the HTTP core is still uSockets (C) plus Bun's uWebSockets fork (C++), on epoll/kqueue, not io_uring. The exact version is unknown (image tag floats at 1.4). Go was built with GOAMD64=v3 while Bun ships a Nehalem-baseline binary with runtime AVX2/AVX-512 dispatch. Routes don't match exactly (Bun 204 vs Go 200 with empty body). Raw Bun.serve with JS callbacks sat below uWebSockets.js on Node in the same run. Multi-core scaling works only on Linux (reusePort ignored on macOS/Windows; node:http ignores reusePort, #43690); Bun needed one process per core while Go used 3.9 cores in one. No published GitHub security advisories; request smuggling #29732 fixed without a CVE (#30921 open). 1.4 is the first release of a Zig-to-Rust port done largely by AI agents in 11 days (~4% unsafe); HTTP/2 and HTTP/3 in Bun.serve are experimental (no gRPC trailers, no WebSockets over h2/h3; HTTP/3 not for production). idleTimeout defaults to 10 s and counts a slow handler as idle (max 255 s, #15589); malformed framing gets 400 and close with no handler call or log; docs disagree on minimum kernel (5.1 vs 3.10).

**How:** Sockets, parsing and routing stay in native code: uSockets (C) runs an epoll (epoll_pwait2) or kqueue loop, not io_uring, and Bun's uWebSockets fork (C++) parses requests with SWAR word-at-a-time scanning (the `hasLess` bit trick on 8-byte words, with 32 bytes of required buffer post-padding) and a Bloom filter over header names, then dispatches through uWS's tree router. The glue layer (Rust since 1.4, Zig before) takes request contexts from a pre-allocated pool of 2,048 and writes response metadata inside uWS 'corked' sections, while ServerRouteList keeps route callbacks in a fixed array and caches one JavaScriptCore Structure per route's params object so the JIT sees a single shape; params are percent-decoded with SIMD. Constant `Response` routes are served with no allocation and no JS. Multi-core throughput comes from one process per core sharing the port through `reusePort` (Linux SO_REUSEPORT), with the kernel spreading connections across them.

**Use it when:**
- JS/TS HTTP APIs on Linux where per-request stack overhead dominates. In the 2026-09-24 the-benchmarker run on 4 cores, Bun.serve with JS route callbacks did 145,897 req/s at c=512 vs 67,239 for Go net/http, with p99 latency of 4.4 ms vs 15.5 ms.
- Node.js services that want more throughput without leaving JavaScript: in the same run raw Bun.serve beat Fastify on Node (68,128 req/s) by ~2.1x and Express (42,586) by ~3.4x.
- Health checks, redirects, fixed JSON and static files: constant `Response` routes are dispatched with no allocation (the docs claim at least 15% faster than returning a new Response), and `{ dir }` routes (1.4+) stream files with sendfile and handle ETag, 304 and Range.
- WebSocket fan-out servers that want built-in topic pub/sub, per-socket backpressure limits and permessage-deflate without extra packages.
- Linux deployments where one worker process per core behind `reusePort` (or node:cluster) is acceptable.

**Skip it when:**
- As a speed-only reason to leave Go: in the same run Go fasthttp (125,657 req/s) and Fiber (123,666) came within ~1.16-1.18x of Bun, and an earlier 2026-09-20 snapshot of this suite, measured differently, showed Bun only ~1.12x ahead of net/http.
- macOS or Windows production, or any host without SO_REUSEPORT: `reusePort` is ignored there, and Bun's docs say node:cluster can only load-balance HTTP on Linux. You get one JS thread per server, while the Go binary in this run used 3.9 cores from a single process with no cluster code.
- CPU-heavy handlers or state shared in memory across requests: each worker is a separate process with its own heap and one event-loop thread, so a slow synchronous handler stalls every connection on that worker.
- gRPC, or anything that needs production HTTP/2 or HTTP/3: both are experimental in Bun.serve. There is no WebSocket over HTTP/2, no server push and no response trailers. The 1.4 notes say not to ship `http3: true` to production yet, since 0-RTT is disabled and server.upgrade() returns false over H3.
- Risk-averse deployments: Bun 1.4 (2026-08-20) is the first release of a Zig-to-Rust port done mostly by Claude agent workflows in 11 days. About 4% of the Rust sits in `unsafe` blocks. Advisories for the 1.4 security fixes are held back until people upgrade, and a request-smuggling bug (issue #29732, fixed 2026-04-27) has an open request for a CVE (#30921).

**Vs siblings:** Pick Bun.serve over fasthttp only when the service is, or should become, JS/TS: staying in Go, fasthttp reached 0.86x Bun's throughput in the same run with no runtime switch. Bun.serve is the zero-dependency base under Elysia, which scored 173,877 req/s largely because its benchmark routes are constants Bun serves natively; uWebSockets.js scored 174,621 on Node with a lower-level API, so pick it instead if you must stay on Node.

**Gotchas:**
- `idleTimeout` defaults to 10 s and counts a handler that is still working but has not written a byte as idle, so slow handlers see connection resets. The maximum is 255 s (open issue #15589 asks to raise it). For SSE or long streams, call `server.timeout(req, 0)` for that request.
- Multi-core scaling fails silently: `reusePort` is ignored on macOS and Windows, and open issue #43690 (2026-09-21) reports that node:http `listen({ reusePort: true })` is ignored even on Bun, while node:net honours it.
- Since 1.3.4, requests with malformed Content-Length, Transfer-Encoding or chunked framing get 400 and the connection is closed without calling your handler or logging anything. Check a hand-written client's framing headers first.
- Constant `Response` routes are cached for the server's lifetime; call `server.reload()` to change them. WebSockets (`server.upgrade()`) work only over HTTP/1.1, so `http1: false` disables them.

**Status:** Very active (last push 2026-09-26, v1.4.2 on 2026-09-05, 96k stars, owned by Anthropic since December 2025) and MIT for Bun's own code, but the binary statically links LGPL-2 JavaScriptCore/WebKit and LGPL-2.1 tinycc, and 1.4 is the first release of the Rust rewrite, so expect a few releases of settling.

[repo](https://github.com/oven-sh/bun) · [benchmark](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/the-benchmarker/web-frameworks/f673364fb30748e5bb8e57319ec2772bc872f78a/data.json)

#### tls

##### OpenSSLNTRU (libsntrup761 + engntru OpenSSL ENGINE)  `C`  `no license`  `abandoned`  `Tier B`

Batched sntrup761/857 post-quantum key exchange for OpenSSL 1.1.1 TLS 1.3; more LAN handshakes/sec than OpenSSL's asm X25519/P-256.

**Beats:** OpenSSL TLS 1.3 key exchange (ASM-optimized X25519 and P-256) — In the USENIX Security '22 paper (Section 4.4, Figure 5), tls_timer ran 100 samples of 8,192 sequential full TLS 1.3 handshakes (RSA-2048 certificate) from an i7-6700 client to a stunnel server on a Ryzen 7 2700X over a Gigabit LAN with Turbo off. The sntrup761 and sntrup857 CDFs sit above OpenSSL 1.1.1k's asm X25519 and P-256 on a 440-620 conn/s axis with no tabulated numbers (the demo page's example run gives about 522 vs 462 vs 449 conn/s), and the paper states no compiler, while the build scripts use gcc/clang -O3 -march=haswell or native; keygen is 156,317 amortized cycles per key at batch size 32 on a Haswell Xeon E3-1275 v3, vs 819,332 unbatched in the same library and 269,191 for CECPQ2's ntruhrss701.

**Known shortcoming:** The headline handshake comparison is CDF plots only; the only numbers are the demo page's example run (sntrup761 ~522 conn/s vs X25519 ~462, P-256 ~449), and the authors say the unloaded LAN hides the 2,197 extra bytes per handshake, so sntrup should not be read as cheaper than ECC overall. No compiler stated in the paper (build scripts use -O3 -march=haswell/native). Dead platform: patches cover OpenSSL 1.1.1f-1.1.1m (EOL 2023-09); ENGINE deprecated in 3.0 and removed in 4.0; OpenSSL 3.5+ ships X25519MLKEM768 instead. Private codepoints, post-quantum only (no ECC hybrid), dynamically linked apps only. A process that forks after filling the key pool can reuse keys (no atfork handling). The handshake that empties the pool pays the whole 32-key refill (~2.5 ms on 2 GHz Haswell) unless async_batch_lib is used.
