- Many small blocks: Lzma_compressBound reserves a constant 16 KB pad per call (open issue #5), so chunked LZMA output buffers can be far larger than with peer codecs.
- Projects that cannot track a vendored-codec fork: AOCL re-releases upstream security fixes on its own schedule (5.3.0 shipped zlib 1.3.1-based code; 5.3.2 moved to zlib 1.3.2 'addressing known security vulnerabilities').

**Vs siblings:** Pick it over zlib-ng or the Cloudflare zlib fork when you also want bzip2 and snappy speedups and AMD support from one library; pick zlib-ng, libdeflate or ISA-L igzip when you only need deflate, need ARM, or want independently measured numbers. For bzip2-compatible output it is faster per thread in the vendor run (about 2.1x) than lbzip2's catalogued 1.6x, though the two were measured on different machines.

**Gotchas:**
- Behaviour depends on environment variables read at first use: AOCL_DISABLE_OPT=ON forces reference paths, AOCL_ENABLE_INSTRUCTIONS caps the ISA, AOCL_ZLIB_QUICK_MODE=ON switches zlib levels 1, 2, 3 and 5 to faster settings with a worse ratio.
- On Windows the CMake Release build compiles everything with /arch:AVX2, and on Linux the Snappy sources are compiled with -msse4.1 and SNAPPY_HAVE_X86_CRC32=1, so not every path honours the 'portable down to SSE2' dispatch claim.
- GCC 15 needs per-file workaround flags (-fno-schedule-insns2 and others) on zlib chunkset_avx512.c and zstd_decompress_block.c; 5.3.2 notes fix 'GCC 15 decompression regressions in ZLIB and ZSTD' and 'LZ4 multi-threaded decompression data corruption', so pin 5.3.2 or later.
- aocl_llc_setup() only reports excluded or unsupported codecs, not allocation failures (lzbench review concern 4), and aocl_lzma_compress() does not check the output size up front and can underflow when outsize < LZMA_PROPS_SIZE (issue #5).

**Status:** Actively maintained by AMD (v5.3.2 released 2026-08-20, regular releases since 4.1) under file-by-file BSD-3-Clause, MIT and NCSA plus upstream codec licences; usable as a library, but it is a vendor fork that lags upstream codec releases and has little outside adoption (44 stars).

[repo](https://github.com/amd/aocl-compression) · [benchmark](https://github.com/inikep/lzbench/pull/321)

##### Firetrail (formerly skim)  `Zig`  `no license`  `active`  `Tier C`

Zig word-hash codec (Density-style) that encodes faster than lz4 --fast=20 and zstd --fast=5, at a lower ratio.

**Beats:** lz4 (also zstd) — The author's end-to-end CLI timings (poop, single thread, warm page cache, Ryzen 7 7800X3D, CachyOS, Zig release-fast build versus distro lz4 1.10.0 --fast=20 and zstd 1.5.7 --fast=5, all -T1) put silesia.tar encode at 1.67 GB/s for White and 1.54 GB/s for Orange versus 0.98 GB/s for lz4 and 0.69 GB/s for zstd, with Orange's ratio 1.54x against lz4's 1.56x; geomean over four corpora is 1.6x lz4 and 2.5x zstd for White. Decoded output was not verified in the harness, and the independent lzbench row covers the predecessor skim 0.1.0, not this codec.

**Known shortcoming:** Tier C: lz4/zstd baselines are distro binaries with flags unstated; the White dictionary is trained on the same input it compresses; the lzbench row is the old skim 0.1.0. No license, so reference.

**Known shortcoming:** Correctness bug: the CLI decoder reads each compressed block into an 8,388,608-byte buffer (main.zig input_data_bound = block_size) but an incompressible 8 MiB block encodes to 8,519,680 bytes, so random or already-compressed files cannot round-trip and ReleaseFast reads past the heap buffer. The decoder has @setRuntimeSafety(false), no input-length checks and no checksum. Algorithm files have no tests and bench.fish never compares decoded output with the original. No LICENSE. Zig 0.16+, no C API. Best possible ratio about 3.76x. Benchmark corpora compress, so the timed runs are unaffected.

**Independent measurement:** verifier

**Independent measurement:** first-party benchmark

**How:** There is no match search or entropy coding: each 64-bit word costs one Fibonacci multiplicative hash, one table load and one compare, and every 8 words share a 1-byte flag header, so the loop is branch-light, unrolled at compile time (inline for) and built with runtime safety off. The README describes the design as inspired by Density. Because only whole words at 8-byte-aligned positions can match, the best possible ratio is about 3.76x (8 bytes become 2 bytes plus 1/8 of a header byte).

**Use it when:**
- Experiments with very fast single-thread encoding of large, repetitive, word-aligned data such as logs (HDFS.log: Orange 2.42 GB/s encode at 2.53x versus lz4 --fast=20 at 1.25 GB/s and 4.53x).
- A deployed static dictionary (White) for streams that share a vocabulary, where the dictionary is trained once with Red and shipped to both ends.
- Pipelines that are encode-bound and can accept a ratio of 1.2-1.5x on mixed data, in a Zig code base.
- Reading the code as a compact reference for Density-style word hashing (about 180 lines per codec).

**Skip it when:**
- Any production or redistributed use: the repository has no LICENSE file, so the code cannot legally be copied.
- Incompressible or already-compressed input with the CLI: an 8 MiB block of random data encodes to 8,519,680 bytes, but the decoder reads each compressed block into an 8,388,608-byte buffer (input_data_bound = block_size in main.zig), so such files cannot be decoded and, in ReleaseFast builds, the read overruns the heap buffer.
- Untrusted input: decompressBlockToBuffer runs with @setRuntimeSafety(false) and never checks the compressed length, and the CLI trusts the per-block sizes in the stream; there is no checksum or format magic.
- Decode-bound workloads: lz4 decodes faster on all four corpora (silesia 2.53 versus 1.89 GB/s for White).
- When ratio matters: lz4 and zstd compress smaller on silesia and HDFS.log, and zstd --fast=5 beats it everywhere on ratio.

**Vs siblings:** Against LZ4, Density and ZXC it only wins on single-thread encode speed for word-aligned repetitive data; pick LZ4 (or memlz for encode-only speed) for anything that needs decode speed, a stable format, a C API or a licence, and Density if you want this style of word-hash codec with a licence and a library API.

**Gotchas:**
- Encoder and decoder must start from identical tables: a White or Orange stream encoded with --import dict.bin decodes to wrong bytes without that same file, and nothing in the stream records which dictionary or codec was used.
- White without an imported dictionary compresses almost nothing, because its table starts zeroed and is never updated.
- No round-trip check anywhere: the algorithm files have no tests, and scripts/bench.fish times decode with poop but never compares the decoded file with the original.
- The published White figures use a dictionary trained on the very file being compressed and leave its 512 KB out of the size, so Orange is the fair cold comparison.

**Status:** Active hobby project (63 commits, last 2026-08-04, version 0.0.0, 1 star) with no licence, so treat it as a reference to read rather than code to vendor.

[repo](https://github.com/VantorreWannes/firetrail) · [benchmark](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/VantorreWannes/firetrail/HEAD/README.md)

#### integer-bitpacking

##### SFVInt  `C++`  `no license`  `unknown`  `Tier C`

DaMoN 2024 paper: BMI2 PEXT/PDEP LEB128 varint decoder claiming up to 2x over Folly and Protobuf; no public code.

**Beats:** Facebook Folly and Google Protobuf LEB128 varint decoders — Only the abstract was seen (as search snippets): up to 2x faster LEB128 decoding than Facebook Folly and Google Protobuf varint decoders on AWS Intel m6i instances, for 32-bit and 64-bit values; one snippet cites 3.1 ms to 1.6 ms on a 'Web2' workload. Compiler, flags, library versions, datasets and per-length results were not readable here.

**Known shortcoming:** Tier C, paper only (arXiv 2403.06898 blocked): BMI2 varint decoding up to 2x over folly and protobuf on m6i; no code found. Candidate for a paper retier.

**Known shortcoming:** No public code, licence or API; the paper body is unreadable here (arXiv blocked, paperhub mirror 403). PDEP/PEXT are microcoded on AMD Zen, Zen+ and Zen 2, so the m6i (Intel) numbers do not carry over. Likely 8-byte loads past the value start with undocumented padding. The Folly baseline (Varint.h) is an unrolled branchy loop with bounds and error checks, so it may not be like-for-like.

**Independent measurement:** verifier

**Independent measurement:** paper, first-party

**How:** Instead of the byte-at-a-time test-and-branch loop, it loads several bytes at once and uses BMI2 PEXT with a continuation-bit mask (search snippets quote masks 0x0000808080808080, 0x0080808080808080 and 0x8080808080808080 for six, seven and eight bytes) to gather the MSBs, then PEXT/PDEP to compact the 7-bit payload groups into the integer in a few instructions. The baseline it beats, folly::tryDecodeVarint, is an unrolled chain of up to ten load/test/branch steps per value.

**Use it when:**
- You must keep the LEB128/protobuf varint wire format (existing files, RPC payloads, column stores) and varint decode shows up in profiles.
- Intel Haswell or later, or AMD Zen 3 or later, where PEXT/PDEP run in hardware.
- Mixed-length 64-bit varints where the scalar loop's data-dependent branches mispredict.
- You are willing to write and fuzz your own decoder from the paper's description.

**Skip it when:**
- AMD Zen, Zen+ and Zen 2: PDEP/PEXT are microcoded there and much slower (varint-simd's README documents this), so a BMI2 decoder can lose to the scalar loop.
- Non-x86 targets (aarch64, wasm): BMI2 does not exist; you need a separate path.
- You control the format: block formats such as Stream VByte, Masked VByte or SIMD bit-packing decode several times faster than any one-at-a-time LEB128 decoder.
- You need drop-in, tested code today: there is no public implementation to vendor.
- Untrusted input: bounds handling, overlong-encoding and malformed-input behaviour are not documented in anything readable here.

**Vs siblings:** Pick the technique over Stream VByte or MaskedVByte only when the LEB128 wire format is fixed; varint-simd (Rust, SSSE3/AVX2, public code and benchmarks on an i7-8850H) solves the same problem and is the safer starting point for a port to C++.

**Gotchas:**
- No code: the 2x figure cannot be reproduced or checked; the verifier and this enricher found nothing under the first author's GitHub account (gangliao).
- A multi-byte load with a PEXT mask likely reads up to 8 bytes past the value start; the paper's padding or tail rule could not be read here, so check this before decoding at buffer ends.
- Folly's baseline already has a bounds-checked fast path only when 10+ bytes remain and reports TooManyBytes/TooFewBytes errors; a faster decoder that drops those checks is not a like-for-like comparison.

**Status:** Peer-reviewed workshop paper (DaMoN 2024, authors from University of Maryland and ByteDance) with no public code, licence or maintenance; treat as a reference design (usability: reference), tier C until the paper body is read.

[benchmark](https://arxiv.org/abs/2403.06898)

#### succinct-structures

##### h0_bv (H0-compressed bitvectors)  `C++`  `no license`  `stale`  `Tier C`

Research C++ RRR-style H0-compressed bitvectors with faster block decoding; beat SDSL rrr_vector on access at block size 63.

**Beats:** SDSL rrr_vector (and SDSL hybrid bitvector) — First-party notebook output from a machine labelled 'laptop' (CPU not stated; g++ -std=c++2b -Ofast -march=native) shows the iterative b=63 decoder against SDSL rrr_vector<63> at equal space: access 249 vs 345 ns on WT-DNA-1GB and 75 vs 94 ns on WT-WEB-1GB (about 1.2-1.4x), rank 262 vs 345 ns on DNA but 179 vs 148 ns on WEB (slower); SDSL's rrr_vector<15> remains faster in absolute terms at more space.

**Known shortcoming:** Downgraded B to C: real numbers live in plotting/results.ipynb (machine 'laptop', CPU unstated) and the win over SDSL rrr_vector is mixed: IT63 vs SDSL b=63 access about 1.2-1.4x faster, rank slower on WT-WEB, b=15 variants slower than RRR15. No license, so reference; 1 star; stale. The SEA 2025 paper (Dagstuhl, arXiv blocked) could restore B.

**Known shortcoming:** The notebook's select times are invalid: the harness sets stop instead of start before the select loop (a bug inherited from SDSL's rrr_time_and_space.cpp), so select includes the rank loop; the access/rank claim is unaffected. The benchmark measures independent-query throughput, not dependent latency. No serialize/load, x86 BMI2 only, no license, hyb_256 checksums mismatch in the notebook. The SDSL patches only add size accessors, so the baseline is fair. Paper: 'Succinct Rank Dictionaries Revisited', SEA 2025 (LIPIcs.SEA.2025.15).

**Independent measurement:** verifier

**Independent measurement:** notebook: IT63 build 3.2 s vs SDSL b=63 21.0 s on WT-DNA-1GB (about 6.5x, derived from page data) at equal space 0.713 bits per bit

**How:** RRR decoding of a block offset into its bit pattern dominates query time at large block sizes. h0_63/h0_it decode a 63/64-bit block iteratively in 8-bit chunks using compile-time binomial and limit tables (constexpr std::array), so a block is decoded with a few table lookups instead of SDSL's bit-by-bit combinatorial walk. h0_gap stores a sampled (gap) lookup table of all block codes for b<32, and the de Bruijn variants assign non-lexicographic codes to blocks (the SEA 2025 paper 'Succinct Rank Dictionaries Revisited' argues these can give faster queries). Select uses BMI2 _pdep_u64 for the in-word step.

**Use it when:**
- Research or prototyping of RRR-style compressed bitvectors for FM-indexes and wavelet trees, where you want SDSL rrr_vector<63> space (about 0.71 bits/bit on WT-DNA-1GB, same as SDSL) with lower access latency (249 vs 345 ns in the notebook).
- Workloads dominated by random access on compressible bitvectors at large block size, where the iterative b=63 decoder beat SDSL b=63 on every dataset in the notebook (for example 75 vs 94 ns on WT-WEB-1GB).
- Build-time-sensitive pipelines: the notebook shows IT63 construction at 3.2 s vs 21.0 s for SDSL b=63 on WT-DNA-1GB (about 6.5x, derived from page data).
- As reference code for the SEA 2025 paper's decoders, to port the iterative or gap-table decoding into your own bitvector.

**Skip it when:**
- Production use: no LICENSE file (all rights reserved by default), 1 star, no releases, debugging code still present, and hyb_256.hpp is marked broken (its checksums disagree in the notebook).
- Rank-heavy workloads on very compressible data: IT63 rank on WT-WEB-1GB was 179 ns vs 148 ns for SDSL b=63, so it is slower there.
- When access speed matters more than space: SDSL's rrr_vector<15> (RRR15 row) was fastest overall (110 ns access, 149 ns rank on WT-DNA-1GB) at about 0.90 bits/bit vs 0.71 for IT63.
- Incompressible or random dense bitvectors: on RND-1 all H0 variants use more than 1 bit per bit (IT63 1.07), worse than a plain bitvector with rank support.
- Non-x86 or pre-BMI2 targets: headers include immintrin.h and select uses _pdep_u64/_pdep_u32 (BMI2).

**Vs siblings:** Pick it over LA-vector or succinct-bitvec-cpp's RRRBitVec only when you specifically need the RRR (block class/offset) representation with faster decoding at b=63; for compressed bitvectors you intend to ship, LA-vector (TALG 2022, select fastest in its comparison) is the better-supported choice, and for uncompressed rank/select SPIDER or rankselect trade more space for speed.

**Gotchas:**
- Select timings in the notebook are not valid: the harness (adapted from SDSL's rrr_time_and_space.cpp, which has the same bug) sets stop = timer::now() where it should reset start before the select loop, so every reported select time also includes the rank loop.
- The benchmark measures independent random queries (sum of results over 10M queries from 2^20 sampled positions), i.e. throughput-like ns/query, not dependent-query latency.
- Each constructor builds four temporary std::vectors copying metadata and block codes (left over from debugging), adding about 8 bytes per 63-bit block of peak memory during construction.
- The SDSL baseline is built from patched sdsl_hacks/rrr_vector.hpp and rrr_helper.hpp; the patches add size accessors and an optional RRR_NO_OPT path that the Makefile does not enable, so the baseline appears unmodified in behavior.

**Status:** Stale research code (last commit 2025-07-17, 48 commits, 1 star) with no license, so it is reference only: read it for the decoding ideas, do not vendor it.

[repo](https://github.com/saskeli/h0_bv) · [benchmark](https://github.com/saskeli/h0_bv/blob/master/plotting/results.ipynb)

##### orzo (Elias-Fano encoded L2 rank/select)  `C++`  `no license`  `stale`  `Tier C`

Research rank/select index for plain bitvectors that Elias-Fano-packs L2 counts, cutting index space below pasta-flat and cs-poppy.

**Beats:** cs-poppy and pasta-flat — Search snippets of the SEA 2025 paper (Hough and Bhatele, LIPIcs vol. 338) say orzo cuts the rank index overhead by about 26.5% relative to cs-poppy and pasta-flat (3.51% overhead with select, 3.125% rank only), at a rank slowdown of about 9-38% versus pasta-flat depending on CPU and input. The repo's benchmark times rank1/select1 for orzo, pasta-flat and pasta's poppy over 10M random queries on 2^24 to 2^34-bit random bitvectors built with clang++-17 -O3 -flto -mavx2, but no CPU model or results are committed, and the paper itself was not opened.

**Known shortcoming:** Downgraded B to C: the win is space only (26.49%, snippet only); the bench (comparison.cc vs pasta-flat and cs-poppy, clang++-17 -O3 -flto) publishes no results and no CPU; no LICENSE. SEA 2025 paper (Dagstuhl) blocked.

**Known shortcoming:** Not a speed win: the SEA 2025 paper (snippet) has rank 9-38% slower than pasta-flat depending on CPU and input; space (about 26.5% less overhead) is the only win. No license; one commit; UPPER_BLOCK_COUNT hard-coded to 259072 for N_L2=10 only; no copy constructor (copies double-free); the destructor frees uninitialised pointers when support_select=false; rank0 returns 1 + (i - rank1(i)), off by one; the bench main checks argc<4 but reads argv[4]; no results.csv or CPU model; needs x86-64 BMI2.

**Independent measurement:** verifier

**Independent measurement:** enricher

**How:** It keeps the cache-centric L0/L1/L2 layout of poppy-style indexes, but each 5632-bit lower block (11 basic blocks of 512 bits) gets one 128-bit entry holding an 18-bit L1 count plus the 10 cumulative L2 counts Elias-Fano encoded (20 upper bits, 90 lower bits). A rank decodes one L2 value with PDEP+TZCNT (BMI2 select-in-word) and then popcounts at most 8 words; by my arithmetic from the source constants the L1/L2 part costs 128/5632, about 2.3% of the bitvector (derived from source constants, not measured). Select uses a separate 2^32-bit upper level, a sample every 8192 ones, a linear scan over L1 entries, a linear Elias-Fano decode of the L2s and a PDEP/TZCNT finish.

**Use it when:**
- Very large static plain bitvectors (the bundled script sweeps 2^24 to 2^34 bits) where index memory matters more than the last nanoseconds of rank latency.
- Moderate to dense bitvectors (the script tests 10%, 50% and 90% ones) on x86-64 CPUs with BMI2 and AVX2.
- Research or prototyping of space-reduced poppy-style indexes, since the code is short (one ~400-line header) and the benchmark harness compares directly against pasta-flat and cs-poppy.

**Skip it when:**
- Latency-critical rank: search snippets of the SEA 2025 paper report rank is about 9-38% slower than pasta-flat depending on CPU and input (snippet only, paper not opened); pick pasta-flat, SPIDER or QuadRank if speed is the goal.
- Production code: no license file (so it cannot legally be copied), a single commit, no tests beyond a CHECK_CORRECTNESS mode in the benchmark, and no issues or releases.
- Non-x86 targets or x86 without BMI2: the header includes immintrin.h and calls _pdep_u64 and _tzcnt_u64 unconditionally; MSVC lacks the __uint128_t it relies on.
- Sparse bitvectors with heavy select traffic: select scans L1 entries linearly from a sample taken every 8192 ones, so long runs of zeros mean longer scans (observed in source, not measured).
- Anything that needs compressed or dynamic bitvectors; the bit array is stored uncompressed and the index is build-once.

**Vs siblings:** Choose orzo over SPIDER, rankselect or succinct-bitvec-cpp only when shaving roughly a quarter off a poppy/pasta-style rank index matters more than rank speed and you can live with unlicensed research code; for compressed sparse sets use LA-vector or h0_bv instead.

**Gotchas:**
- Template parameters are not really tunable: UPPER_BLOCK_COUNT is hard-coded to 259072 with a comment that it is 'temporarily hardcoded' for the default N_L2 = 10, and the L1 field is only 18 bits wide.
- Class owns raw new[]/calloc buffers with no copy or move constructor, so copying an Orzo double-frees; with support_select = false the destructor still deletes and frees the uninitialised select pointers.
- rank0 returns 1 + (i - rank1(i)), which looks off by one against rank1's exclusive convention; the constructor reads whole 512-bit basic blocks, so the bit array must be padded to a multiple of 512 bits (both observed in source, not tested).
- The benchmark main checks argc < 4 but reads argv[4], and the repo commits no results.csv, so the paper's numbers cannot be reproduced from the repo alone.

**Status:** Single-commit research artifact (2025-05-12, 2 stars) with no license file, so reference only; read it to learn the Elias-Fano L2 trick, do not vendor it.

[repo](https://github.com/hpcgroup/orzo) · [benchmark](https://github.com/hpcgroup/orzo/blob/master/benchmarking/comparison.cc)

##### SPIDER (Succinct Predictive InDEx for Rank and select)  `C`  `no license`  `stale`  `Tier C`

Research C code for a ~3.8%-overhead rank/select bit vector that interleaves rank counters with data and predicts select positions.

**Beats:** pasta-flat and pasta-wide, poppy (cs-poppy), Vigna's rank9 and SDSL rank/select structures (competitor list from WebSearch snippets of the SEA 2024 paper; paper not opened) — The SEA 2024 paper (seen only as search snippets; Dagstuhl and arXiv are blocked here) reports 3.82-3.83% space overhead, the fastest rank for bit vectors of 8 billion bits or more (22% better than pasta-flat) and select up to 41% faster than existing succinct structures while nearly matching the best 12.5%-space select; compiler, flags beyond the Makefile's gcc -O9 -march=native, and CPU are not visible. An independent Rust reimplementation in QuadRank's repo (i7-10750H at 3.0 GHz, n=2^35 bits) measured the SPIDER-style block at 29.39 ns/query in a single-thread loop vs 17.75 ns for sux-rs Rank9 and 33.99 ns for RankSmall<1,11> at similar 3% space (derived from page data).

**Known shortcoming:** Downgraded B to C: the repo has no numbers and the SEA 2024 paper (LIPIcs.SEA.2024.21, Dagstuhl blocked) is known only from snippets (22% faster than pasta-flat at 8B+ bits; select only near the best 12.5%-space structure, not faster). No license, x86-only. Retier to B when the paper is readable.

**Known shortcoming:** Not a library: global state in non-static helper.h globals, an fgetc builder and an MSB-first bit layout; speedtest.h times only SPIDER with clock() over an independent-query loop. Issue #1 (2025-12-18) asks for competitor bench code, a reproduction command and why latency looks low, with no reply. No LICENSE.

**Independent measurement:** verifier

**Independent measurement:** independent Rust reimplementation in quadrank's evals/rank-laptop.csv (n=2^35, 1 thread, plain loop): Spider-style block 29.39 ns vs Rank9 17.75 ns vs RankSmall<1,11> 33.99 ns (derived from page data)

**How:** Each 512-bit cache line stores 496 data bits plus a 16-bit rank counter relative to a 64-bit top-level count kept every 63,488 bits, so a rank query costs one cache-line access plus a small top-level array that usually stays in cache, then up to 8 popcounts. Select samples the position of every k-th one (16-bit low-level and 64-bit high-level sample arrays), linearly interpolates between samples to predict the target cache line, corrects with a short scan of the interleaved counters, and finishes inside the 64-bit word with PDEP + LZCNT. The ni-* variants keep the counters in a separate array for comparison.

**Use it when:**
- Reference design when you are writing your own rank/select for very large bit vectors (the paper reports the gain at 8 billion bits or more, snippet only) and want low space overhead.
- Studying or porting the interleaved-counter layout; QuadRank's BinaryBlock16Spider is a Rust reimplementation of the same block layout.
- Prototyping select with prediction (linear interpolation from sampled positions) on x86-64 with BMI2.

**Skip it when:**
- Any production use: there is no LICENSE file, so the code cannot legally be copied, and it is not packaged as a library.
- Programs that need more than one bit vector or thread-safe reentrant objects: all state lives in non-static globals declared in helper.h, so even including the header in two translation units collides.
- Non-x86 targets: it includes x86intrin.h and uses _pdep_u64 and _lzcnt_u64 (BMI2/LZCNT), built with -march=native.
- Small or cache-resident bit vectors, where the single-cache-miss layout gives little; or workloads needing the fastest rank at any space, where 25%-overhead Rank9 still led in plain loops in QuadRank's measurements.
- When you need reproducible competitor numbers: the repo only times SPIDER itself, and a reproduction question in issue #1 is unanswered.

**Vs siblings:** Only as a design reference: for a usable ~3.3%-overhead single-cache-miss rank, QuadRank/BiRank (MIT, Rust crate) implements the same layout and in its own benchmark streamed 2.63 ns vs 2.81 ns for its SPIDER-style block at 12 threads; for select, SPIDER's predictive scheme is the distinctive part, and splatlab rankselect (PTSelect) is the sibling to compare for in-word select.

**Gotchas:**
- Bits are packed MSB-first: the builder shifts each input byte in from the low end of a 64-bit word, and the 16-bit counter occupies the top 16 bits of the first word of every cache line, so input layout differs from SDSL/sux LSB-first bit vectors.
- The builder reads the file one byte at a time with fgetc and ignores a failed fopen beyond printing perror, so construction is slow and a bad path crashes.
- speedtest.h times independent random queries in a loop with clock() (CPU time, not wall time) and generates indices from two 31-bit rand() calls, so the figure is loop throughput rather than dependent-query latency; issue #1 (Dec 2025, Ragnar Groot Koerkamp) asks why the paper's numbers sit between typical latency (~80 ns) and loop throughput, and is unanswered.
- The 16-bit in-line counter limits each top-level block to 63,488 bits; this is fixed by #define, not configurable.

**Status:** Stale research artifact (10 commits, last 2024-05-28, 5 stars, no releases) with no license, so treat it as a reference to read, not code to vendor.

[repo](https://github.com/williams-cs/spider) · [benchmark](https://drops.dagstuhl.de/entities/document/10.4230/LIPIcs.SEA.2024.21)

### crypto-and-hashing

#### aead-and-ciphers

##### HiAE (High-throughput Authenticated Encryption)  `C`  `no license`  `active`  `Tier C`

Reference C code for HiAE, Huawei's AES-round AEAD; 2-6.6x OpenSSL AES-256-GCM on 16 KB messages on recent x86/ARM.

**Beats:** OpenSSL AES-256-GCM — The comparison comes from the designers' non-peer-reviewed ePrint 2025/377, Table 10. It measures single-core AEAD encryption at 16 KB with 48-byte AD, built with -O3 and GCC 11.4 on the x86 machines. HiAE reached 340.02 Gbps against 51.90 for OpenSSL 3.0 AES-256-GCM on a Ryzen 9 7950X (about 6.6x), 253.19 vs 38.80 on an EPYC 9334, and 171.46 vs 36.49 on a Xeon W9-3495X. The GCM baseline swings widely (114.07 Gbps on an i7-11700, where HiAE's lead falls to about 2.2x), decryption was not measured, phones used a hand-written AES instead of OpenSSL, and the repo's harness times only HiAE.

**Known shortcoming:** ePrint preprint only; the harness times HiAE alone (no OpenSSL code in the repo), so ratios against AES-GCM are derived from separately reported numbers. The repo has no license; hiae-aead/libhiae is an MIT-licensed alternative implementation. New 2025 design with little cryptanalysis yet.

**Known shortcoming:** Designer's preprint measures encryption only; libhiae shows decryption ~35-45% slower. At 64 bytes OpenSSL AES-GCM beats HiAE on every CPU in the paper's Table 10, and AEGIS-128L beats it on all 7 x86 CPUs. Reference HiAE_AEAD_decrypt releases plaintext without checking the tag (RUP setting), where ePrint 2025/1180 (ToSC 2026) gives key recovery. Init changed Oct/Nov 2025, so current ciphertexts differ from the paper version; no runtime ISA dispatch; individual Internet-Draft only, not CFRG-adopted.

**How:** HiAE is an NFSR-style stream cipher with a 2048-bit state (16 x 128-bit blocks). Each 16-byte block costs two AES rounds plus a few XORs, arranged in an 'XAXX' shape (AESL(a xor b) xor c xor d). That shape matches x86 aesenc and fuses well with ARM aese+aesmc, so neither ISA pays the extra XOR that aesenc-shaped designs such as AEGIS and Rocca pay on ARM. The keystream tap position was picked to leave four dependency-free rounds of parallelism during decryption. The code unrolls 16 state updates, so the shifting state costs no index arithmetic. On x86 with VAES and AVX-512 it switches to inline assembly that keeps all 16 state blocks in xmm0-xmm15 and uses xmm16-31 for message and ciphertext blocks. The paper says this is why older CPUs, where aesenc can only use xmm0-15, fall behind.

**Use it when:**
- Point-to-point links where you control both endpoints and messages are 1 KB or larger, on CPUs with VAES and AVX-512 (Ice Lake, Sapphire Rapids, Zen 4). In the designers' Table 10 at 16 KB AEAD, HiAE runs at 340.02 Gbps against 51.90 for OpenSSL 3.0 AES-256-GCM on a Ryzen 9 7950X, and 195.02 against 43.85 on a Xeon Gold 6326.
- ARMv8/v9 servers and laptops with crypto extensions, where the gain over other AES-based AEADs is largest. On Kunpeng 920 at 16 KB, HiAE does 53.72 Gbps, against 23.11 for AEGIS-128L and 14.66 for OpenSSL AES-256-GCM. On Apple M3 Pro it does 189.19, against 70.95 for GCM.
- Reproducing or extending the ePrint 2025/377 measurements on your own hardware. make benchmark times encryption-only, AEAD and MAC-only runs at 16 B to 16 KB.
- Designs that want a 256-bit key-recovery target with a 128-bit tag and can guarantee unique nonces and verify-before-release decryption.

**Skip it when:**
- Interoperating with TLS, IPsec, QUIC or any existing protocol. HiAE has no RFC. Its specification is an individual Internet-Draft (draft-pham-cfrg-hiae-06, May 2026) that CFRG has not adopted.
- Small messages. At 64 B, OpenSSL AES-256-GCM beats HiAE on every CPU in Table 10 where OpenSSL was used (7950X 18.35 vs 12.12 Gbps, M3 Pro 28.05 vs 9.72), and AEGIS-128L beats it on all seven x86 chips. On Kunpeng 920 and 920X, GCM still wins at 256 B. The fixed 32-round initialization and 32-round finalization dominate short messages.
- x86 without VAES (Cascade Lake, Haswell). Rocca is faster there: 156.60 vs 133.19 Gbps on a Xeon Gold 6242R and 75.97 vs 63.90 on a Xeon E5-2620 v3, both at 16 KB AEAD.
- Any setting where a nonce might repeat, unverified plaintext might be released, or an attacker can submit many forged decryptions. ePrint 2025/1180 (a minor revision of a ToSC 2026 paper) recovers the full 256-bit key with 2^128 data and at most 2^129 time using nonce-respecting decryption queries, and with only a small constant number of repeated nonces or unverified decryptions. The designers' rebuttal (2025/1235) says these settings are outside HiAE's model.
- Decrypt-heavy workloads or shipping this repo. The paper benchmarks encryption only, while libhiae's own numbers show decryption about 35-45% slower (Zen 4 at 16 KB: 129.71 vs 222.32 Gbps). This repo also has no LICENSE file.

**Vs siblings:** Use HiAE over Rocca, Rocca-S and AEGIS-128L for bulk (1 KB and up) traffic on ARM or VAES-capable x86, where Table 10 shows it ahead. Stay with Rocca on pre-VAES Xeons, with AEGIS-128L or AES-GCM for messages of 256 B or less, and with libaegis (RFC-published AEGIS, including the wider AEGIS-128X variants the HiAE paper never measured) when you need a standardized, licensed library. To deploy HiAE itself, take the MIT-licensed hiae-aead/libhiae rather than this repo. intel-ipsec-mb and SNOW-V-GCM target different needs: standard IPsec algorithms and a 5G-style stream cipher.

**Gotchas:**
- HiAE_AEAD_decrypt never checks the tag. It writes the plaintext, then overwrites the caller's tag buffer with the computed tag and always returns 0. The caller has to save the received tag first, compare the two in constant time, and wipe the plaintext on mismatch. As written, the API is the release-of-unverified-plaintext setting in which 2025/1180 recovers the key. libhiae's HiAE_decrypt does verify and returns non-zero on failure.
- The algorithm changed after the paper. The October and November 2025 commits changed how key and nonce are loaded during initialization, and a July 2025 fix made finalization encode lengths in bits. Ciphertexts and tags from older checkouts will not match the current draft test vectors. The round count is the same, so throughput should be unaffected.
- Building with -march=native on a VAES/AVX-512 machine emits EVEX instructions that fault on older x86 CPUs, and there is no CPUID check. Build per target, or use libhiae, which dispatches at run time.
- Every HiAE_stream_encrypt, HiAE_stream_decrypt and HiAE_stream_proc_ad call pads its own trailing partial block. When streaming, every chunk except the last must therefore be a multiple of 16 bytes. The header does not document this; it follows from the code.

**Status:** This is a 21-star designer reference repo, last changed 2025-11-11 to match the updated initialization and IETF test vectors. It has no LICENSE file, so it is study-only. For real use, take the MIT-licensed hiae-aead/libhiae (59 stars, pushed 2026-09-20), which adds runtime dispatch, tag verification and a portable fallback.

[repo](https://github.com/Concyclics/HiAE) · [benchmark](https://eprint.iacr.org/2025/377.pdf)

#### encoding

##### Faster CRC32 on Apple M1 (dougallj, PMULL multi-chain)  `C++`  `no license`  `abandoned`  `Tier C`

Single-file C++17 AArch64 CRC-32/CRC-32C kernel with 12 PMULL folding chains; about 2.5x zlib's crc32 on Apple M1.

**Beats:** zlib crc32() function — On a 3.2 GHz Apple M1 the author measured zlib's crc32 (a separate, unpublished test of Apple's system zlib, version unknown) at about 30 GB/s; the companion 12-chain gist reached about 70-75 GB/s on a 2 MiB buffer (clang++ -std=c++17 -O3), and this cleaner template/asm version about 76 GB/s. corsix/fast-crc32 independently measured this gist at 77.55 GB/s on M1 (512 KiB default buffer) against 25.03 GB/s for Chromium zlib's scalar code and 26.57 GB/s for its vector code, but only 17.41 GB/s on Ampere Altra, where the Chromium scalar code wins at 22.68 GB/s.

**Known shortcoming:** A gist, not a library: Apple M1 only (PMULL multi-chain), untouched since 2022-06-06. ~76 GB/s is this gist's own figure (70/75 GB/s from an earlier test gist); zlib is not in the harness, so the ~2.3x over zlib is derived. clang++ -O3.

**Known shortcoming:** No license. Builds only with Apple clang as published (corsix had to add <cstring> and -flax-vector-conversions). Loses on Ampere Altra (17.41 vs 22.68 GB/s); inputs under 192 bytes take a serial path. Superseded by corsix/fast-crc32 (~85 GB/s on M1).

**Independent measurement:** corsix/fast-crc32 independent run: 77.55 GB/s on M1 vs Chromium zlib 25-27 GB/s; Ampere Altra 17.41 vs 22.68 GB/s.

**How:** It uses Intel's 2009 carry-less-multiply folding ("Fast CRC Computation for Generic Polynomials Using PCLMULQDQ") ported to ARM PMULL/PMULL2, but with 12 independent 16-byte accumulators (192 bytes per iteration) instead of the usual 4. The chain count is sized to M1 Firestorm's latency: the Apple core fuses PMULL/PMULL2 with a following EOR into one 3-cycle uop, so each chain costs 6 cycles and 2 fused uops, and 12 chains fill the 4-per-cycle SIMD pipes. The fold step is inline asm to keep valid fusion pairs. The final 128-to-32-bit reduction uses two CRC32X/CRC32CX instructions, or a Barrett reduction for other polynomials.

**Use it when:**
- Bulk CRC-32 or CRC-32C over large buffers (the author profiled 128 KB and up; the test harness uses 2 MiB) on Apple M-series cores, where the checksum is the throughput bottleneck, e.g. zip/PNG/gzip writers or storage checksums on macOS/iOS.
- Studying or porting the N-chain PMULL+EOR folding technique: about 270 readable lines, with the constants derived by constexpr code rather than magic numbers.
- Arbitrary reflected 32-bit CRC polynomials on AArch64: pass the polynomial as a template parameter (NO_CRC_INSNS builds without the ARMv8 CRC instructions, using a table plus Barrett reduction).

**Skip it when:**
- Non-Apple ARM cores. The PMULL+EOR fusion it depends on is, per the author, probably unique to Apple CPUs. corsix/fast-crc32 measured it at 17.41 GB/s on Ampere Altra, slower than Chromium zlib's scalar CRC32X loop at 22.68 GB/s.
- x86 or any non-AArch64 target: there is no fallback path, since it includes arm_neon.h and uses PMULL inline asm unconditionally.
- Small or latency-sensitive buffers. Below 192 bytes (after 16-byte alignment) it drops to a single serial CRC32X chain, and the author warns its 5 ops per 16 bytes (vs 3 for CRC32X) can hurt when the checksum shares the core with other work.
- Shipping code that needs a clear license. The gist carries only an 'AS IS' warranty disclaimer and no license grant.
- When you want the fastest M1 result: the author's 2024 update points to corsix/fast-crc32 at 85.05 GB/s vs 77.55 GB/s for this gist.

**Vs siblings:** corsix/fast-crc32 is the direct successor: it ships explicit license files, is about 10% faster on M1 (85.05 vs 77.55 GB/s by blending EOR3 and CRC32X) and covers x86 and non-Apple ARM, while crc-fast and crc32fast are packaged libraries. Pick this gist only as a compact, readable C++17 reference for 12-chain PMULL+EOR folding; for shipping code use corsix/fast-crc32.

**Gotchas:**
- It does not build as-is outside Apple clang. corsix/fast-crc32's vendored copy had to rewrite the asm to standard syntax (`pmull v0.1q, %[val].1d, %[consts].1d`), add the missing `#include <cstring>` for memcpy, add an extern "C" wrapper, and compile with `-march=armv8-a+crypto+crc -flax-vector-conversions` under g++ on Linux.
- Speed depends on fusion pairs, i.e. each PMULL immediately followed by its dependent EOR. The author reports about 70 GB/s without them and about 75 GB/s with them; the inline asm pins this order, so do not 'clean it up' into intrinsics without re-measuring.
- The final fold from 12 accumulators to one is serial (about 72 cycles, per the author's TODO), a fixed cost per call on top of the small-buffer fallback.
- This gist has no test or harness of its own. The companion gist's harness checks only one 2 MiB buffer against a slice-by-4 table, but corsix's bench.c (which checks every length from 1 to 4,160 bytes and every split point against a table CRC) runs this code before benchmarking it.

**Status:** Abandoned: last edited 2022-06-06, and the author's 2024 blog update names corsix/fast-crc32 as the new state of the art. With no license grant it is a reference implementation, not code to vendor.

[repo](https://gist.github.com/dougallj/263f132023f590aec31a11bbc746b897) · [benchmark](https://dougallj.wordpress.com/2022/05/22/faster-crc32-on-the-apple-m1/)

#### signatures-kem

##### GOLF: GPU-accelerated Optimization for Lattice-based FALCON  `CUDA`  `no license`  `unknown`  `Tier C`

CUDA batch port of Falcon-512 signing and verification, one signature per GPU thread; 70x/369x the reference's published CPU throughput.

**Beats:** Falcon reference implementation throughput as published on falcon-sign.info (Intel Core i5-8259U @ 2.3 GHz, TurboBoost off), cited as Fouque et al. (Ref) in Table II and not re-run by the authors; also prior CPU/GPU Falcon papers — On an RTX 4090 (CUDA 12.1, sm_89, -maxrregcount=127, 128x512 threads), GOLF measures 420,250 sign/s and 10,311,039 verify/s for Falcon, with parameters implied to be 512 by the baseline. That baseline (5,948.1 sign/s, 27,933.0 verify/s) was copied from falcon-sign.info for the reference implementation on an i5-8259U at 2.3 GHz with TurboBoost off and compiler flags not given, so 70.65x/369.13x compares a GPU batch against one CPU. On an A100 GOLF reaches 157,995 sign/s and 4,180,879 verify/s, which is 2.69x/1.53x over Lee et al.'s published A100 figures (not re-run).

**Known shortcoming:** No public code. GPU vs CPU comparison: the 58.05x/73.14x ratios are against Nguyen et al. on an Apple M1, and the 70.65x/369.13x ratios against the reference use numbers copied from falcon-sign.info (i5-8259U, flags unknown). The ePrint page shows signing as 42.02 kops/s; the PDF says 420.25.

**Known shortcoming:** Paper never names the parameter set (baseline is falcon-sign.info's Falcon-512 row) and its ratios are inconsistent (abstract 58x/73x vs Apple M1; 70.65x/369.13x vs reference; intro 387.84x). Batch latency ~156 ms. Side channels argued away, not measured. The possibly related russdrh/FP-GOLF repo (no license) reuses one salt across threads and its benchmark clones one key/message 65,536 times and checks only thread 0.

**Independent measurement:** IEEE TIFS 2025: signing 420.25 kops/s; vs Nguyen et al. (M1) 58.05x/73.14x; vs reference 70.65x/369.13x.

**How:** The main gain is coarse-grained parallelism: one thread per signature, 128 blocks x 512 threads (65,536 signatures per launch), with -maxrregcount=127 so that 512 threads fit in a block. A 2-threads-per-signature fine-grained variant that swaps data with __shfl_sync reached only 177,027 sig/s, against 361,726 for coarse-grained. Kernel fusion avoids repeated launches and global-memory round trips, and the recursive ffSampling is rewritten as an explicit stack-frame loop (Lee et al.'s method) so that NVCC will compile it. Finally, the FFT/iFFT butterfly units run in depth-first rather than layer-by-layer (breadth-first) order to shorten data reuse distance. This added 14.51% signing throughput (361,726 to 414,216 sig/s at 128x512) and, per Nsight, cut L2-to-DRAM traffic by 18%.

**Use it when:**
- Cloud or server backends that queue tens of thousands of Falcon-512 signatures at a time, where aggregate ops/s matters and roughly 156 ms of batch latency is acceptable (RTX 4090 figure).
- Bulk Falcon-512 verification, e.g. checking large signature sets. Verification shows the largest gain (10.3M verify/s on an RTX 4090, about 6.4 ms batch latency) and needs no secret material on the GPU.
- You are building your own GPU Falcon and want proven, simple tricks: one thread per signature, a stack-frame iterative ffSampling, and depth-first butterfly ordering for FFT/iFFT cache locality.
- You need published RTX 4090 and A100 throughput numbers to size GPU capacity for Falcon against Lee et al.'s earlier GPU work.

**Skip it when:**
- Single-signature or latency-bound signing. Each 65,536-signature batch takes about 156 ms on an RTX 4090 (415 ms on an A100), while the CPU reference produces one Falcon-512 signature in about 0.17 ms (5,948 sign/s on an i5-8259U).
- You need usable, licensed code. The paper links none. The candidate repo russdrh/FP-GOLF has no license, 0 stars and a single benchmark/KAT driver, and has per-thread indexing bugs (see gotchas).
- Falcon-1024 or FIPS 206 FN-DSA interoperability. The paper never names a parameter set (its baseline row is Falcon-512), cites the 2018 NIST submission, and FP-GOLF hard-codes logn=9 (Falcon-512).
- Shared or multi-tenant GPUs with side-channel concerns. The paper argues GPU global-memory side channels are 'not practical' rather than measuring leakage, and does not analyze the floating-point Gaussian sampler's timing on GPU.
- Tight GPU memory. The FP-GOLF tree mode allocates 7,169 doubles (about 56 KB) of expanded key per thread, about 3.8 GB for its 65,536-thread batch, plus a 36 KB per-thread scratch union.

**Vs siblings:** Pick GOLF over VecFalcon only when you have a CUDA GPU and large batches and need Falcon throughput far beyond a CPU core. VecFalcon (CPU SIMD, 1.13-1.59x faster signing, released code) is the practical choice for per-signature latency or deployable code. GRASP is the matching GPU batch design for SPHINCS+ and also ships no code; if you need working GPU Falcon code today, Lee et al.'s benlwk/Falcon-Mitaka (GPL-3.0, Falcon-512), the prior work GOLF benchmarks against, is released.

**Gotchas:**
- Headline ratios are easy to misread. The abstract's 58.05x/73.14x is against Nguyen et al.'s Apple M1 NEON code, not the reference. Against the reference (falcon-sign.info) the gain is 70.65x/369.13x, though the introduction says 387.84x. The ePrint web abstract prints 42.02 kops/s where the PDF says 420.25 kops/s.
- Throughput depends heavily on batch size. Across nine grid/block configurations from 16,384 to 65,536 threads, the best signing throughput is 2.93x the worst (1.47x for verification). Keys are generated ahead of time and shipped to the GPU in bulk, and the paper does not say whether host-device copies are inside the timed region.
- In FP-GOLF, the sign kernels read the 40-byte nonce (salt) with no per-thread offset, so every thread in a batch hashes and emits the same host-supplied salt. They also memmove thread 0's message into every signed-message output. Falcon (the paper's Algorithm 1) needs a fresh uniform salt per signature.
- The FP-GOLF benchmark copies one key, one message, one seed and one nonce into all 65,536 slots, checks only thread 0's signature against the CPU result, and times kernel launch plus cudaDeviceSynchronize only. Its grid is 256x256, not the paper's 128x512.

**Status:** This is a peer-reviewed reference design (IEEE TIFS vol. 20, pp. 9441-9453, 2025; ePrint revised 2025-08-15) with no linked code, license or maintenance. The first author's russdrh/FP-GOLF (3 commits on 2026-05-25, 0 stars, no license) contains the paper's depth-first FFT/iFFT loops (logm/loghm counters) and stack-based ffSampling, so it is probably related. It is unconfirmed as the paper's artifact and not usable as-is.

[benchmark](https://eprint.iacr.org/2025/749)

##### GRASP: GPU-based paRallel Accelerated SPHINCS+  `CUDA`  `no license`  `unknown`  `Tier C`

Single-kernel CUDA SPHINCS+-SHA256-f-simple batch signer/verifier; 1.37-3.45x over Kim et al.'s GPU code, 1,820-3,659x the single-core reference.

**Beats:** NIST PQC SPHINCS+ reference C code (version 3.0), SHA-256 simple fast parameter sets, run by the authors on a single core of an AMD Ryzen 5 5600G; also the open-source GPU SPHINCS+ of Kim et al. (re-run on the same GPU) plus prior GPU/FPGA works — On an RTX 4090, timing kernels only (host-device copies excluded, averaged over 1,000 runs, NVCC version and flags unstated), GRASP signs 146,363 / 82,621 / 40,489 and verifies 1,499,590 / 933,696 / 886,362 SPHINCS+-SHA256-128f/192f/256f-simple signatures per second. That is 3,114-3,659x (signing) and 1,820-2,029x (verification) the NIST reference C code v3.0 on one Ryzen 5 5600G core. The like-for-like result is 1.37-1.79x signing and 1.53-3.45x verification over Kim et al.'s open-source GPU code re-run on the same RTX 4090.

**Known shortcoming:** No public code. The >1000x ratios compare an RTX 4090 against one Ryzen 5 5600G core running the NIST SPHINCS+ reference; the headline numbers exclude memcpy, and NVCC/CPU flags are not given. Against other GPU code (Kim et al., re-run on the same RTX 4090) the gain is 1.37-3.45x.

**Known shortcoming:** Only SHA256-f-simple is measured; including memcpy, level-1 signing drops from 146k to 118k/s. Needs a 128x512 launch grid (128x64 reaches 45% of peak). Level-3 verify figure differs between text (1,408,846) and table (933,696). Baseline is the portable reference v3.0 on one core, with no optimized CPU build compared. SLH-DSA (FIPS 205) compatibility not documented.

**Independent measurement:** IEEE TC 2026: signing 3659x/3178x/3115x, verifying 2029x/1898x/1820x vs SPHINCS+ ref v3.0 (1 core); 1.37-3.45x vs Kim et al. GPU.

**How:** Kernel fusion runs FORS, WOTS+ and the MSS hypertree in a single CUDA kernel. This avoids the global-memory hand-offs of Kim et al.'s multi-kernel design. The thread-team size is chosen so that both the hypertree layer count d and the FORS tree count k divide evenly (gcd(22,33)=11), with one thread per layer or subtree, so no threads sit idle during node merging. When the root of the layer below is already known, WOTS+ signing is folded into that leaf's public-key chain computation, which removes about 33% of the hash calls for those leaves and cuts separate WOTS+ signings from d to t per thread. The n-byte hash blocks move with 16-byte int4 loads and stores at levels 1 and 5, and with int2 at level 3, where 24-byte blocks would misalign.

**Use it when:**
- High-volume SPHINCS+ signing on a data-center GPU (e.g. a code- or firmware-signing farm) that accepts SHA-256 fast-simple parameters: 146,363 / 82,621 / 40,489 signatures/s at levels 1/3/5 on an RTX 4090.
- Mass verification of SPHINCS+-SHA256-f signatures: 1.5M/s at level 1 on an RTX 4090, one thread per signature.
- A GPU signer that needs per-signature latency: the low-latency mode signs in 0.512 ms at level 1 (25 ms for the CPU reference, 4.8 ms for Kim et al.), at the cost of dropping to 19,521 ops/s.
- Reference techniques for your own GPU or CPU hash-based signer. Kernel fusion, gcd-sized thread teams and merging WOTS+ signing into leaf keygen are all described in enough detail to reimplement, and the paper says the WOTS+ merge also helps CPU code.

**Skip it when:**
- You need code. None was released and there is no license. The only open GPU SPHINCS+ code found is Kim et al.'s kindongsy/TCAS-SPHINCSp_GPU, which is unlicensed and consists of per-security-level Visual Studio projects.
- You need SHAKE, Haraka, 'robust' or small (s) parameter sets. Only SHA-256 fast-simple was measured; the claim that it is 'equally effective in all modes' is asserted, not benchmarked.
- You need FIPS 205 SLH-DSA compliance. The work targets SPHINCS+ round 3 (reference code v3.0), and compatibility with the final SLH-DSA standard is not documented.
- Small batches in the throughput mode. The peak needs a 128x512 grid; at 128x64, level-1 signing drops to 66.4 kops/s, 45% of the peak.
- Sizing end-to-end PCIe throughput from the headline. It excludes host-device copies: with memcpy, RTX 4090 level-1 signing falls from 146,363 to 117,723 ops/s, and with-memcpy verification numbers are not reported.

**Vs siblings:** Pick GRASP when you are committed to hash-based SPHINCS+ signatures and need GPU batch throughput. GOLF is the same group's GPU design for Falcon; it reaches 420k sign/s on the same RTX 4090 with 666-byte Falcon-512 signatures versus 17,088 bytes for SPHINCS+-128f, and it also ships no code. The CPU siblings (VecFalcon, ENG25519, UltrafastSecp256k1) release code and suit per-signature latency on CPUs.

**Gotchas:**
- Level-3 verification is reported inconsistently: the text says 1,408,846 ops/s, while Table VI and Fig. 13 say 933,696 (933.7 kops/s). The table value drives the 1897.76x and 1.80x ratios.
- The 1,820-3,659x ratios are against the portable reference C code on one Ryzen 5 5600G core with unstated flags (40/26/13 sign/s, 739/492/487 verify/s). No optimized CPU SPHINCS+ implementation was compared.
- The gap over Kim et al. shrinks with apples-to-apples conditions: 1.37/1.79/1.58x kernel-only on an RTX 4090 (Kim's open-source code re-run), 1.36/1.65/1.49x with memcpy, and 1.22/1.25/1.30x on an RTX 3090 against Kim's published with-memcpy figures.
- The low-latency and high-throughput modes are separate thread configurations. Low-latency gives 5.5x lower throughput than Kim et al. on the RTX 4090, so pick one per deployment.

**Status:** This is unreleased research code from a peer-reviewed paper (IEEE TC vol. 75 no. 4, pp. 1579-1592, 2026; ePrint revised 2025-01-16) with no repo, license or maintenance, so treat it as a technique reference only. Both the ePrint and the journal version are titled 'GRASP: Accelerating Hash-based PQC Performance on GPU Parallel Architecture'; the catalog name is the expanded acronym.

[benchmark](https://eprint.iacr.org/2024/1030)

##### moduletto (NEON i16 ML-KEM-512)  `Rust`  `PolyForm-Noncommercial-1.0.0`  `active`  `Tier C`

Rust modular-arithmetic/NTT crate whose NEON ML-KEM-512 example edges out liboqs 0.16.0 on Apple M5 (~1.18x).

**Beats:** liboqs 0.16.0 (ML-KEM-512, built from source at tag 0.16.0, Release, -O3 -march=native, on aarch64/Apple M5) — On an Apple M5 (macOS 25.5), the author's 10,000-iteration example times its NEON i16 ML-KEM-512 at 4.07/3.84/5.80 us (keygen/encaps/decaps, about 13.7-14.1 us per session), built with the Cargo release profile (LTO, codegen-units = 1) and an unstated rustc. That is compared with liboqs 0.16.0 built from source (-O3 -march=native) at 16.19 us, about 1.18x. The liboqs number comes from an unpublished C harness and is hardcoded in the example, so the comparison is first-party and not reproducible from the repo.

**Known shortcoming:** liboqs and Kyber-ref times are hard-coded constants in examples/kyber_benchmark.rs, measured by a C harness that is not in the repo; rustc version not stated (retiered A to C). The '2.96x' is Kyber-ref vs liboqs, not moduletto (moduletto vs Kyber-ref is ~3.4-3.5x, derived). The KEM lives in an example, not the library; FIPS 203 conformant only since 2026-08-11. PolyForm-Noncommercial license: reference use only. NEON (aarch64) only.

**Known shortcoming:** Security bug (found in enrichment, by code reading): the decapsulation mask `!(a^b).wrapping_neg()` evaluates to (a^b)-1 rather than 0x00/0xFF in all three backends, so a ciphertext differing in one byte can leak real-key bits into the implicit-rejection output; ACVP vectors did not catch it and it is not reported upstream. Do not use for real keys. No API (KEM lives in an example), not on crates.io, no zeroize or RNG. Library NTT converts i64/i16 on every call; the x86 i64 path is ~2x slower than liboqs.

**How:** A pq-crystals-style int16 Montgomery NTT (R = 2^16, QINV = -3327) runs eight butterflies per NEON instruction (vmull_s16 / vmovn_s32 / vshrn_n_s32). The two narrow layers (len 4 and 2) are vectorised with uzp/zip deinterleaving, and lazy reduction plus a branchless rounding Barrett step removes per-layer reductions. Most of the session-level gain came from outside the NTT: grouped bit-packing codecs (43.6 to 27.7 us); a two-lane Keccak-f1600 that uses ARMv8.2 FEAT_SHA3 (EOR3/RAX1/XAR/BCAX) to pair independent SHAKE streams, with right-sized squeezing (to 16.1 us); and dropping round-3 Kyber's final KDF during the FIPS 203 fix (to 13.9 us).

**Use it when:**
- Studying how a Rust ML-KEM-512 reaches liboqs-level speed on Apple Silicon: int16 NEON NTT, uzp/zip narrow layers, two-lane FEAT_SHA3 Keccak
- Non-commercial research or benchmarking on aarch64 with FEAT_SHA3 (Apple M-series), where the ~13.9 us session figure was measured
- Needing a small no_std-capable NTT/ModN arithmetic crate for q = 3329 experiments, with Coq proofs of the Barrett and constant-time primitives and fuzz targets
- Porting ideas (grouped codecs, streaming rejection sampler, paired Keccak lanes) into a permissively licensed ML-KEM implementation you write yourself

**Skip it when:**
- Any commercial product: PolyForm Noncommercial 1.0.0 forbids commercial use without a separate license
- Production key exchange: the KEM is benchmark example code with no public KEM API, no RNG integration, no zeroization, no independent review, and the decapsulation mask defect listed under gotchas
- x86-64 or other non-aarch64 targets: the NTT falls back to a portable i64 kernel and the i64 KEM backends measured 34.7-36.8 us on the M5, about 2x slower than liboqs
- ML-KEM-768/1024: only the 512 parameter set (k = 2) is implemented
- Needing a published package: the crate is not on crates.io (the README's moduletto = "0.1" snippet will not resolve), so it has to be a git dependency

**Vs siblings:** Among the catalogued KEM/signature entries, this is the only ML-KEM one that times against liboqs on Apple Silicon NEON. sntrup is a usable, MIT/Apache crate for a different KEM (NTRU Prime) with a reproducible liboqs harness, and the Plantard-NTT paper targets formally verified NTTs compared against pq-crystals reference C. Pick moduletto only to learn aarch64 ML-KEM-512 optimisation techniques under a non-commercial license.

**Gotchas:**
- Decapsulation's constant-time equality mask is wrong in all three backends of the example (eq &= !(a ^ b).wrapping_neg() computes (a^b)-1 per byte, not 0x00/0xFF). A ciphertext whose only byte difference from the re-encryption is 0x02 yields mask 0x01, so the output mixes bits of the real key K' into the implicit-rejection key. The ACVP VAL vectors did not catch this. This is from reading the source; not reported upstream as of this review.
- The library's NEON NTT takes and returns [ModN<3329>; 256] (i64 per coefficient) and converts to and from i16 on every call (about 30 ns each way, per the source comment), so building a KEM on the public API will not reach the example's numbers
- Until 2026-08-11 the code implemented round-3 Kyber with a hardcoded zero implicit-rejection seed and eta1 = 2. The 2026-03-19 tables and the Platform Notes in BENCHMARKS.md describe that older, non-conformant code
- The LibOQS (16.19 / 20.43 us) and Kyber-ref (47.87 us) figures are hardcoded constants printed by the example. Running it re-times only moduletto

**Status:** One developer, 11 commits (the burst of 2026-08-11 changes delivered the FIPS 203 fixes and the speedups, and the last commit was 2026-09-03), no issues filed, not on crates.io, and noncommercial-licensed, so treat it as reference code to read, not a dependency.

[repo](https://github.com/crabnebula-dev/moduletto) · [benchmark](https://github.com/crabnebula-dev/moduletto/blob/main/BENCHMARKS.md)

### interpreters-and-vms

#### bytecode-vms-and-wasm

##### EOS VM  `C++`  `EOS VM License v1.0 (MIT-derived text with an added clause requiring source release of any covered work used for non-EOSIO blockchain purposes; not OSI-approved)`  `stale`  `Tier C`

Header-only C++ WebAssembly interpreter and x86-64 single-pass JIT for Antelope blockchains; vendor claims up to 16x over the Binaryen interpreter.

**Beats:** Binaryen and WABT WebAssembly interpreters — The only numbers are block.one's EOSIO 2 announcement, seen as search snippets: 'EOS VM runs the EOS Mechanics WASM CPU benchmarks up to 16x faster than Binaryen' (the EOSIO 1.0 interpreter), with no runtime, hardware, compiler or method given; the EOSIO v2.0.0 release notes on GitHub carry no numbers and recommend EOS VM JIT for block producers and the EOS VM Optimized Compiler, which is not in this repo, for other nodes. The repo's bench-interp tool prints a single parse time and execution time with no published results.

**Known shortcoming:** Vendor 16x claim is snippet only (medium.com blocked) and it is unclear which runtime produced it (the Optimized Compiler is not in this repo); the VM Matters paper puts it far behind wasmtime and WAVM. LICENSE is the custom non-OSI 'EOS VM License V1.0', not MIT, so usability is reference. Fork of EOSIO/eos-vm.

**Known shortcoming:** Enricher: the cited EOS Mechanics CPU contract (AlohaEOS/eos-mechanics contracts/eosmechanics.cpp) has is_prime never returning false for odd p (prime = BOOL(p)), Lucas-Lehmer overflow for p over 32, '1LLU << p' undefined up to 375, a discarded result and self-reported cpu_usage_us timing, so the 16x claim (snippet only, runtime unknown, no numbers in the v2.0.0 notes) rests on a broken harness. MVP-only opcodes, 8 GiB virtual reservation per allocator, process-wide signal handlers, JIT x86-64 only.

**How:** The interpreter's parser rewrites Wasm into an internal bitcode of fixed-size variant opcodes with branch and call targets pre-resolved (br_table_data, call_imm), dispatched through a statically derived visitor instead of virtual calls, and keeps module data in non-owning bump allocators that live as long as the module. Linear memory sits in an 8 GiB PROT_NONE reservation with guard pages, so loads and stores need no bounds checks and host functions need no pointer validation. The JIT is a single-pass x86-64 code writer driven directly by the parser (memory base kept in rsi, no IR or LLVM), which keeps compile time linear. Time limits cost nothing in the hot loop: on expiry the watchdog makes the code pages non-executable and the resulting SIGSEGV unwinds the run.

**Use it when:**
- Antelope/EOSIO-compatible chains, or any system that needs bit-identical Wasm results across machines (softfloat on by default) and consensus-matching limits such as call depth 250 and per-section caps in `options`.
- Embedding untrusted Wasm in a C++ host where predictable, linear load and validation time matters more than peak speed (the README contrasts this with WAVM's long, unpredictable LLVM compiles).
- Hard per-call CPU deadlines without instruction counting: the watchdog revokes execute permission on the code pages when time runs out.
- Many short calls into small contracts with cheap host-function transitions on x86-64 Linux (JIT) or other 64-bit Unix hosts (interpreter).

**Skip it when:**
- Peak throughput: the peer-reviewed 'VM Matters' study (snippet only) measured EOS VM at about 20 s on a matrix benchmark against about 70-170 ms for WAVM and Wasmtime, so it only beats the old Binaryen and WABT interpreters.
- Modern Wasm modules: the opcode table is MVP only (no sign-extension, saturating float-to-int, bulk memory, reference types or SIMD), so modules from toolchains that enable post-MVP features by default will not load unless built for the MVP target.
- Windows (CMake stops with an error on WIN32) or a JIT on anything but x86-64; AArch64 gets only the interpreter.
- Projects that cannot accept the EOS VM License v1.0: its share-alike clause covers any work adapted for other blockchain purposes and it is not OSI-approved.
- Hosts that install their own SIGSEGV/SIGFPE handlers or whose host functions need destructors to run when a trap unwinds.

**Vs siblings:** Pick EOS VM over wasm3, WAMR or Wasmi only when you need Antelope consensus compatibility, softfloat determinism and zero-overhead watchdog deadlines in a header-only C++ engine; for general embedding those interpreters have measured numbers, permissive licences and wider platform support, and WAVM or WasmEdge win on peak speed.

**Gotchas:**
- Each wasm_allocator reserves 8 GiB of virtual memory (max_memory = 4ull << 31) plus guard pages; it had no destructor until April 2025 (commit 'Add destructor to wasm_allocator to release memory'), so older copies leaked the mapping.
- Static initialization installs process-wide SIGSEGV, SIGFPE (and SIGBUS outside Linux) handlers and traps unwind with siglongjmp; the README warns host functions must be able to 'fail hard' without destructors, and the watchdog starts a new std::thread for every timed run.
- A timeout disables code pages for the whole module: other threads running the same module take SEGVs and retry until the timed-out run re-enables them (signals.hpp comment), so one slow contract stalls its siblings briefly.
- Harness flaw in the cited benchmark: the EOS Mechanics CPU action (AlohaEOS/eos-mechanics contracts/eosmechanics.cpp) has is_prime assign `prime = BOOL(p)` inside its test, so it never returns FALSE for odd p, and the Lucas-Lehmer step overflows 64 bits for p > 32 and shifts 1LLU by up to 375 (undefined behaviour); the work is about 35,000 iterations of a 64-bit multiply and remainder whose result is discarded (a code comment warns it could be optimized out), timed by self-reported on-chain cpu_usage_us that the repo's own disclaimer says producers can manipulate.

**Status:** Stale since 2025-07-30 (sync-call work for Antelope's node software), maintained by the EOS Network Foundation for its own chain with 5 open issues; the custom non-OSI licence and MVP-only Wasm make it a reference design rather than a general-purpose engine.

[repo](https://github.com/AntelopeIO/eos-vm) · [benchmark](https://medium.com/eosio/introducing-eosio-2-enhancing-performance-improving-security-and-new-developer-tools-38ca29c7ab4c)

##### Mitey JIT (csjh/mitey-jit)  `C++`  `no license`  `active`  `Tier C`

Experimental Arm64/macOS WebAssembly JIT with a fused validate-and-compile pass; starts big modules about 3x faster than Wasmtime.

**Beats:** wasmtime, V8 (Node.js) — Author's own blog post (csjh.blog, unreachable here; numbers relayed by search snippets) timed load+validate+instantiate with hyperfine on an M1 MacBook Air: SpiderMonkey 52.8 ms (unrolled JIT) and 65.8 ms (single-pass JIT) vs Wasmtime 183.3 ms, Wasmtime single-pass 197.4 ms and Node 66.3 ms; Figma 159.7 / 198.8 ms vs Wasmtime 710.4 ms and Node 92.5 ms. Execution (median of three): the single-pass JIT ran esbuild in 3.126 s vs Wasmtime 3.316 s and Node 3.694 s but lost to Wasmtime on Coremark and SpiderMonkey; compiler flags, Wasmtime and Node versions and Wasmtime cache settings are not known.

**Known shortcoming:** The record credited the esbuild win to the wrong backend: the unrolled JIT is 'too slow' for esbuild and the single-pass baseline backend wins it, 3.126 s vs 3.316 s Wasmtime (1.06x) and 3.694 s Node. The single-pass backend loses to Wasmtime on SpiderMonkey (347 vs 577) and Coremark. No licence file, so reference only; Arm64 macOS only; no benchmark code in the repo and the blog is blocked here.

**Known shortcoming:** Enricher: HEAD main.cpp and test/executor.cpp wire only the baseline backend; nothing includes the minimal backend and backend/current.hpp includes a missing ./arm64.hpp, so the blog's 'unrolled JIT' numbers are not reproducible from HEAD. Branch-range checks are assert-only and 2x too loose (bcond/cbz/cbnz allow under 2 MiB against a real +-1 MiB range), so an NDEBUG build would silently wrap out-of-range branches. One global 5 MB value stack, a global trap jmp_buf, process-wide SIGBUS/SIGILL handlers, no SIMD, no LICENSE, no build file. Codegen fixes landed January to February 2026 (i64.sub bug, br_table register overlap, fuzzing fixes) and the post date is unreadable, so it is unknown whether the numbers predate them.

**Independent measurement:** licence, committed harness, independent run

**Independent measurement:** reproducible build of the measured backend

**How:** Startup: validation and code generation happen in one linear pass per function (validate_and_compile), with no IR and no optimizer, which is why it beats Wasmtime's Cranelift compile on large binaries. The current 'baseline' backend is a single-pass compiler whose validation stack also tracks where each value lives (register, stack slot, immediate or condition flags): locals live in callee-saved registers, temporaries come from an LRU register cache, constants fold into immediates, and comparisons stay in flags until a branch consumes them. Bounds checks are removed by reserving 16 GiB of PROT_NONE address space per linear memory (guard regions on both sides, mprotect to grow), and stack overflow is caught by a guard page instead of per-push checks. The older 'minimal' backend emits a chain of calls into precompiled C++ handlers ([[clang::musttail]], preserve_most on cold trap paths), an unrolled interpreter.

**Use it when:**
- Research or teaching: a compact, readable single-pass Wasm-to-Arm64 compiler (register cache, flag tracking, guard-page bounds checks) to study or borrow ideas from.
- Short-lived runs of very large Wasm binaries on an Apple Silicon Mac where compile latency dominates (author's numbers: SpiderMonkey starts in 65.8 ms vs 183.3 ms for Wasmtime).
- Comparing baseline-compiler design choices against Wasmtime Winch or Cranelift on the same Arm64 machine.

**Skip it when:**
- Anything shipped: no LICENSE file (all rights reserved by default), README says 'Not meant for production use', no build file in the repo.
- Linux, Windows or x86-64: the pager uses MAP_JIT, pthread_jit_write_protect_np and SIGBUS from macOS; backend/current.hpp errors out on x86.
- Peak-throughput workloads: the single-pass backend loses to Wasmtime on Coremark (26616 vs 28260) and the SpiderMonkey score (347 vs 577); only esbuild was faster (3.126 s vs 3.316 s, 1.06x).
- Modules that use SIMD (v128 is commented out in spec.hpp), threads or multiple concurrent instances/threads (one process-wide value stack and trap jmp_buf).
- Multi-tenant or embedding hosts: it installs process-wide SIGBUS and SIGILL handlers and reserves 16 GiB of address space per memory plus 400 bytes of executable space per code-section byte.

**Vs siblings:** Pick it over Wasmi or wasm3 only to study an Arm64 single-pass JIT design, since those are portable, licensed and maintained interpreters with near-zero startup; pick WAMR or Wasmtime itself for anything that must ship. Against wisp (another baseline compiler compared with Winch and Singlepass), mitey-jit's distinctive part is guard-page bounds checks and flag/register tracking during validation on Arm64.

**Gotchas:**
- Code-reading finding: the shipped main.cpp and test/executor.cpp both include backend/arm64/baseline.hpp, and nothing includes the minimal backend (minimal.cpp, backend/minimal/composer.hpp); backend/current.hpp includes a non-existent ./arm64.hpp. The post's 'unrolled JIT' numbers are therefore not reproducible from HEAD without restoring an older wiring.
- Branch-range checks are assert()-only and twice too loose: bcond/cbz/cbnz accept byte offsets below 2 MiB although the 19-bit field reaches only +-1 MiB (b/bl accept 256 MiB vs a +-128 MiB range), and a release build with NDEBUG drops them, so a branch that is out of range would silently wrap. The minimal backend's put_br encodes stack offsets in a 9-bit field with only a comment ('should be handled better when src/dst are higher than 1<<9'). Not observed failing; it bites only very large functions or deep value stacks.
- Trap handling is longjmp out of signal handlers (SIGBUS for guard regions, SIGILL for encoded trap instructions); the handlers are installed process-wide, and the heap registry never removes freed memories, so a later SIGBUS in a reused address range could be taken for a Wasm trap.
- The JIT region is reserved as 400 bytes per code-section byte plus 400 per function, and its size is stored in a uint32_t header, so code sections above about 10.7 MB unmap only part of the region on free; the instruction cache is never invalidated after writing code (sys_icache_invalidate is commented out; the source comment reasons fresh pages cannot hold stale lines).

**Status:** Active (457 commits, last 2026-02-13, with many Jan-Feb 2026 codegen fixes such as 'fix i64sub bug', 'fix br_table to avoid temporary reg overlap' and 'fix validation bugs found by fuzzing', so the post's numbers may predate them; post date not readable here), but unlicensed and macOS-Arm64-only, so reference reading only.

[repo](https://github.com/csjh/mitey-jit) · [benchmark](https://csjh.blog/posts/a-tale-of-three-wasm-runtimes/)

#### embedded-scripting

##### Zef  `C++`  `no license`  `active`  `Tier C`

Toy AST-walking interpreter tuned with inline caches; its leaky Yolo-C++ build beats CPython 3.10 and QuickJS-ng on four benchmarks.

**Beats:** QuickJS-ng 0.14.0 (release binary qjs-linux-x86_64), Lua 5.4.7 (built with GCC 11.4.0), CPython 3.10 (Ubuntu 22.04 package) — On the author's ScriptBench1 (nbody, splay, richards, deltablue; mean wall-clock seconds over 30 interleaved runs on an Intel Core Ultra 5 135U, Ubuntu 22.04.5), the GCC 11.4.0 Yolo-C++ build's geomean was 0.0686 s against CPython 3.10 0.1296 s (1.89x faster), Lua 5.4.7 0.0577 s (1.19x slower) and QuickJS-ng 0.14.0 0.2036 s; the QuickJS-ng margin is about 1.40x once richards.js's 20 iterations are divided out (derived from page data). The memory-safe Fil-C++ 0.677 build (geomean 0.2759 s) is slower than all three baselines.

**Known shortcoming:** ScriptBench/richards.js runs runRichards() 20 times while the other language ports run it once, so the QuickJS-ng richards row is inflated about 20x; the win over QuickJS-ng is about 1.40x after correction, not 2.97x (derived from page data). The fast yoloBuild is an incomplete port that never frees memory (the author calls it unsound) built from a separate checkout of unstated revision; the memory-safe Fil-C++ build is slower than QuickJS, CPython and Lua. No licence file, so reference only. CPU Intel Core Ultra 5 135U, GCC 11.4.0.

**Known shortcoming:** Enricher: deltablue.js runs one extra projectionTest and splay.js uses Math.random() keys while the other ports use seeded xorshift; richards.lua prints FAILURE without a non-zero exit and run-benchmarks checks only exit status, so a wrong Lua result still gets timed. The Yolo-C++ build allocates through calloc and never frees (src/utils.h FIXME 'unsound'), and it beats Lua only on splay and deltablue, the allocation-heavy rows that therefore pay no GC cost. Dormant since 2026-04-22, no embedding API.

**Independent measurement:** corrected richards iteration count, licence

**Independent measurement:** like-for-like ports with result checks and a freeing build

**How:** It stays a recursive AST walker but adds the machinery a JIT would use: NaN-style tagged 64-bit values (doubles offset by 0x1000000000000, inline int32s), hash-consed Symbols instead of std::string lookups, a Storage/Offsets object model computed in a resolve pass, and inline caches implemented by placement-constructing specialized AST nodes over generic ones (constructCache<>), guarded by watchpoints for scope-chain and subclass invariants. The rest is grinding: per-operator Binary<>/Unary<> nodes, getter/setter inference, a global (class, symbol) to callee table, Zero/One/TwoArguments specializations, and constant array-literal specialization. The final 4x comes from compiling with an ordinary C++ compiler instead of Fil-C++, where GC allocations become calloc and are never freed.

**Use it when:**
- You are writing your own dynamic-language interpreter and want a worked, diff-by-diff example of inline caches and watchpoints in an AST interpreter, with measured gains per step.
- You want evidence of what each classic trick buys in an interpreter without a JIT: object model plus inline caches gave 4.55x, symbols 18%, argument specialization about 4%, per the write-up.
- Teaching or research on memory-safe C++ (Fil-C++) overheads: the write-up documents Fil-C pathologies (std::optional unions and stack Values becoming heap allocations) and their workarounds.
- Short-lived scripts in a hobby setting where a self-contained interpreter in about 100 source files is acceptable.

**Skip it when:**
- Embedding a scripting language in an application: there is no host API, no sandboxing and no documented C++ interface; Lua, Luau or QuickJS are the realistic choices.
- Any long-running workload on the fast build: the Yolo-C++ path allocates with calloc and never frees (src/utils.h marks it 'FIXME: This is unsound'), so memory grows until the process dies.
- Wanting speed with memory safety: the documented Fil-C++ build (with GC) is 2.13x slower than CPython 3.10, 4.78x slower than Lua 5.4.7 and 1.36x slower than QuickJS-ng 0.14.0 on the author's geomean.
- Anything needing a licence: the repo has no LICENSE file and the README names none, so the code cannot be reused.
- Production maturity: single-author side project, 82 commits, last commit 2026-04-22, no releases, one open issue (broken localhost links in the docs).

**Vs siblings:** Pick Zef only as reading material on interpreter optimization; for an actual embedded engine Lua or Luau (faster than Zef's fast build on nbody and richards, with an embedding API) or QuickJS (a real JS engine) win, and Daslang or LuaJIT Remake (Deegen) are the catalogued choices when interpreter speed itself is the goal.

**Gotchas:**
- Harness flaw: ScriptBench/richards.js calls runRichards() 20 times while the Zef, Lua and Python ports run it once, so QuickJS-ng's richards time (0.7193 s) covers 20x the work. Per run QuickJS-ng takes about 0.036 s vs 0.0309 s for Yolo-C++ Zef, and the headline 2.97x geomean win over QuickJS-ng shrinks to about 1.40x (derived from page data). deltablue.js also runs one extra projectionTest(100) after its 20 rounds, and splay.js keys come from Math.random() while the other ports use a seeded xorshift.
- The Yolo-C++ build never reclaims memory, and it beats Lua 5.4.7 only on splay (0.3992 vs 0.4393 s) and deltablue (0.0784 vs 0.0832 s), the two allocation-heavy rows, so those wins carry no collection cost while CPython, Lua and QuickJS-ng do collect (inference from the write-up and src/utils.h). The benchmarked binary came from a separate checkout (pizlscript/yoloBuild) whose revision is not stated.
- Result checks are uneven: ScriptBench/richards.lua tests 'qpktcount == QPKTCOUNT or holdcount == HOLDCOUNT' and only prints FAILURE without a non-zero exit, and run-benchmarks only checks exit status, so a wrong Lua result would still be timed. The Python and Zef ports do fail the run on a wrong count.
- Timing is wall-clock of the whole process via Ruby Time.now, including interpreter startup; several rows run only 14-40 ms (nbody: Lua 0.0142 s, QuickJS-ng 0.0214 s, Yolo Zef 0.0233 s), so startup compresses the ratios. The script defaults to --repeat 3; the write-up says 30 runs.

**Status:** Single-author demonstration project, dormant since 2026-04-22 after a month of commits; no licence, so reference only, and its fast configuration leaks all memory by design.

[repo](https://github.com/pizlonator/zef) · [benchmark](https://github.com/pizlonator/zef/blob/master/website/source/implementation.md)

#### jits

##### HHVM  `C++`  `PHP-3.01 AND Zend-2.0 (core); MIT (Hack typechecker and Hack Standard Library)`  `active`  `Tier C`

Meta's JIT virtual machine for Hack; reported 1.6x over the 2014-era Zend PHP interpreter on real applications.

**Beats:** PHP reference interpreter (Zend Engine), 2014-era version per the OOPSLA 2014 paper (version not seen); HPHPc as a second comparison — No numbers exist in the repo; the claim rests on search snippets of the peer-reviewed but first-party OOPSLA 2014 paper: HHVM about 1.6x faster than the PHP (Zend) interpreter of that time on real-world applications in sandbox mode, and 2.64x (sandbox) and 2.79x (production) geometric-mean speedups on its benchmark suite against 1.93x for the earlier HPHPc static compiler; PHP version, hardware and flags were not visible. A later first-party figure (PLDI 2018, snippet) is a 21.7% gain on the Facebook website from the region-based PGO JIT over HHVM's earlier tracelet JIT.

**Known shortcoming:** Raised D to C on the OOPSLA 2014 abstract (1.6x over PHP on real-world apps in sandbox mode), snippet only since the paper is blocked; the baseline is 2014 PHP and current HHVM runs Hack only. Zend-2.0 licence is not OSI-approved, so usability is mixed. Off-baseline.
