For production use, the vkrasnov AVX2 fork, httparse or httpp (about 2.26x at -O3) have stronger benchmark evidence and more complete APIs.

**Gotchas:**
- Header-array overflow: parseRequest ignores params.num_headers and slices the many-item pointer as headers[0..100]. A request with more headers than your array writes past its end, and Zig cannot bounds-check a [*]T slice in any build mode. The repo's own bench and a zig-httpuring test pass 32 slots, and test.zig passes 4-14. Always supply at least 100
- Looser than picohttpparser on the request line. test.zig asserts success for an empty method (' / HTTP/1.0') and an empty target ('GET  HTTP/1.0'), where upstream test.c expects -1. The method is not checked against token characters, so ':GET' is accepted. Multiple spaces between tokens, which upstream accepts, are rejected
- Header values keep trailing spaces and tabs (upstream trims them). A request whose final empty line is a lone LF at the end of the buffer returns -2 (incomplete) until more bytes arrive. test.zig asserts this for 'GET / HTTP/1.0\nHost: example.com\n\n'
- HttpRequest.body is never filled in. Errors come back only as i32 codes, because the internal ParseError is not surfaced. The bundled response formatter heap-allocates a StringHashMap and an ArrayList for every response

**Status:** Counts as active under the 12-month rule (last commit 2025-10-11, a port to Zig 0.15.1). In practice it is a 9-commit, single-author, unlicensed side project that only the author's own repos use (zig-httpuring and buddy-blocks, via a relative ../zig-pico path), so treat it as reference code rather than a dependency.

[repo](https://github.com/solenopsys/zig-pico) · [benchmark](https://github.com/solenopsys/zig-pico/blob/master/readme.md)

##### SynapServe  `Rust`  `no license`  `unknown`  `Tier C`

Closed-source zero-allocation Rust HTTP/1.1 parser inside the SynapServe io_uring server; claims 1.11-1.25x faster tokenization than httparse.

**Beats:** httparse — First-party Criterion runs (100 samples, single core) against httparse 1.10 on three synthetic requests, where SynapServe also extracts content_length, chunked and keep_alive: 42 vs 52 ns at 35 B, 200 vs 230 ns at 368 B and 420 vs 466 ns at 733 B (1.25x/1.15x/1.11x). With a matching extraction loop added to httparse it is 220 vs 304 ns and 413 vs 604 ns (1.38x/1.46x), and known-header lookup is about 0.6 ns vs 20.5-23.1 ns. No CPU, OS, rustc version, flags or benchmark code is given for these parser runs; the site's separate static-file server benchmark ran on an Intel i7-8550U laptop under Linux 6.17.

**Known shortcoming:** No code and no licence: the SynapServe GitHub org (created 2026-02-20) has 0 public repos, no crates.io crate, 'All rights reserved' footer, and the benchmark crate the founder mentioned on HN was never published. The page misdescribes the baseline: httparse 1.10 selects AVX2/SSE4.2 at runtime and enables NEON on aarch64, not 'SSE4.2 compile-time only'. Internal inconsistencies (medium request 200 vs 220 ns; large request faster with extraction than without; response-writer claims with no baseline numbers). The 1.38-1.46x relies on an unpublished extraction loop added to httparse; raw parsing alone is 1.11-1.25x. No CPU, OS, rustc or flags for the parser runs. O(1) lookup covers only 21 unpublished headers; 64 KB header cap and 64-header table; 'not production-battle-tested', no fuzzing documented; server Linux-only (io_uring, 6.1+). Only activity: one blog post (2026-02-21) and a Show HN; solo founder's pitch site, partly AI-generated per the founder. Design reference only.

**How:** The output is compact. Fields are Span{off: u16, len: u16} (4 bytes, Copy), so a header entry is 10 bytes in a [Header; 64] stack table (640 bytes) instead of httparse's 32-byte &str/&[u8] pairs, and a reset clears 29 bytes instead of re-initializing a 2 KB header array. Scanning uses hand-written SIMD with runtime dispatch (AVX2 or SSE4.2 on x86-64, NEON on aarch64, SWAR elsewhere), memchr for delimiters, and fused passes: the CRLF search also rejects NUL and bare CR, and tchar validation of header names runs in the same loop as the colon search. Known headers are recognized by length, then first byte, then word-sized compares (u64/u32 with |0x20 case folding), and recorded in a u32 presence bitmap plus a known_index[21] array, so a lookup is one bit test and one array load instead of a case-insensitive linear scan.

**Use it when:**
- As a design reference for your own Rust HTTP/1.1 front end: u16 span output, a parse-time known-header bitmap index, and fused CRLF plus validation scans are the ideas worth copying.
- If you get the code from the vendor and every request handler checks the same few headers (Content-Length, Transfer-Encoding, Connection, Host). The page reports 0.59-0.67 ns vs 20.5-23.1 ns per lookup and 60-112 ns saved per handler, which is more than the parse gain.
- Small-to-medium request heads (35-733 B tested, 1-20 headers) where you would otherwise parse with httparse and then loop over the headers to find framing fields.
- Evaluating SynapServe itself as a Linux (kernel 6.1+) io_uring HTTP/1.1 server or reverse proxy, since the parser ships only inside it.

**Skip it when:**
- You need a dependency now: there is no public repo (the GitHub org, created 2026-02-20, has 0 public repositories), no crate on crates.io under any synapserve name, and no named license. The site promises an open-source core but its footer says 'All rights reserved'.
- Request heads over 64 KB or more than 64 headers: the founder calls the 64 KB header area, which follows from the u16 spans, a hard limit, and the header table is [Header; 64]. Neither case's behavior is documented.
- You need httparse's API inside hyper, axum or actix-web: the output type is different (buffer-relative spans, not slices), and nothing can be linked anyway.
- You need reproducible numbers: the page gives no benchmark code, CPU, OS, rustc version or flags for the parser runs. The honest parse-only gain is 1.11-1.25x, and the 1.38-1.46x figure depends on an unpublished extraction loop the author bolted onto httparse.
- Security-sensitive or production parsing: the founder says it is 'not production-battle-tested', and no fuzzing, conformance testing or request-smuggling handling (e.g. Content-Length plus Transfer-Encoding conflicts) is documented.

**Vs siblings:** In practice, never as a dependency. httparse (catalogued, the baseline here) is what you would actually ship, and thhp and picohttpparser-rs are public Rust parsers with code you can benchmark yourself. SynapServe is only worth reading for its parse-time header index and fused semantic extraction, which none of those siblings do.

**Gotchas:**
- The comparison table misstates the baseline. It lists httparse SIMD as 'SSE4.2 (compile-time only)', but in httparse 1.10's default std build src/simd/runtime.rs picks AVX2 or SSE4.2 at runtime via is_x86_feature_detected!, and build.rs turns on NEON for aarch64 with rustc 1.59+.
- The numbers do not agree with each other. The medium request parses in 200 ns in the tokenize chart but 220 ns in the equal-work chart. The large request takes 420 ns alone but 413 ns with extraction. The 'Response writer: 46% faster' heading and the '1.38-1.40x on responses' claim come with no baseline numbers, only absolute times (3.9 / 33.5 / 41.3 ns).
- O(1) lookup covers only the 21 headers recognized during parsing, and the list is not published (the benchmark shows it includes Content-Type, Content-Length and X-Request-Id). Lookup cost for any other header is not documented.
- Zero allocations is not a difference from the baseline: httparse also never allocates (the caller provides the header array), as the page's own table says. The real differences are entry size (10 vs 32 bytes) and reset cost.

**Status:** Usable only as a reference. The GitHub org has been empty since 2026-02-20, nothing is on crates.io, and the license is unknown despite the promised open-source core. The only activity is a Feb 2026 blog post and a Show HN (2 points), and the roadmap on the site still lists its Q1 2026 milestone as in progress, so maintenance status is unknown for a solo-founder startup seeking seed funding.

[benchmark](https://synapserve.io/posts/http-parser-performance/)

#### http-servers-frameworks

##### uhttp (io_uring-http-benchmark)  `C++`  `no license`  `active`  `Tier C`

Single-route io_uring static HTTP server in C++20; 40-54% more req/s than tuned nginx serving one 10 KB file on loopback.

**Beats:** nginx — On loopback, with 2 server workers pinned to 2 physical cores of an unnamed 8-core SMT 'mobile CPU' and wrk on the other 6, uhttp served a 10,240-byte file at 276-358k req/s against 184-256k for tuned nginx (reuseport, sendfile on or off, open_file_cache, logging off, same cores), +40% to +54% at 64-4,096 connections, as medians of 3 interleaved 45 s runs after a 15 s warmup. The build was CMake Release (-O3 -march=native, LTO) on a kernel with CONFIG_INIT_ON_ALLOC_DEFAULT_ON=y; compiler, kernel, nginx and wrk versions are not stated, and the raw CSVs are gitignored, so only the README's medians are published.

**Known shortcoming:** A benchmark server, not a library: serves one route from memory; nginx has the better p99 at 64 connections. No licence (reference only).

**Known shortcoming:** No LICENSE file (reference only); two commits on 2026-08-17, no tests or CI. CMake accepts liburing 2.5 but the code calls io_uring_register_napi(), which needs 2.6; DEFER_TASKRUN needs Linux 6.1+ (undocumented). More than 32 pipelined requests in one write may stall (code reading). ETag/Last-Modified/Accept-Ranges are sent but conditional and Range requests are ignored; the file is read once at startup. Serves GET on one exact path, IPv4 only, no timeouts, TLS, HTTP/2, bodies or logging. Loopback-only numbers without CPU, compiler, kernel, nginx or wrk versions; raw CSVs gitignored; -march=native; results bimodal run to run (~350k vs ~389k). bench/tune_system.sh lowers perf_event_paranoid and kptr_restrict system-wide until restored. nginx has the better p99 at 64 connections and higher IPC.

**How:** Shared-nothing worker threads each own one io_uring ring (SINGLE_ISSUER + DEFER_TASKRUN, registered ring fd, CQ 4x the SQ) and use multishot accept into direct (fixed-file) descriptors plus multishot recv over a provided buffer ring, so a connection is accepted and read repeatedly without new submissions and completions are drained and acknowledged in batches. Each response is pre-serialised into one buffer, kept as two copies so only the Date field is patched once a second; SO_REUSEPORT with a classic-BPF steering program keeps each connection on the core that handled its SYN; and per-connection state is a packed 20-byte struct. perf puts syscall entry/exit at 0.07% of uhttp's cycles against 8.71% for nginx, and instructions per request at 17,583 vs 35,831. nginx still has the higher IPC (0.86 vs 0.64), so the author's own summary is that the gain comes from doing less work, not from doing it faster.

**Use it when:**
- Learning or prototyping io_uring networking: a small C++20 codebase (about 1,400 lines in src/) that shows multishot accept/recv, provided buffer rings, direct descriptors, DEFER_TASKRUN and generation-tagged user_data for recycled descriptor slots.
- Measuring io_uring against nginx on your own kernel and hardware: the harness interleaves targets, gives the client 3x the server's cores, flags client-bound runs and reports server CPU microseconds per request.
- A synthetic load-test target that must return one small fixed response at very high request rates on Linux 6.1+ where you control both ends.
- Ablation studies: structural io_uring options are compile-time switches in src/config.hpp and bench/ablation.sh rebuilds and measures each one.

**Skip it when:**
- Serving a real site or directory: one route, one file read at startup, GET only, exact path match (a query string gets 404), no MIME mapping, index files, Range or conditional requests.
- Anything that needs TLS, HTTP/2 or HTTP/3, request bodies, access logging, config reload, IPv6 (the listener is AF_INET only) or idle/read timeouts; none are implemented, so idle or slow clients hold connection slots (default 4,096 per worker) indefinitely.
- Shipping or vendoring code: there is no LICENSE file, and the repo has two commits (both 2026-08-17), no tests, no CI and 0 stars.
- Low-concurrency tail-latency work: nginx had the better p99 at 64 connections (333 us vs 360 us).
- As evidence that io_uring beats sendfile on a real network: every number is loopback, where nginx's sendfile zero-copy path gives no benefit, and the author says the NIC case was not tested.

**Vs siblings:** Pick it over epoll-httpd when the question is specifically io_uring versus nginx's epoll model at 64-4,096 connections with perf-level attribution; epoll-httpd is the better base for real code because it is MIT-licensed and serves arbitrary files. For serving actual traffic, use H2O (static files, TLS, HTTP/2/3) or Sogou Workflow (C++ backend) instead.

**Gotchas:**
- Build floor is wrong: CMakeLists.txt accepts liburing >= 2.5, but server.cpp calls io_uring_register_napi(), which first appears in liburing 2.6's header (the 2.6 CHANGELOG adds NAPI busy-poll support), so a build against 2.5 should fail to compile.
- Pipelining is capped at 32 queued responses per connection. From reading server.cpp, bytes beyond that are carried over and only parsed when the next recv completes, so a client that pipelines more than 32 requests in one write and then waits for all of them can stall.
- It sends ETag, Last-Modified and 'Accept-Ranges: bytes' to match nginx's headers, but ignores If-None-Match, If-Modified-Since and Range and always returns a full 200. The file is never re-read, so edits need a restart.
- The harness's `sudo bench/tune_system.sh apply` sets kernel.perf_event_paranoid=-1 and kernel.kptr_restrict=0 system-wide (plus the performance governor and larger backlogs) until you run `restore`.

**Status:** A one-shot research dump (two commits on 2026-08-17, none since, no issues, releases or stars) with no LICENSE file, so it is reference-only: read it to learn the io_uring techniques, but do not copy or vendor it.

[repo](https://github.com/SquiggleKernel/io_uring-http-benchmark) · [benchmark](https://github.com/SquiggleKernel/io_uring-http-benchmark/blob/main/README.md)

#### websocket-grpc-rpc

##### Courierust  `Rust`  `PolyForm-Perimeter-1.0.1`  `active`  `Tier C`

Zero-dependency Rust HTTP/WebSocket stack; its WebSocket codec encodes small masked frames ~2.5x faster than tungstenite.

**Beats:** tokio-tungstenite / tungstenite — WS_BENCHMARK.md reports one `cargo bench` release run (thin LTO, codegen-units=1) on a shared Windows machine with no CPU model or rustc version, against tungstenite 0.30 and tokio-tungstenite 0.30 in the same process: masked encode 15.2 vs 40.0 ns at 64 B, 9.5 vs 90-99 us at 256 KiB and parity at 16 KiB; loopback echo at 64 B is 26.5 us against 37.2 us for tokio-tungstenite (2 worker threads) and 26.5 us for sync tungstenite. The repo's own Linux CI report (commit d7d52b3, complexity bench) shows smaller or reversed codec gaps: 64 B masked encode 32.8 vs 40.8 ns (1.24x) and 256 KiB masked encode 100.0 vs 20.5 us (4.9x slower), in a noisy run.

**Known shortcoming:** The repo's own Linux CI run does not reproduce the codec claims: 64 B masked encode only 1.24x (claimed 2.6x) and 256 KiB masked encode 4.9x slower (claimed ~10x faster); headline speedups come from one Windows run. Echo and push benchmarks use the deprecated one-job-per-connection server path (event_driven: false), not the default. The echo win over tokio-tungstenite is sync vs async; sync tungstenite ties it. The UTF-8 loss row is stale (now at parity). The CI has no performance thresholds despite the README. Loses 256 KiB echo (297.6 vs 165.0 us) and 16 KiB echo (9%) to tungstenite. PolyForm Perimeter 1.0.1 licence (noncompete, not OSI) with an extra term. Blocking API only (select/poll), no RFC 8441. First published 2026-08, 5 stars. Filed under WebSocket: it is an HTTP/TLS/gRPC/WebSocket stack, not an event loop.

**How:** Masking XORs 16-byte lanes against one precomputed u128 per key phase: 16 is a multiple of the 4-byte key, so every lane starts at the same phase and the loop autovectorizes in safe Rust (25-37 GB/s on the page). The per-byte `i & 3` key lookup does not vectorize. The masked writer masks in place into a reused staging buffer, while tungstenite 0.30's masked `format` allocates and masks a new copy of the payload for every frame. Other techniques: frames up to 64 KiB go out in one write syscall, payloads over 8 KiB are read straight into the message buffer, and the DEFLATE match-finder tables are reused for each message. The echo win over tokio-tungstenite comes from blocking threads against a 2-worker Tokio runtime, not from the codec, because sync tungstenite ties it (26.5 vs 26.5 us at 64 B).

**Use it when:**
- WebSocket clients that send many small masked frames (64 B-1 KiB) and where the CPU cost per frame matters: the page shows 15.2 vs 40.0 ns at 64 B and 1.3-1.5x at 1 KiB
- Client uploads of large masked messages where allocation churn matters: courierust allocates 0 bytes per masked frame, while tungstenite allocates a full copy of the payload (1 MiB per 1 MiB message)
- Threaded or blocking Rust programs outside Tokio that need lower small-message latency than tokio-tungstenite: 64 B echo 26.5 vs 37.2 us and 1 KiB echo 26.6 vs 39.0 us, the same as sync tungstenite
- Builds that need a dependency-free or no_std + alloc WebSocket framing core, with strict RFC 6455 validation and incremental UTF-8 checks across fragments
- Programs already on Courierust's HTTP server that need WebSocket on the same port; in the event-driven driver an idle socket costs a poller slot, not a thread

**Skip it when:**
- Async or Tokio code (axum, hyper, tokio-tungstenite users): there is no Future/Stream API, and the benchmark win against tokio-tungstenite is sync against async, not codec against codec
- Bulk transfers of 256 KiB or more with Courierust at both ends: echo is 297.6 vs 165.0 us for tungstenite, and 16 KiB echo is 9% behind (39.3 vs 35.8 us)
- Any product that could compete with Courierust: PolyForm Perimeter 1.0.1 has a noncompete clause and is not OSI-approved, so many OSS distributions and commercial networking products cannot ship it
- WebSocket over HTTP/2 (RFC 8441) is not implemented. The encoder never uses context takeover, so compression ratio is lower on streams of small repetitive messages
- Risk-averse production: the crate was first published 2026-08-21, has 5 stars, 990 crates.io downloads and no issues filed, and its TLS stack is from scratch with no documented third-party audit. Readiness uses select/poll only, and no epoll/kqueue/io_uring backend is documented

**Vs siblings:** Among the siblings, uWebSockets (C++) is the WebSocket server to pick for raw server throughput. monoio or ringline are the picks when the Tokio runtime itself is the bottleneck, which is most of the gap measured here against tokio-tungstenite. Pick Courierust only for a dependency-free, blocking Rust WebSocket client or server where masked-encode cost and allocation per frame matter and the PolyForm license is acceptable.

**Gotchas:**
- The echo and push benchmarks start the server with `event_driven: false`. The README calls this one-job-per-connection model deprecated for production, so the default event-driven server path was not measured
- On Windows, the client keeps `ClientConfig::read_timeout` (30 s by default) armed as SO_RCVTIMEO. The authors measured this at about 2x slower on 256 KiB bulk transfers; for bulk use, set `read_timeout: None` and rely on ping keepalive
- In the event-driven driver, a bulk push loop inside `on_message` blocks the reactor worker, and the bounded send queue then closes the connection. Push fan-out from another thread with `WsConn::sender()`
- The UTF-8 loss row in WS_BENCHMARK.md (1.9x slower than std) is stale. utf8.rs now hands the bulk scan to core::str::from_utf8, and COMPLEXITY.md reports 891.5 vs 890.3 ns (Windows); the Linux CI report gives a ratio of 1.04

**Status:** Actively developed: last commit 2026-09-15, 1.0.7 on crates.io (main is at 1.0.8) and a CI bench/interop/fuzz suite. Its PolyForm Perimeter 1.0.1 license bars competing products, so treat it as reference code to study unless your use clearly does not compete.

[repo](https://github.com/blueokanna/Courierust) · [benchmark](https://github.com/blueokanna/Courierust/blob/main/benches/WS_BENCHMARK.md)

##### grpc_homa (Homa transport plugin for gRPC)  `C++`  `no license`  `stale`  `Tier C`

gRPC C++ transport plugin that replaces HTTP/2-over-TCP with the Homa kernel RPC protocol; reports ~40% lower short-RPC round-trip time.

**Beats:** gRPC (default TCP transport) — The README's 'initial performance measurements' put a short gRPC RPC at about 55 us round trip over Homa versus about 90 us over the stock TCP transport (~40% faster), with no hardware, NIC, kernel, compiler, load level or method given; the repo's rtt test (a mean over 50,000 sequential unary Sum calls on one client thread) is not tied to those numbers. On the Homa wiki the author separately puts ~60 us of an unloaded small gRPC round trip in gRPC software and ~30 us in TCP plus the network, which suggests the remaining 55 us is mostly gRPC itself and that Homa's tail-latency-under-load advantage was not measured here.

**Known shortcoming:** The ~40% (55 vs 90 us) claim gives no hardware or method; development was suspended in late 2023; insecure channels only; the C++ code has no licence (reference only).

**Known shortcoming:** The author suspended work and does not recommend using it (#17, 2025). Open bugs: release-only segfault in BuildAndStart (#15), Homa RPC timeouts where TCP works (#16). A burst of outstanding RPCs exhausted kernel memory and hung a host (#14). Compiles against internal gRPC src/core headers with branches only for gRPC 1.41/1.43/1.57, and HomaModule has changed incompatibly since. Makefile hard-codes the author's paths; x86-64 only (rdtsc); insecure channels only. Homa messages capped at 1 MB, oversized metadata fails the RPC. The 55 vs 90 us figure has no hardware, kernel, NIC or load stated and is a mean over sequential unary calls; tail latency under load, Homa's main claim, is not measured. No licence for the C++ code.

**How:** Homa is a connectionless, message-based datacenter transport. A sender transmits the first rtt_bytes of a message at once as 'unscheduled' bytes. After that, the receiver sends GRANT packets that pace the rest of the message and set its network priority, so a short RPC needs no handshake and has no byte-stream head-of-line blocking. The plugin drops HTTP/2 framing for a packed 21-byte header (stream id, sequence number, metadata and body lengths, flags), sends gRPC slices through one gathered sendmsg iovec, and hands gRPC received slices that point into a kernel-shared mmapped buffer (SO_HOMA_RCVBUF), so contiguous payloads are not copied.

**Use it when:**
- Research or prototyping on Linux clusters where you control the kernel and can load HomaModule on every client and server host.
- Unary gRPC C++ services with small messages inside one datacenter, where tens of microseconds per round trip matter.
- Measuring how much of gRPC's round-trip time comes from TCP. The bundled test_client 'rtt' test runs over Homa, or over TCP with --tcp.
- As a starting point for reviving Homa support in gRPC, if you can build gRPC 1.57.0 from source and are ready to own the code.

**Skip it when:**
- When you need TLS or per-call auth: only insecure channel and server credentials exist.
- In production. The author suspended work in late 2023, and in 2025 (issue #17) he wrote that he does not recommend anyone try to use it. Open issues include a release-build segfault in BuildAndStart (#15) and Homa RPC timeouts on a setup where TCP works (#16).
- Across data centers, on mixed or public networks, on non-Linux hosts, or on managed platforms where you cannot load a custom kernel module on both ends.
- For bursty servers with many outstanding RPCs. Issue #14 reports kernel memory exhaustion that hung the host, and the author said poor application behavior can exhaust Homa kernel resources.
- For Java or other gRPC languages: Java support is only partly done, and the C++ code compiles against gRPC 1.57.0 internals, so newer gRPC releases are untested.

**Vs siblings:** Pick this only if you must keep the gRPC C++ API and want the transport itself to cut small-RPC latency. brpc, grpcxx and Kitex beat gRPC in user space over plain TCP, need no kernel module and are maintained, while this plugin is only the gRPC front end for the catalogued HomaModule, so every gain depends on that driver.

**Gotchas:**
- The Makefile hard-codes the author's paths (HOMA_DIR, GRPC_INSTALL_DIR), so you must edit it by hand; there is no CMake or Bazel build.
- It tracks two moving targets: gRPC internals (branches exist only for gRPC 1.41.0, 1.43.0 and 1.57.0) and the HomaModule API. The last commit (Aug 2025) says 'Homa API has gone through several incompatible changes', and HomaModule has changed since, including a protocol change in Sept 2026.
- Homa messages are capped at 1,000,000 bytes (HOMA_MAX_MESSAGE_LENGTH). Larger gRPC messages are split across several Homa messages, and initial or trailing metadata that does not fit in one Homa message fails the RPC.
- Each socket mmaps a 1000 x 64 KB (~64 MB) receive-buffer region. A server that leaves many RPCs outstanding can exhaust Homa kernel memory (issue #14).

**Status:** Stale: work stopped in late 2023 and the last commit (Aug 2025) only ported the code to the Homa API of that time; the C++ code has no LICENSE file or license headers, so treat it as reference only, not something to vendor.

[repo](https://github.com/PlatformLab/grpc_homa) · [benchmark](https://github.com/PlatformLab/grpc_homa)

### numerics-and-science

#### autodiff-and-ml-kernels

##### CodeJeNN (Keras-to-C++ inference header generator)  `C++ (generated); generator in Python`  `NRL Open License Agreement (custom, non-OSI)`  `active`  `Tier C`

Python tool that turns a trained Keras MLP/CNN into one dependency-free C++ header; snippet-reported 2-25x over Keras eager on one core.

**Beats:** Keras eager-mode inference (TensorFlow backend for the MLP case, PyTorch backend for the CNN case) — The repo's speed test (tutorials/06_speed_test) times 10,000 single-sample calls of a small MLP and CNN in Keras eager or JIT mode against the generated C++ (g++-15 -O3 -march=native -ffast-math, one thread, MacBook M1 Pro) but publishes no numbers. The figures come only from search snippets of arXiv 2607.02746: MLP 0.48 s vs 12.01 s Keras/TensorFlow eager (about 25x) and 1.21 s with JIT (about 2.5x), CNN 1.05 s vs 19.14 s eager (about 18x) and 2.17 s JIT (about 2.1x). The C++ timing loop discards outputs, and the measured models hit the stale-output code path described above.

**Known shortcoming:** Numbers from an arXiv snippet only (MLP 0.48 s vs 12.01 s eager and 1.21 s JIT; CNN 1.05 s vs 19.14 s and 2.17 s JIT); the 38x CNN figure is not confirmed. README backend labels contradict test.py. NRL licence is non-OSI, so reference only.

**Known shortcoming:** Correctness bug: code_generate.py emits `static std::array<Scalar,N> model_output = layer_K_output;` for 1-D outputs without output normalization; a static local initialises once, so every call after the first returns the first result. Both speed-test models (MLP 1000->100, CNN ->100) take this path, and test.cpp discards results while --debug calls the model once, so neither catches it; whether the timed loop still does the work (or is optimised away) is unproven without a build. Every layer buffer is a function-local static (not thread-safe). src/generate.sh passes --double, which main.py's argparse lacks.

**Independent measurement:** verifier

**Independent measurement:** enrichment

**How:** It removes the framework entirely: no Python dispatch, no tensor allocation and no graph runtime per call, which is what dominates single-sample inference of small models in Keras eager mode. Weights are emitted as constexpr std::array literals, layers are small inline function templates (a plain scalar dot-product loop for Dense) with activations passed as lambdas so the compiler can inline everything, and intermediate buffers are preallocated function-local statics. The README says vectorization and threading are deliberately left out, on the assumption that the host solver is already parallel.

**Use it when:**
- Calling a small Keras-trained MLP or CNN once per cell or per sample inside a C++ physics or CFD code, where linking TensorFlow, libtorch or ONNX Runtime is unwanted
- Single-sample, single-thread latency on CPU with models small enough that the weight arrays stay in cache (the speed test uses a 1000-64-32-100 MLP and a 10x100 input CNN)
- Supported layer sets only: Dense, Conv1D/2D/3D and their transposes, separable and depthwise conv, pooling, Batch/Layer/Unit/Group normalization, Reshape/Flatten/Rescaling, common activations
- Research or government projects that can accept the NRL Open License Agreement

**Skip it when:**
- Calling the generated function more than once with a 1-D output and no output normalization file: the generator emits `static std::array<Scalar, N> model_output = layer_K_output;`, a static local initialized only on the first call, so every later call returns the first result (this is the configuration of both speed-test models)
- Multithreaded callers: every layer buffer and the output are function-local statics, so concurrent calls from OpenMP or MPI+threads code race
- Large models or batched throughput: Dense is an unvectorized scalar loop with strided weight access, the README warns large static arrays make it memory-bandwidth bound, and against Keras JIT the snippet-reported gain is only about 2-2.5x
- Recurrent, attention or multi-input/multi-output models: only single-input, single-output sequential or functional MLP/CNN graphs are supported (ConvLSTM2D is commented out)
- Projects needing an OSI license: the NRL agreement restricts redistribution to its own terms, takes an irrevocable grant-back of modifications to the US Government, and can be terminated by the Government

**Vs siblings:** RTNeural is the catalogued alternative for small-model C++ inference, with measured comparisons against libtorch, ONNX Runtime and TensorFlow Lite; pick CodeJeNN only when you want a single dependency-free header generated straight from a Keras .h5/.keras file, including 3D and transposed convolutions, and can accept the NRL license and fix the static-buffer issues. Kaoken and tiny-ml-runtime take the same baked-weights approach for other model types.

**Gotchas:**
- Stale-output bug: with a 1-D output and no output_*.npy normalization files, the returned array is a static initialized once, so results after the first call are wrong; the --debug comparison calls the model once and does not catch it, and the speed test discards results
- Weights are non-static constexpr locals inside the inline function; for large models check stack use and code size, since the compiler may materialize them per call
- Custom activations need a hand-written C++ version pasted into the header; until then the header prints 'WARNING: CUSTOM ACTIVATION HAS NOT BEEN IMPLEMENTED' on every call
- Docs disagree with the scripts: the speed-test readme says the CNN used PyTorch and the MLP TensorFlow, but the checked-in test.py files set the opposite; src/generate.sh passes --double, which main.py's argparse does not define (it takes --bit=32|64), so the shipped default script should exit with an unrecognized-argument error

**Status:** A single-commit code drop (2026-06-22, 'final draft for paper') from a US Naval Research Laboratory project with 1 star; the NRL Open License makes it reference-only for this catalog, and the generated header may count as a derivative work under that agreement.

[repo](https://github.com/jarcities/codejenn) · [benchmark](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/jarcities/codejenn/HEAD/tutorials/06_speed_test/readme.md)

##### cuEquivariance  `Python (frontends; CUDA kernels ship as separate pip packages)`  `Apache-2.0`  `active`  `Tier C`

NVIDIA's CUDA kernels for equivariant tensor products (MACE, NequIP, Allegro); an independent study puts MACE inference about 3x faster than e3nn.

**Beats:** e3nn (PyTorch equivariant tensor products for MACE, NequIP and similar models) — An independent preprint (arXiv 2510.23621, 'Speeding Up MACE', read only as a search snippet) profiles MACE end to end and finds the cuEquivariance backend cuts inference latency by about 3x versus e3nn, with roughly 4x more from casting linear layers to BF16/FP16. GPU, compiler and exact model size were not visible. The repo's own tutorial times e3nn against cuEquivariance (1000 nodes, 10000 edges, multiplicity 128, FP32) but stores no output.

**Known shortcoming:** Raised D to C on the abstract of an independent arXiv 2510.23621 (about 3x MACE inference latency vs e3nn), seen only as a snippet. The kernel pip package ships under NVIDIA's proprietary Math Libraries SDK license, so usability stays mixed.

**Known shortcoming:** The kernel wheels are proprietary binaries (NVIDIA Math Libraries SDK license forbids reverse engineering and derivative works); the README says Beta and releases 0.4.0 and 0.9.0 broke the API. uniform_1d/fused_tp compute only in FP32/FP64; the tutorial says linear layers get no large speedup and issue #45 found no gain over e3nn for a 3000x0e linear; issue #244 open: out of shared memory on Blackwell at embedding size 128. The 3x MACE figure (arXiv 2510.23621) stays snippet-only, and the snippet attributes about 4x more to BF16/FP16 linear layers.

**Independent measurement:** verifier

**Independent measurement:** enricher

**How:** Every supported operation is lowered to one segmented-polynomial descriptor and run by a JIT-compiled 'uniform_1d' CUDA kernel (or fused_tp / indexed_linear kernels) instead of e3nn's chain of small PyTorch ops. The uniform_1d kernel fuses the gather of sender features and the scatter-add of messages into the tensor-product call, so the edge-sized intermediates of the e3nn message-passing path are not written to memory. It uses an ir_mul (component-major) layout so channels are contiguous, and indexed linear layers (per-species weights) run as one kernel instead of e3nn's FullyConnectedTensorProduct against a one-hot vector.

**Use it when:**
- Inference or training of MACE-style interatomic potentials on NVIDIA GPUs, where MACE already exposes cuEquivariance as a backend
- Large graphs (thousands of nodes, tens of thousands of edges) with multiplicities around 128, where the tutorial says the kernels do best
- Message-passing layers where you can fuse gather, channelwise tensor product and scatter into one uniform_1d call
- Symmetric contraction and per-species (indexed) linear layers in MACE's product basis and skip connections
- Protein-structure models (OpenFold3/Boltz-style) that need triangle attention or triangle multiplication on Ampere through Blackwell

**Skip it when:**
- You need AMD GPUs, CPUs or source-level control of the kernels: the kernel wheels are NVIDIA-only binaries under a proprietary license, and the open-source OpenEquivariance covers AMD and is BSD-3
- Plain equivariant linear layers or scalar-only irreps: the tutorial says it does 'not provide a large speedup' there, and issue #45 reported no gain over e3nn for a 3000x0e linear case
- Small inputs: the tutorial says the kernels do best on very large inputs, and triangle kernels fall back to PyTorch below sequence length 100 by default
- Code that must stay in e3nn's mul_ir layout end to end: each TransposeIrrepsLayout call costs time, which the tutorial calls 'quite expensive'
- Production code that cannot absorb API breaks: the README says Beta, and 0.4.0 and 0.9.0 removed or renamed public classes

**Vs siblings:** Pick cuEquivariance over OpenEquivariance when you run MACE or AlphaFold-style models on NVIDIA hardware and want the vendor-maintained backend with JAX bindings and triangle kernels. OpenEquivariance claims parity with it, is BSD-3 and runs on AMD. batmobile's 11.8x-20x e3nn numbers come from a much smaller single-author kernel set.

**Gotchas:**
- uniform_1d and fused_tp compute only in FP32 or FP64; FP16/BF16 inputs are upcast to FP32 math unless you choose another method.
- The triangle-multiplication Triton kernels can run ahead-of-time tuning that 'may take several hours'; the cache lives in ~/.cache/cuequivariance-triton and is lost on container restart unless it is persisted.
- Open issue #244 reports out-of-shared-memory failures on Blackwell at embedding size 128, and 0.9.1 fixed an index overflow in uniform_1d at large index values; 0.9.1 also turned parallel kernel compilation off by default after multi-GPU problems.
- Deprecated primitives (TensorProduct, EquivariantTensorProduct, SymmetricTensorProduct) raise ImportError since 0.9.0; use SegmentedPolynomial or the high-level modules.

**Status:** Actively developed by NVIDIA (0.12.0 on PyPI 2026-09-23, roughly monthly releases) and still labelled Beta; the Apache-2.0 Python frontends are usable, but the speed comes from closed binary kernel wheels under the NVIDIA Math Libraries SDK license, which forbids reverse engineering and derivative works, so usability is mixed.

[repo](https://github.com/NVIDIA/cuEquivariance) · [benchmark](https://arxiv.org/abs/2510.23621)

##### learn-cuda attention (hand-written SM120 flash attention)  `CUDA C++ with inline PTX (PyTorch harness)`  `no license`  `active`  `Tier C`

Educational ~300-line CUDA C++ FlashAttention-2 forward kernel; 4-6% faster than flash-attn on one RTX 5090 shape, 3% slower than cuDNN.

**Beats:** flash-attn (FlashAttention-2 package) and PyTorch F.sdpa FlashAttention backend; PyTorch F.sdpa cuDNN backend is NOT beaten — On one RTX 5090 capped at 400W (CUDA 12.9, bf16, head_dim 128, 8 heads, 4096 queries x 8192 keys, non-causal), the author's harness timed v5 at 197.74 TFLOPS (median from triton do_bench), against 190.58 for the flash-attn package (about 1.04x) and 186.73 for PyTorch SDPA's FlashAttention backend (about 1.06x), but behind SDPA's cuDNN backend at 203.61 TFLOPS (about 0.97x). PyTorch and flash-attn versions and the host CPU are not stated.

**Known shortcoming:** Slower than cuDNN SDPA (197.74 vs 203.61 TFLOPS); learning repo with no license.

**Known shortcoming:** Correctness: no tail handling or KV masking, so sequence lengths not divisible by 64 read out of bounds and give wrong output; head_dim != 128 calls exit(1); no dtype or contiguity checks. Launches on the default stream, not torch's current stream. Uses sm80 mma.sync PTX with nothing SM120-specific, so 'SM120 flash attention' overstates it. No licence.

**Independent measurement:** enrichment

**How:** FlashAttention-2 partitioning: each 128-thread block owns a 64-row query tile, the four warps split those rows, and every warp streams through 64-row K/V tiles with an online softmax (running row max and sum, rescaling the output accumulator) so the attention matrix is never materialized. Data moves global to shared with cp.async into XOR-swizzled shared memory to avoid bank conflicts, then to registers with ldmatrix.x4 (transposed for V), and both matmuls use bf16 mma.sync.m16n8k16 tensor-core instructions with fp32 accumulators. v5 double-buffers K and overlaps the next K and V loads with the softmax and the matmuls (2-stage cp.async pipeline).

**Use it when:**
- You want a short, readable reference for a near-roofline FlashAttention-2 forward pass in raw CUDA C++ and inline PTX, with each optimization isolated in its own file (swizzling, pipelining, ldmatrix.x4).
- You are writing your own attention kernel for consumer Blackwell (RTX 5090, sm_120) or Ampere/Ada-class GPUs and need a working baseline to modify, for example to try MXFP8/NVFP4 MMA, which the author cites as the reason for using CUDA C++ instead of Triton.
- Non-causal bf16 prefill-style attention with head_dim 128 and sequence lengths that are multiples of 64, where you can verify the result yourself against F.scaled_dot_product_attention.

**Skip it when:**
- Production inference or training: use PyTorch SDPA with the cuDNN backend (203.61 vs 197.74 TFLOPS on the author's own benchmark), flash-attn or FlashInfer, which handle masks, varlen, GQA and backward.
- Any head_dim other than 128: the host wrapper prints an error and calls exit(1), terminating the Python process.
- Sequence lengths not divisible by 64: the kernel has no tail handling or KV masking, so partial tiles read out of bounds and produce wrong results.
- Causal attention, masks, dropout, fp16 or fp8 inputs, or training (no backward kernel).
- Anything you need to redistribute: the repository has no license file.

**Vs siblings:** Pick this over FlashAttention-3, ThunderKittens or SageAttention only when you want to learn from or fork a minimal kernel: FA3 targets Hopper, SageAttention trades precision for speed on RTX 5090-class GPUs, and both are maintained libraries, whereas this is roughly 300 lines you can read in one sitting.

**Gotchas:**
- attention.cpp does not check dtype, device or contiguity and takes raw data pointers, flattening batch x heads; a transposed or non-contiguous tensor gives silently wrong output.
- Kernels launch with <<<>>> on the default stream, ignoring torch.cuda.current_stream(); code running on other streams can race or serialize.
- Softmax uses the fast-math __expf and P is rounded to bf16 before the P@V matmul (as in FA2); the harness checks output only with torch.testing.assert_close defaults on one random shape.
- The harness default is --bs 4 while the README table states bs=1; reproduce with --bs 1 to compare numbers.

**Status:** The repo gets commits (last 2026-09-07), but this is a personal learning repository with no license, so treat it as reference reading only; the attention kernel was written up in an August 2025 blog post (gau-nernst.github.io/fa-5090, blocked here and known only from search snippets).

[repo](https://github.com/gau-nernst/learn-cuda) · [benchmark](https://github.com/gau-nernst/learn-cuda/blob/HEAD/07_attention/README.md)

##### Mini-Attention (FlashAttention-2 from scratch in CUDA C++ for SM120)  `C++ (CUDA/PTX)`  `no license`  `active`  `Tier C`

Hand-written FlashAttention-2 forward kernel for RTX 5090 (SM120); beats cuDNN SDPA at N<=1024, 3-5% slower beyond.

**Beats:** cuDNN fused attention via PyTorch SDPA (SDPBackend.CUDNN_ATTENTION) — On one RTX 5090, fp16 non-causal attention with H=16, D=128 and batch 16/16/16/8/4 for N=512/1024/2048/4096/8192 (5 warm-ups, mean of 20 CUDA-event timings with a 200 MB L2 flush), K7 took 0.185 vs 0.247 ms for cuDNN through PyTorch SDPA at N=512 (1.33x) and 0.658 vs 0.739 ms at N=1024 (1.12x), but 2.588 vs 2.515 ms at N=2048 and 10.310 vs 9.904 ms at N=8192 (about 213 vs 222 TFLOPS, derived from page data). The exact PyTorch, cuDNN and CUDA versions and the host CPU are not stated beyond the torch>=2.11.0 cu128 requirement.

**Known shortcoming:** README contradicts itself (133.2% vs 134.7%; 'beats ~35%' at N=1024 vs 112.2%). One profiler line (0.003 ms) is physically impossible (~2,900 TFLOPS vs 419 peak), so at least one measurement is wrong. Beats cuDNN SDPA only at N<=1024. No licence.

**Known shortcoming:** tests/test_correctness.py checks the SM86 inline kernels, not the benchmarked SM120 kernel, which is checked only in the bench script at 0.05 tolerance. The baseline timing counts the `with sdpa_kernel()` context manager inside the CUDA-event window, inflating cuDNN at short N where this kernel wins. Non-causal, d=128, forward only.

**Independent measurement:** verifier

**Independent measurement:** enrichment

**How:** Standard FlashAttention-2 tiling with an online softmax in registers, using Ampere-style mma.sync.m16n8k16 tensor-core instructions (consumer Blackwell has no WGMMA or tcgen05), ldmatrix.x4(.trans) fragment loads, XOR-swizzled shared memory to avoid bank conflicts, cp.async.cg global-to-shared copies with an L2::256B prefetch hint, eager first K/V tile load and optional double buffering. SM120 tuning uses Bc=128 tiles (fits within about 100 KB shared memory), exp2-based softmax and one hoisted reciprocal for the final 1/l normalization, with K7 picked by a static scan over Br/Bc/warp configs.

**Use it when:**
- Studying how to write a FlashAttention-2 forward kernel by hand for consumer Blackwell (RTX 5090, SM120), with each optimization isolated in K1-K7.
- Short-sequence, non-causal fp16 prefill-style attention with head dim 128 (N=512 to 1024) on an RTX 5090, where the README measures 1.12x to 1.33x over cuDNN via PyTorch SDPA.
- As a reference for SM120 tile-size and PTX choices (mma.sync instead of WGMMA, Bc=128, L2::256B hints) when tuning your own kernel.

**Skip it when:**
- Sequences of 2048 tokens or more: the README table shows K7 at 95-97% of cuDNN there, so cuDNN is faster.
- Causal or masked attention, dropout, training (no backward pass), GQA/MQA with different K/V head counts, head dims other than 128, or sequence lengths that are not multiples of the 64/128 tile sizes; the SM120 kernel rejects or does not implement these.
- Any code you plan to ship: there is no LICENSE file (it returns 404), so the code cannot be copied, and the project has 1 star and one author.
- Datacenter Blackwell (B200/SM100) or Hopper: the SM100 kernel is work in progress and FlashAttention-3 or cuDNN target those parts directly.

**Vs siblings:** Pick it over learn-cuda's SM120 attention only for N<=1024 non-causal d=128 forward on an RTX 5090, since learn-cuda reaches about 94% of speed-of-light at long sequences but does not beat cuDNN; for anything production use cuDNN via SDPA or FlashAttention, and SageAttention if quantized attention is acceptable.

**Gotchas:**
- tests/test_correctness.py (the 'All K1-K7 passed' output in the Readme, tolerance 1e-3) loads the SM86 inline kernels, not the SM120 kernel that was benchmarked; the SM120 kernel is only checked inside _bench_sm120.py at B=4, N=1024 with a 0.05 tolerance.
- The baseline timing wraps each call in a 'with sdpa_kernel(...)' context manager inside the CUDA-event window, so Python-side overhead is charged to cuDNN at sub-millisecond sizes where K7 wins; the probe also silently falls back to FLASH_ATTENTION or MATH if cuDNN is unavailable.
- Several Readme figures disagree or are implausible: K7 at N=1024 is 112.2% in the latency table, 114.4% in the progression table and 'beats by ~35%' in the NCU section; the torch.profiler line (0.003 ms) is physically impossible; and the 'NCU-equivalent' metrics come from an analytical script, not Nsight Compute.
- Design notes contradict the code in places, for example notes/why_mma_sync.md cites 228 KB shared memory per block on SM120 while the bench script says 100 KB per SM.

**Status:** Active as of the last commit on 2026-03-31 (59 commits, 1 star), but unlicensed, so treat it as reference reading rather than vendorable code.

[repo](https://github.com/shlokgpu/Mini-Attention) · [benchmark](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/shlokgpu/Mini-Attention/HEAD/Readme.md)

##### oneDNN Graph Compiler  `C++`  `no license`  `unknown`  `Tier C`

Intel's tensor compiler backend for oneDNN Graph API that fuses MLP/MHA subgraphs; beat oneDNN post-op fusion and TVM. Removed in oneDNN 3.8.

**Beats:** oneDNN primitives with post-op fusion; TVM auto-scheduler — Intel's own arXiv paper (2301.01333) measured on a 32-core Xeon Platinum 8358: BERT-Large 1.12x and DLRM 1.15x end to end over oneDNN post-op fusion, MHA 2.3x (FP32) / 2.4x (Int8) lower time than post-op fusion, and 2.4x (MLP) / 6.2x (MHA) average over TVM with auto-scheduler; FP32 MLP was 4% slower than oneDNN primitives and Int8 MLP 6% faster. No compiler, flags or benchmark scripts are given.

**Known shortcoming:** Intel's own arXiv paper, no venue, compiler or flags; code lives inside the oneDNN repo (itself a baseline), no subdirectory named.

**Known shortcoming:** Discontinued: deprecated in oneDNN v3.7 and removed in v3.8; code (Apache-2.0) only in v3.7 tree; always experimental; build refuses the DPCPP CPU runtime.

**How:** It lowers through two IRs: a Graph IR that keeps op semantics for graph-level passes (layout propagation, constant-weight preprocessing, FP32-to-Int8 conversion with quantization-parameter folding) and a C-like Tensor IR for code generation. Compute-heavy ops are expanded from expert-written templates around tuned microkernels instead of being searched by an auto-scheduler. Fine-grain fusion inserts neighbouring ops at anchor points inside the template loops, and coarse-grain fusion merges the parallel outer loops of several fused ops, with buffer reuse by liveness analysis.

**Use it when:**
- Only if you are pinned to oneDNN 3.0-3.7 on Intel Xeon and run Int8 or FP32 BERT-style MHA blocks through the Graph API (the paper reports 2.3-2.4x lower MHA time than post-op fusion).
- As a reference design for template-plus-fusion tensor compilers, if you are building your own fused MLP/attention codegen for CPUs.
- Reproducing the paper's BERT-Large / DLRM numbers on a Xeon Platinum 8358-class machine with a matching oneDNN 3.x build.

**Skip it when:**
- New projects: oneDNN 3.7 deprecated the backend and 3.8 removed it; current oneDNN covers SDPA and gated MLP through its regular Graph API backend.
- FP32 MLP: the paper measured it 4% slower than plain oneDNN primitives.
- Non-Intel or non-x86 targets: the paper only measured a Xeon Platinum 8358 and the docs list no other supported platforms.
- Builds with the DPC++/SYCL CPU runtime: its CMake fails with an unsupported CPU runtime error for DPCPP.
- Anything that needs stability: the backend was always labelled experimental.

**Vs siblings:** LIBXSMM and Optimizing-DGEMM are kernel libraries you call directly, while this was a graph-level fuser behind the oneDNN Graph API; pick it only for whole-subgraph MHA/MLP fusion on an old oneDNN, since it is no longer maintained.

**Gotchas:**
- Off by default; it had to be enabled at CMake time, and runtime env vars ONEDNN_EXPERIMENTAL_GRAPH_COMPILER_CPU_JIT (llvm/c/builtin) and _OPT_LEVEL change codegen.
- Removed in oneDNN v3.8, so upgrading oneDNN silently drops back to the regular dnnl backend's fusions.
- The 'c' JIT mode is unavailable on Windows and macOS per its CMake file.

**Status:** Discontinued: deprecated in oneDNN 3.7 and removed in 3.8 (2025); the code remains readable at the v3.7 tag under Apache-2.0, but it is a reference, not something to adopt.

[repo](https://github.com/uxlfoundation/oneDNN/tree/v3.7/src/graph/backend/graph_compiler) · [benchmark](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2301.01333)

##### ThunderMittens  `C++ (Metal Shading Language) with Python/MLX bindings`  `no license`  `stale`  `Tier C`

Metal port of the ThunderKittens tile DSL for Apple GPUs; its bf16 GEMM is about 9% faster than MLX's mx.matmul.

**Beats:** MLX mx.fast.scaled_dot_product_attention and mx.matmul (Apple's MLX Metal kernels) — First-party only, read as a WebSearch snippet because the Hazy Research blog is egress-blocked: on an Apple M2 Pro, the bf16 GEMM is about 9% faster than mx.matmul on most square sizes, and the forward attention kernel is within +-15% of mx.fast.scaled_dot_product_attention (B=16, H=16, N 512 to 2560, D 64/128 in time_attn.py). The repo stores no results, and both kernels are built with MLX's default Metal compilation, with no extra flags.

**Known shortcoming:** Raised D to C on the Hazy Research blog (domain-restricted snippet only: GEMM about 9% faster than MLX, attention within +-15%). No license, 24 stars, last commit 2025-08-26, stale.

**Known shortcoming:** Shape checks are assert() only (compiled out in release builds, no tail handling); attn_fwd uses a fixed 1/sqrt(D) scale while time_attn.py passes scale=1 to MLX, so the attention comparison is not like for like; float16 matmul passes the host check but its Metal kernel is commented out; no backward kernel; eval_cpu ends in assert(false); no license.

**Independent measurement:** verifier

**Independent measurement:** enricher

**How:** The base tile shrinks from ThunderKittens' 16x16 to 8x8 so tiles map directly onto Metal's simdgroup_matrix multiply-accumulate; per the blog snippet this was needed because the M2 Pro allows at most 128 registers per thread. Each threadgroup is one 32-thread SIMD group. The GEMM computes a 32x32 output tile from 32x16 and 16x32 register tiles with FP32 accumulators, reads straight from device memory with no threadgroup-memory staging, and fully unrolls the K loop. The attention kernel is FlashAttention-style: online softmax over 8-row query tiles, with Q pre-scaled by 1/sqrt(D)*log2(e) so it can use exp2.

**Use it when:**
- Learning or porting ThunderKittens-style tile kernels to Apple Silicon (M-series GPUs) through Metal
- Experimenting with a custom bf16 square GEMM inside MLX where every dimension is a multiple of 32 (time_gemm.py sweeps 1024 to 16384)
- Prototyping fused Metal kernels for MLX with tile primitives instead of hand-written simdgroup_matrix code (the blog says the GEMM is 11 lines against MLX's 100+)
- Non-causal, unmasked bf16 forward attention with head dim 64 or 128 and equal Q/K/V shapes, for inference experiments

**Skip it when:**
- Any shipped product: the repo has no license file for its own code (only the vendored MLX tree is MIT), so legally it is reference-only
- Attention speed: the first-party claim is only 'within +-15%' of mx.fast.scaled_dot_product_attention, so it is not a reliable win
- Training or autodiff: there is no backward kernel, and the JVP transform in attn_fwd.cpp is a commented-out template stub
- Causal or masked attention, GQA/MQA (Q, K and V must share one shape), head dims other than 64/128, or FP16/FP32 attention
- CPU fallback or ragged shapes: eval_cpu ends in assert(false), and sequence lengths and GEMM sizes that are not tile multiples have no tail handling

**Vs siblings:** Pick it over ThunderKittens (CUDA) or HipKittens (AMD) only when the target is an Apple GPU and you want the same tile programming model there. Effort (bucketMul) is the other Apple Silicon entry but does approximate matrix-vector products for LLM decoding, not exact GEMM or attention.

**Gotchas:**
- Shape and dtype checks are plain assert() calls (N a multiple of 8 for attention; GEMM M/N multiples of 32 and K a multiple of 16), which disappear in release builds, so wrong shapes can produce silent garbage or out-of-bounds reads.
- matmul_custom accepts float16 in its host-side check, but the float16 Metal instantiation is commented out; only float32 and bfloat16 kernels exist.
- time_attn.py warms up MLX's SDPA instead of the ThunderMittens kernel and passes scale=1 to MLX while the TK kernel scales by 1/sqrt(D); neither timing script checks correctness, and each iteration calls mx.eval, so launch overhead is included.
- The repository vanished and was restored on 2025-08-26 (two 'revive thundermittens' commits; ThunderKittens issue #132), so there is no history, issue tracker activity or tests to lean on.

**Status:** Stale (two restore commits on 2025-08-26, 24 stars) and unlicensed, so it is reference code for reading and re-implementing, not for vendoring.

[repo](https://github.com/HazyResearch/ThunderMittens) · [benchmark](https://hazyresearch.stanford.edu/blog/2024-11-28-tk-mlx)

##### yalm (Yet Another Language Model, C++/CUDA LLM inference)  `C++ (CUDA)`  `no license`  `stale`  `Tier C`

Educational single-GPU C++/CUDA LLM inference engine; about 2.4x Hugging Face transformers FP16 decode, roughly tied with llama.cpp.

**Beats:** Hugging Face transformers (PyTorch) GPU inference; llama.cpp GPU also measured — Author-run table (README, Mistral-7B-Instruct-v0.2 FP16, 4k context, RTX 4090 + EPYC 7702P): yalm 63.8 and 58.7 tok/s at ~120 and ~4800 generated tokens vs Hugging Face transformers 25.9 and 25.7 (about 2.5x and 2.3x, derived from page data), llama.cpp 61.0 and 58.8, calm 66.0 and 65.7. Transformers, llama.cpp, CUDA and compiler versions are not given and no script reproduces the cross-engine table; the build uses -O3 -ffast-math -mavx2 -mfma -mf16c and nvcc -O2.

**Known shortcoming:** Only clearly beats HF transformers (2.5x); ties llama.cpp at ~4800 tokens and calm is faster. No script for the cross-engine table. No licence.

**Known shortcoming:** README benchmark table predates commit 6cd1ef6 (2025-08-26), which fixed out-of-bounds prefetch reads in att_mix and CUDA graph node updates, so the numbers come from pre-fix code (tier C rule). yalm's tok/s counts prompt plus generated tokens over total time with the prompt run one token at a time, not llama.cpp's metric. fp8 offered by convert.py but rejected by the loader; MoE asserts on CUDA; default build targets sm_80/sm_90 only.

**Independent measurement:** verifier

**Independent measurement:** enrichment

**How:** Decode at batch 1 is memory-bandwidth bound, so the CUDA path is a set of hand-written GEMV-style kernels: one warp per output row with a warp-shuffle reduction (`matmul_row`), a block transpose so 32 row results go out in one coalesced 128-byte store, and fused kernels for QKV projection + clipping, RoPE + KV-cache write, SwiGLU w1/w3 + activation, and output projection + residual add. The whole per-token forward pass is captured once into a CUDA graph and replayed, updating only the kernel-node parameters that change with position, which removes per-kernel launch overhead. The KV cache is FP16 and the attention value-mix kernel unrolls 16-deep register prefetches over the sequence; the design follows zeux/calm, which the README credits.

**Use it when:**
- Learning or teaching how a fast single-GPU decoder is built: small codebase (src/infer.cu is about 1,250 lines) with heavily commented kernels and an accompanying blog post.
- Batch-1, single-sequence FP16 decode of Mistral-7B or Llama-3.2 on an NVIDIA GPU with enough VRAM for the whole model, where you want about 2.4x the token rate of Hugging Face transformers eager inference.
- Profiling experiments with Nsight Compute: `./build/test -k [matmul,mha,ffn]` benchmarks individual kernels and `-b`/`-b2` measure memory bandwidth.
- Long-context experiments with a sliding-window KV cache (`-T`) plus two attention-sink tokens, or the built-in perplexity and passkey modes.

**Skip it when:**
- Production serving: the README says it is an educational exercise 'not meant to be run in production', and there is no license file, so the code cannot be reused.
- Anything needing more speed than llama.cpp: the README's own table has llama.cpp at 61.0/58.8 tok/s vs yalm 63.8/58.7 (a tie at ~4800 tokens) and calm ahead of both at 66.0/65.7.
- Batched or multi-user serving, quantized weights (only fp32/fp16 load; fp8 in convert.py is rejected by the loader), multi-GPU or models larger than VRAM.
- Long prompts: the prompt is hydrated one token at a time through the decode path (no batched prefill), so time-to-first-token grows linearly with prompt length.
- Mixtral/MoE on GPU: the CUDA path asserts 'Mixture of experts not yet supported for CUDA'; Mixtral works on CPU only.

**Vs siblings:** Pick yalm over llm.c or ik_llama.cpp only to study a compact, documented single-GPU FP16 decode engine; for actual inference ik_llama.cpp/llama.cpp, CTranslate2 or PowerInfer are licensed, maintained and support quantization, batching and more models.

**Gotchas:**
- The README benchmark table dates from Dec 2024 - Jan 2025 README commits and was not re-measured after commit 6cd1ef6 (2025-08-26) fixed att_mix loop bounds (its 16-deep prefetch read past the attended sequence) and CUDA-graph node updates.
- The program's own 'throughput' line divides prompt plus generated tokens by total time including prompt hydration, so it is not the same metric as llama.cpp's separate prompt-eval and eval rates.
- Error handling is `assert(false)`/`abort()`: an unsupported dtype or model aborts, and a build with NDEBUG would let some of those paths continue silently.
- CFLAGS include -Werror, so newer compilers that add warnings can break the build; issue #1 (CPU-only build) is unanswered.

**Status:** Stale (last commit 2025-08-26, 117 commits, three open unanswered issues) and unlicensed, so read it as reference material rather than vendoring it.

[repo](https://github.com/andrewkchan/yalm) · [benchmark](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/andrewkchan/yalm/HEAD/README.md)

#### big-integer-arbitrary-precision

##### AVX-512IFMA large integer multiplication (Edamatsu and Takahashi)  `unknown`  `no license`  `unknown`  `Tier C`

Peer-reviewed AVX-512IFMA large-integer multiplication method, reported up to about 2.97x faster than GMP; no code released.

**Beats:** GMP — Two search-engine summaries of the abstract (paper not opened) report large-integer multiplication with AVX-512IFMA up to about 3.07x faster than the authors' AVX-512F implementation and about 2.97x faster than GMP on a Cannon Lake processor. GMP version, operand sizes, compiler and flags are not documented.

**Known shortcoming:** No public code; snippet-only evidence (ICA3PP 2019 paper unreachable here); 'up to' best-case ratios (2.97x over GMP, 3.07x over own AVX-512F); discontinued CPU (Cannon Lake); GMP version, flags and operand sizes unknown.

**Independent measurement:** verifier

**How:** AVX-512IFMA (VPMADD52LUQ / VPMADD52HUQ) multiplies 52-bit fields in each of eight 64-bit lanes and adds the low or high 52 bits of the product into a 64-bit accumulator. Storing operands in radix 2^52 leaves 12 spare bits per lane, so many partial products can be summed before any carry has to be propagated, and carry normalization is deferred. That gives eight 52x52-bit products per instruction instead of GMP's scalar 64x64-bit multiply-with-carry chain, and products wider than the 32x32-bit VPMULUDQ products an AVX-512F-only kernel is limited to. Whether it uses schoolbook, Karatsuba or Toom-style splitting is not documented in anything readable this session.

**Use it when:**
- You are writing your own mpn-level multiply kernel for x86 cores with AVX-512IFMA (Cannon Lake, Ice Lake and later Intel parts that kept it, AMD Zen 4/5 per the record) and want a peer-reviewed design reference for radix-2^52 vector multiplication.
- Sizing the payoff before adding an IFMA path to a bignum library: the paper's reported best case is about 2.97x over GMP and 3.07x over an AVX-512F implementation on one CPU.
- Comparing against the authors' earlier AVX-512F (Knights Landing) design to see how much IFMA adds over a 32-bit-multiply vector kernel.

**Skip it when:**
- You need code you can run: nothing is published, so has_code is false and every number is the authors' own.
- CPUs without AVX-512IFMA (anything before Cannon Lake/Ice Lake and later parts that dropped the extension): the technique cannot run there.
- Very large operands where GMP switches to Toom-Cook or FFT multiplication: the operand-size range of the reported speedup is not documented, so it may not hold there.
- Constant-time or cryptographic use: no side-channel properties are documented; for RSA-size modular work OpenSSL's IFMA almost-Montgomery routines (benchmarked in the VROOM sibling entry) are shipping code.
- Decisions that need typical rather than best-case gains: both ratios are 'up to' figures.

**Vs siblings:** Read it when designing a general (non-modular) IFMA multiply for single large operand pairs; for runnable code, DigitsOnTurbo patches GMP's multiplication (1.41x geomean at 512-32768 bits), lea-gl's truncated batch AVX-512 Montgomery code beats GMP 3.95-5.34x on batched modular products, and FLINT is the practical pick for very large sizes.

**Gotchas:**
- Evidence is snippet only: the chapter (DOI 10.1007/978-3-030-38991-8_5) could not be opened because link.springer.com and semanticscholar are egress-blocked, so GMP version, operand sizes, compiler, flags and exact CPU are unknown.
- A radix-2^52 kernel needs conversion from and to GMP's 64-bit limbs (split and recombine passes); whether that cost is inside the reported times is not documented.
- Cannon Lake, the test CPU, was a short-lived discontinued microarchitecture, so the ratios may differ on Ice Lake, Sapphire Rapids or Zen 4/5.
- No public repository is attributable: github.com/topics/avx512ifma lists no repositories, and Hibari-K's AVX-512F multiply repos (no IFMA variant, no license) are not linked to the authors.

**Status:** A 2019 peer-reviewed paper with no released code or license, so it is reference material only; it could be re-tiered to B once a verifier can read the paper.

[benchmark](https://www.semanticscholar.org/paper/Accelerating-Large-Integer-Multiplication-Using-Edamatsu-Takahashi/ee766c654ad4acc8d42340ff3b5fd37f1229dff3)

##### DigitsOnTurbo (DoT)  `C`  `no license`  `unknown`  `Tier C`

Research SIMD (AVX-512/IFMA) kernels for bignum add/sub and base-case multiply, patched into GMP and OpenSSL.

**Beats:** GMP 6.3.0 (also OpenSSL 3.5.2 bignum) — Against stock GMP 6.3.0, DoT-patched GMP gives geomean 3.81x add, 3.73x sub and 1.41x multiply over 512-32,768-bit operands, up to 48.7% on large multiplies and +19.3% on pi. Against OpenSSL 3.5.2 it gives 2.95x add and 4.08x sub. All results are from clang 14 -O2 -march=native on Xeon Gold 6548Y+ (Emerald Rapids) and Xeon Max 9462 (Sapphire Rapids), measured by the authors.

**Known shortcoming:** Code only at an anonymous review link that blocked fetch (unverified); no license; preprint with no venue named.

**Known shortcoming:** Without AVX-512 gains mostly vanish (SSE add 0.7x, AVX2 1.2x); whole-program gains small (pi +19.3%, GMPbench +7.8%, RSA/FFDH/DSA +3-5%); constant-time behaviour not analysed.

**Independent measurement:** DoTMP (the GMP integration in arXiv 2604.21566) reports +7.8% on GMPbench (search snippet only); code still only at anonymous.4open.science.

**How:** Add/sub runs in four phases: lane-parallel limb add, carry detection with SIMD compares, a single parallel carry-propagation step, and a deferred scalar slow path for cascading carries. A cascade requires limbs equal to 2^64-1, so on random inputs it practically never fires. Multiplication uses a 'vertical and crosswise' scheme that exposes all m^2 partial products as independent AVX-512 IFMA multiplies (52-bit radix, with conversion from 64-bit limbs) before reducing columns, which removes read-after-write chains on a shared accumulator. Karatsuba/Toom recursion in GMP bottoms out in this base case.

**Use it when:**
- Research or prototyping on AVX-512 (Sapphire/Emerald Rapids class) Xeons where GMP mpn add/sub dominates the profile
- Mid-size operands (about 6,144-32,768 bits), where the paper reports its largest gains
- Reproducing or extending SIMD bignum work; the four-phase carry design is a clear reference
- Estimating headroom before investing in your own SIMD mpn kernels

**Skip it when:**
- Production work: there is no public repository or license, and the code sits at an anonymous review URL
- CPUs without AVX-512: the paper reports SSE addition at 0.7x (slower than scalar) and AVX2 at only 1.2x
- Huge-operand multiplication dominated by FFT: DoT replaces only the base case, so whole-program gains shrink (GMPbench +7.8% overall)
- Crypto code that needs constant time: the data-dependent cascading-carry slow path is not analysed for timing leaks
- Adversarial inputs built to trigger cascading carries, where the paper's advantage drops to 0.7-2.0x versus prior SIMD methods

**Vs siblings:** Pick it over ctbignum or mp++ only if you want faster stock GMP/OpenSSL arithmetic at thousands of bits on AVX-512 without changing your code, and you can live with unpublished code. FLINT is the shippable choice for big-number workloads, and the truncated-batch AVX-512 Montgomery code fits better when you batch modular exponentiations.

**Gotchas:**
- The code was not verifiable: anonymous.4open.science blocks fetchers, and no license is stated
- The headline 3.81x/3.73x geomeans are for the add/sub primitives alone; end-to-end gains are much smaller (pi +19.3%, divide +8.4%, RSA/FFDH/DSA throughput +3-5%)
- The multiply needs a 64-to-52-bit radix conversion for the 4x4 routine to stay compatible with GMP/OpenSSL limbs, which adds overhead

**Status:** Preprint with no stated venue and code only at an anonymous review link with no license, so treat it as a reference design, not a dependency; maintenance status unknown.

[benchmark](https://arxiv.org/html/2604.21566v1)

##### Large integer multiplication with Intel AVX-512 on Knights Landing  `unknown`  `no license`  `unknown`  `Tier C`

Peer-reviewed AVX-512F reduced-radix large-integer multiplication for Xeon Phi Knights Landing, reported about 2.5x faster than GMP; no code.

**Beats:** GMP — Two search-engine summaries of the abstract (paper not opened) say the AVX-512F implementation is about 2.5x faster in execution time than GMP for large-integer multiplication on Knights Landing, also comparing instruction counts. GMP version, operand sizes, compiler, flags and the exact Xeon Phi model are not documented.

**Known shortcoming:** No linked public code (github.com/Hibari-K/bigint_mul_avx512f looks related but is unattributed, unlicensed and has no GMP comparison); snippet-only evidence (IEEE HPCC 2018 unreachable here); best-case ~2.5x over GMP on discontinued Xeon Phi Knights Landing; GMP version, flags and sizes unknown.

**Independent measurement:** verifier

**How:** AVX-512F has no 64x64-bit vector multiply; VPMULUDQ (_mm512_mul_epu32) gives eight 32x32-to-64-bit products per instruction. With a reduced-radix representation (limbs narrower than 32 bits) each 64-bit accumulator keeps headroom, so the column sums of the product can be built from many vector multiply-adds before carries are propagated in a final normalization pass. On Knights Landing, whose scalar cores are weak, this vector path beats GMP's scalar mpn code; the exact limb width and multiplication algorithm used in the paper are not documented in anything readable this session.

**Use it when:**
- Designing a multi-precision multiply for cores that have AVX-512F but not AVX-512IFMA, such as Knights Landing, where GMP's scalar path is slow.
- Throughput-oriented number crunching on many-core Xeon Phi nodes that still run, as a reference for vectorizing the column sums of a multi-limb product.
- As the baseline when evaluating the same authors' later AVX-512IFMA paper, which reports up to about 3.07x over this AVX-512F approach.

**Skip it when:**
- You need code you can run: nothing is published and attributed, so has_code is false.
- CPUs with AVX-512IFMA: the authors' own IFMA version (sibling entry) reports up to about 3.07x over their AVX-512F one.
- Mainstream x86 cores with fast scalar 64-bit multiply and carry chains: the 2.5x is specific to Knights Landing, and the gain elsewhere is not documented.
- Very large operands where GMP uses Toom-Cook or FFT multiplication: the operand-size range of the result is not documented.
- New deployments: Knights Landing (Xeon Phi) is discontinued.

**Vs siblings:** Read it only as a design reference for AVX-512F-only hardware; on IFMA-capable CPUs prefer the same authors' AVX-512IFMA design, and for runnable code CGBN (GPU, 43.5x average on low multiplication vs 20-core GMP), lea-gl's batched AVX-512 Montgomery code or FLINT (large sizes) are the practical picks.

**Gotchas:**
- Evidence is snippet only: ieeexplore document 8622797 and semanticscholar are egress-blocked, so GMP version, operand sizes, compiler, flags and the exact CPU are unknown.
- Reduced-radix limbs need split and recombine passes to and from 32- or 64-bit limbs; whether the reported time includes that conversion is not documented.
- Hibari-K/bigint_mul_avx512f matches the topic and period (28-bit split/combine, _mm512_mul_epu32, 'naive algorithm', Makefile for Intel icc -xMIC-AVX512 on Knights Landing) but names no authors or paper, has no timing harness, no GMP comparison and no license; do not treat it as this paper's artifact.
- Knights Landing results lean on its weak scalar cores, so a 2.5x win over GMP there says little about Skylake-SP or later server parts.

**Status:** A 2018 peer-reviewed paper with no released code on discontinued hardware, so it is reference material only; it could be re-tiered to B once a verifier can read the paper.

[benchmark](https://ieeexplore.ieee.org/document/8622797/)

##### libMetalFloat64 (philipturner/metal-float64; emulated FP64 on Apple GPUs)  `Metal Shading Language (Swift package)`  `MIT`  `abandoned`  `Tier D`

Archived plan for emulated FP64 on Apple GPUs in Metal; no arithmetic is implemented, only theoretical peaks versus CPU FP64.

**Beats:** Native hardware FP64 on the Apple Silicon CPU (NEON) in the README table, and OpenCL FP64 in the precision table; the listed baselines GMP and MPFR are not compared — Nothing was measured: the README table gives theoretical scalar Gops for an unnamed reference system (8-core 3.064 GHz ARM CPU and 32-core 1.296 GHz Apple GPU), derived from instruction counts, comparing CPU hardware FP64 with GPU double-single FP32x2 (e.g. FMUL 196 vs 758, FADD 196 vs 482). The IEEE eFP64 column is empty, most of the precision table is '???', and the code that would produce those numbers does not exist in the repository.

**Known shortcoming:** Tier D: the README Performance table is theoretical peak derived from instruction counts, not a measurement, and the baseline is the CPU's hardware FP64 peak rather than GMP or MPFR. It is FP64 emulation on Apple GPUs, so it sits oddly in the arbitrary-precision category. Archived 2024-08-11, last commit 2023-05-17.

**Known shortcoming:** HEAD has no FP64 arithmetic: float64_t/float59_t/float43_t are empty ulong wrappers with no operators, the only MetalFloat64 source is a placeholder increment(uint) marked 'TODO: Remove this entire file', and the README's float32x2_t does not exist. MetalAtomic64 fetch_add ignores the type id (an f64 add would be an integer add) and the device store has no lock. The header copies Apple Metal stdlib code under Apple copyright, so MIT does not cover all of it. openmm/openmm#3889: the Metal compiler optimizes away double-single emulation. Usability corrected to reference (retier-09).

**Independent measurement:** verifier

**Independent measurement:** enricher

**How:** The intended speed comes from emulating FP64 with FP32 and 32-bit integer ALU instructions on the GPU's wide FP32 units: an IEEE path modeled on Berkeley SoftFloat and LLVM compiler-rt fp_lib.h, and a faster double-single (float-float, e8m48) path with flushed denormals. The README's speedups over the CPU's NEON FP64 are instruction-count estimates (for example 11 FP32/integer instructions per double-single add, 7 per multiply), multiplied by the GPU's ALU count and clock; none of that arithmetic is in the repository.

**Use it when:**
- As a design reference when planning your own FP64 or double-single emulation in Metal: the README lists per-operation instruction counts and the dylib-versus-inline split.
- As a starting point for lock-buffer 64-bit atomics on Apple GPUs (MetalAtomic64 hashes addresses into a lock buffer, borrowing the idea from Kokkos desul's Lock_Array), after finishing and testing it yourself.
- Not for production numerics in any form: there is no working FP64 add, multiply or FMA to call.

**Skip it when:**
- Any real workload: the README opens with 'Still in the planning stage - this is not a finished library!' and the sources confirm it.
- Arbitrary-precision or big-integer work: it is fixed 64-bit floating point, not a GMP or MPFR alternative, so it is in the wrong category for that comparison.
- Code that needs correct 64-bit atomics: __metal_atomic64_fetch_add_explicit ignores its type argument and always does integer addition (so f64 adds would be wrong), and the device-memory store has its lock acquire and release left as comments.
- Pre-Metal 3 hardware: it needs function pointers and Metal dynamic libraries, so Apple6-family GPUs (A13 and later) or macOS 13 Ventura on Intel Macs.
- Fast-math builds of double-single code: the author notes in openmm/openmm#3889 that the Metal compiler optimizes away double-single FP64 emulation.

**Vs siblings:** Do not pick it for computation: sibling entries such as MultiFloats.hpp, DoubleFloats.jl or libQD3 ship working double-double arithmetic with measurements, while this repository has none. It is only worth reading if you target Metal, which none of the siblings do, and plan to write the emulation yourself.

**Gotchas:**
- The README warns that forgetting useResource(_:usage:) on the atomics lock buffer can freeze half of the GPU until a restart, or silently draw half its maximum TDP in the background.
- The library header copies parts of Apple's Metal Standard Library and says Apple owns the copyright of that code, so the MIT license does not cover all of it.
- README and code disagree: the README documents float64_t and float32x2_t, while the headers define float64_t, float59_t and float43_t, and the atomics enum adds f32x2 and f32.
- Clients must ship libMetalFloat64.metallib in the same directory as their own library, because it is linked with @loader_path.

**Status:** Archived and read-only since 2024-08-11 with the last commit on 2023-05-17; MIT-licensed but unusable as shipped, since it contains only type scaffolding, a placeholder function and partial 64-bit atomics.

[repo](https://github.com/philipturner/metal-float64) · [benchmark](https://github.com/philipturner/metal-float64)

#### blas-lapack

##### Aliaksei Sala C++ GEMM (C++Now 2025 / CppCon 2025 talk)  `C++`  `no license`  `unknown`  `Tier C`

C++Now/CppCon 2025 talk building a C++ DGEMM step by step to roughly OpenBLAS speed; slides only, no code.

**Beats:** OpenBLAS — C++Now 2025 slides (PDF): final version 0.336 s / 142.2 GFLOPS vs OpenBLAS 0.310 s / 154.1 GFLOPS for 2880^2 FP64 on a 4-core i5-6300HQ under Linux with -O3 -march=haswell -ffast-math, so OpenBLAS is about 8% faster. CppCon 2025 deck (Keynote, text extracted): on a 16-core, 5.7 GHz Zen 5 CPU (kernel named zen5_packed_kernel; consistent with a Ryzen 9 9950X, though the slide text does not name the model) 'Matmul: 1.7 TFLOPS' vs 'Openblas: 1.58 TFLOPS' in FP64 (about 1.08x, derived from page data), a tie at 3.57 TFLOPS in FP32, and 3.09 TFLOPS in bfloat16 with no OpenBLAS counterpart; first-party, no code.

**Known shortcoming:** Not faster on the opened slides: OpenBLAS 154.1 GFLOPS vs the talk's final version 142.2 (i5-6300HQ). The Ryzen 9950X win (1.70 vs 1.58 TFLOPS) is only a Medium snippet. No code repository.

**Known shortcoming:** The CppCon 2025 keynote file (CppCon/CppCon2025 Presentations, Matrix_Multiplication.key) shows FP64 1.70 vs OpenBLAS 1.58 TFLOPS (~1.08x, derived), an FP32 tie at 3.57 vs 3.57, and bf16 3.09 TFLOPS with no OpenBLAS figure; kernel zen5_packed_kernel (16 cores, 5.7 GHz); CPU model, matrix size and compiler not given. The talk's code is C++ (AVX2 intrinsics, then std::experimental::simd), not hand-written assembly; no code repository.

**Independent measurement:** verifier

**Independent measurement:** enrichment
