Factor and triangular-solve arrays are stored in FP32 (optionally scaled FP16) while PCG vectors stay FP64; the CUDA build adds a synchronization-free dataflow triangular solve and a GPU-resident PCG.

**Use it when:**
- Large graph Laplacians from social, web or collaboration networks with skewed degrees: in the authors' GH200 table it takes 4.68 s on com-LiveJournal against 149 s for BoomerAMG and 83.7 s for AMGCL, and 0.76 s on as-Skitter against 69.8 s and 6.8 s.
- Interior-point Laplacian/SDDM systems that change every iteration, where AMG setup is expensive: about 0.3 s against 7.6-9.9 s for AMGCL on the iter0020-iter0040 matrices.
- Many right-hand sides on one fixed Laplacian (factor once with cpu_solver, then solve or apply repeatedly), from C++, Python or Octave.
- Multicore CPU servers where you can pin threads across NUMA domains; the solver is memory-bandwidth bound and the README gives placement guidance.

**Skip it when:**
- General SPD matrices that are not Laplacian or SDDM (for example elasticity or most higher-order FEM systems): only Laplacian and SDDM inputs are supported.
- Regular grids and FEM meshes where AMG already works well: AMGCL matched or beat it on grid_500, grid3d_100, grid_5000, parabolic_fem, kron_g500-logn16 and com-Orkut, and BoomerAMG needs 7-9 PCG iterations where apxchol needs 30-50.
- Projects that need bit-reproducible results across thread counts: the docs state a fixed seed does not give byte-identical parallel factors, so iteration counts can vary between runs.
- Licensing-sensitive or GPL projects: the BSD-4-Clause advertising clause is not OSI-approved and is GPL-incompatible.
- Expecting a GPU win for a single right-hand side: in the historical GH200 campaign the CPU build was faster than its own GPU build (CPU/GPU total-time ratio 0.461, solve-only 0.853).

**Vs siblings:** Pick apxchol over AMGCL when the systems are graph Laplacians of skewed-degree networks or interior-point SDDM matrices, where it wins by up to 31x in the authors' tables; keep AMGCL for general SPD problems and for grids and FEM meshes, where it ties or wins. Against LAMG+, which also targets graph Laplacians, apxchol offers a C++ library with OpenMP and CUDA builds and Python bindings, but no head-to-head between the two was found.

**Gotchas:**
- The library's default build uses -march=native, so binaries are not portable to older CPUs; turn off APXCHOL_NATIVE_ARCH for redistributable builds.
- Thread placement matters more than thread count: on an EPYC 7742 socket, 32 threads spread over 4 NUMA domains took 0.77 of the 16-threads-on-one-domain time, and all 64 cores were slower than 32; pin threads explicitly with OMP_PLACES.
- For a singular (connected) Laplacian the returned x is the minimum-norm solution with mean zero, whatever constant component the warm start had; a wrong-length x0 throws std::invalid_argument.
- APXCHOL_POOL_FP32=OFF does not make it an all-FP64 solver: the assembled factor stays FP32 and GPU triangular solves default to scaled FP16.

**Status:** Active ETH Zurich research code (354 commits, last commit 2026-09-30, PyPI 0.2.2 from 2026-07-27, 8 stars, no issues filed); usable from source or pip, but the BSD-4-Clause advertising clause limits it to reference use in this catalog.

[repo](https://github.com/AlgOptGroup/apxchol) · [benchmark](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/AlgOptGroup/apxchol/HEAD/benchmarks/daint/results.csv)

##### CKTSO-GPU  `C++ (CUDA; solver shipped as prebuilt x86-64 Windows/Linux binaries, demos in C++)`  `None stated: no LICENSE file, and README.md and ug.pdf give no terms; prebuilt x86-64 Windows/Linux binaries only, used on top of the separately distributed CKTSO library`  `abandoned`  `Tier C`

Closed-source CUDA add-on to CKTSO for sparse LU refactorization and solve; first-party 13.3x geomean refactorization speedup over KLU.

**Beats:** KLU 1.3.9 (SuiteSparse; run with CKTSO's ordering); also CKTSO version 20221123 on 1 CPU thread — First-party results.pdf (CKTSO-GPU 20221207), 29 SuiteSparse circuit matrices with Flops/NZ(L+U) > 50: refactorization on an RTX 3090 is 13.29x faster on geometric mean (28.80x arithmetic) than sequential KLU 1.3.9 given CKTSO's ordering, and 6.11x (12.01x) faster than CKTSO on one thread of a Xeon Gold 6130. Solve is 1.72x (2.41x) faster than KLU and 1.46x (1.98x) faster than one-thread CKTSO. Built with gcc 4.8.5 and nvcc 11.0 on CentOS 7.9; flags are not stated, there is no benchmark code, and per-matrix results appear only as bar charts.

**Known shortcoming:** Tier C: every ratio (refactor 28.80x/13.29x vs KLU, solve 2.41x/1.72x) comes from the vendor's results.pdf with no benchmark code or flags; binaries only, no license stated. Per ug.pdf the GPU module only pays off when flops/NNZ(L+U) > 50; on sparse matrices the multicore CKTSO is the better pick. It is the GPU add-on of the already-listed CKTSO.

**Known shortcoming:** GpuRefactorize does no pivoting. V100 gives wrong results unless the L1-cache-disabled libraries are used (about 20% slower). Compute capabilities are listed only up to 8.0 with CUDA 11.0 builds. Benchmarked only against 1-thread CKTSO and sequential KLU; the CKTSO README claims over 25x over KLU at 16 threads on a different matrix set, above the GPU's 13.29x geomean, and lists 'Faster GPU acceleration method' as ongoing work.

**Independent measurement:** verifier

**Independent measurement:** enricher

**How:** Refactorization reuses the pivot order and LU pattern fixed by the CPU factorization, so there is no pivot search and the column dependencies are known in advance; the GPU can then factor independent columns in parallel. The guide exposes a threshold (iparm[1], default 128) that switches refactorization between a 'bulk' and a 'pipeline' mode, and it picks blocks per multiprocessor and threads per block automatically. This matches the author's published GPU left-looking LU (DAC 2012, TPDS 2015), which uses a cluster mode for early dependency levels with many sparse independent columns and a pipeline mode for late levels with few, denser columns (per search snippets; the source is closed, so the exact algorithm is not visible). Gains come from matrices with enough work per factor nonzero; the guide's threshold is flops/NNZ(L+U) > 50.

**Use it when:**
- SPICE Newton/transient loops that refactor the same circuit-matrix pattern thousands of times while the pivot order from one CPU factorization stays acceptable.
- Slightly dense circuit matrices that pass the user guide's flops/NNZ(L+U) > 50 test, the only class it was benchmarked on.
- You already use CKTSO on x86-64 Windows or Linux and have an NVIDIA GPU of compute capability 3.5-8.0 with a CUDA 11 driver.
- Real or complex matrices with a single right-hand side per solve.

**Skip it when:**
- Highly sparse circuit matrices: the user guide itself says it cannot accelerate them efficiently and that multicore CKTSO is best there.
- You have a many-core CPU: the GPU was compared only with one-thread CKTSO and sequential KLU. The CKTSO README separately claims more than 25x over KLU at 16 threads (66 matrices, a different set), which exceeds this module's 13.29x geomean over KLU, so multithreaded CKTSO may match or beat it (cross-document, not like-for-like).
- You need pivoting on the GPU: factorization with pivoting stays on the CPU, and every CPU refactorization that changes the LU structure requires calling InitializeGpuAccelerator again.
- You need source code, a license, non-x86-64 hosts, AMD GPUs, or post-Ampere GPUs: it ships only prebuilt x86-64 binaries with no license terms, built with CUDA 11.0, and the listed compute capabilities stop at 8.0.
- Long-term support: the last commit was 2023-04-01, and the CKTSO README lists a 'faster GPU acceleration method' as work in progress.

**Vs siblings:** Use it only if you already run CKTSO and your matrices pass the flops/NNZ(L+U) > 50 test. Otherwise multithreaded CKTSO (same author, maintained, TCAD 2025 paper) or BSD-licensed Basker on the CPU is the safer choice, and GLU is a public-source GPU circuit LU you can build and modify.

**Gotchas:**
- Wrong results on some GPUs: disabledL1cache/readme.txt says the V100 needs the L1-cache-disabled libraries, which cost about 20% performance. Check residuals on your GPU.
- GpuRefactorize does no pivoting. If changed values make a pivot unacceptable, fall back to CKTSO factorization with pivoting on the CPU and re-initialize the accelerator; CKTSO's scaling option (its iparm[7]) is not supported on the GPU.
- Values and vectors are passed in host memory, and results.pdf does not say whether its timings include host-device transfers; oparm[1]/oparm[2] report the module's own timings.
- Return codes are mixed: negative values are CKTSO errors (-51 to -53 are GPU-specific), and positive values are raw cudaError_t codes (e.g. 209, no kernel image, on an unsupported GPU). Call CKTSO_SortFactors before initializing, or initialization is slower.

**Status:** Abandoned since 2023-04-01 (22 commits, 6 stars), binary-only with no license terms, so reference only; tied to CUDA 11.0-era builds and an external licensed CKTSO library.

[repo](https://github.com/chenxm1986/cktso-gpu) · [benchmark](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/chenxm1986/cktso-gpu/HEAD/results.pdf)

##### GSS (GRUS Sparse Solver, trial binaries)  `C`  `no license`  `abandoned`  `Tier C`

Closed-source Windows x64 sparse direct solver (LU/Cholesky/LDLt) with optional CUDA offload; about 2.9x PARDISO on large SPD-type factorizations.

**Beats:** Intel MKL PARDISO (Intel Composer XE 2013 SP1), CPU only — Vendor user guide (GSS 2.4, 2014), Table 1: numeric-factorization time only, GSS 2.4 in CPU+GPU hybrid mode vs CPU-only PARDISO from Intel Composer XE 2013 SP1, on a Core i7-4770 with 24 GB, a GTX 780 and CUDA 5.5 under Windows 7 x64. Over 12 SuiteSparse matrices the totals are 315 s vs 904 s (about 2.9x, derived from page data), with GSS losing on the 3 shortest jobs; no harness, compiler flags or thread settings are published.

**Known shortcoming:** Not like-for-like: GPU-hybrid GSS (GTX 780) measured against CPU-only PARDISO (Composer XE 2013 SP1); GSS slower on 3 of 12 matrices (msdoor, inline_1, boneS10); 2014 hardware (i7-4770, Win7, CUDA 5.5).

**Known shortcoming:** Closed-source Windows trial DLLs with a trial .lic file: no license, no source, no harness or flags, so not reproducible; abandoned since 2021-10-05.

**Known shortcoming:** Closed-source trial: gss_spd.lic contains 'Thu Dec 31 10:11:11 2015', apparently an expiry date; only a Windows x64 double-precision real DLL ships. Guide says both solvers used default parameters, yet GPU hybrid mode is off by default (setting[20]=0), so Table 1's settings are unclear. The '64-bit' (_l) API still takes int* index arrays (2^31 nonzero limit). Claim cannot be reproduced.

**Independent measurement:** User guide Table 1: 12 SuiteSparse matrices, numerical factorization only, 315.1 s vs PARDISO 904.2 s, about 2.9x (derived from page data); best case nd24k 5.4x.

**Independent measurement:** enrichment

**How:** Supernodal elimination-tree factorization in which an 'adaptive task-load-tree split' carves out a subtree of heavy supernodes small enough to factor entirely on the GPU (via cuBLAS), so CPU-GPU transfers stay small, while light independent supernodes run on CPU threads. A dynamic scheduler hands more tasks to whichever device is faster and splits a long-running GPU task to give child tasks to idle CPU threads. The README and the author's 2021 arXiv preprint (2109.14929) describe Q-learning for ordering, task scheduling and pivoting; the 2014 guide that carries the benchmark describes only adaptive scheduling, so how much of the Q-learning work is in this DLL is not documented.

**Use it when:**
- Historical or comparative interest: a 2014-era data point for CPU+GPU hybrid supernodal factorization against PARDISO
- Windows x64 with an old CUDA-capable NVIDIA card (compute capability 3.0+, CUDA 5.5) and large SPD or structurally symmetric matrices whose numeric factorization takes tens of seconds; the guide shows 1.5x-5.4x there
- Repeated factorizations of the same sparsity pattern, where the symbolic phase is reused and numeric factorization dominates
- If you can obtain a current commercial licence from the vendor; the repository itself grants no rights

**Skip it when:**
- Anything that needs source, a licence grant or Linux/macOS: there is no LICENSE file, no source, and only a Windows x64 DLL
- Short factorizations: the guide says PARDISO is faster when computing time is short, and GSS loses on msdoor (1.061 vs 0.424 s), inline_1 and boneS10
- General unsymmetric, symmetric-indefinite or complex matrices if you want the GPU path: hybrid mode supports only types 10 and 11
- Modern GPUs and toolchains: built against CUDA 5.5 and bundles cublas64_55.dll; behaviour on current drivers and GPUs is not documented
- Matrices with more than 2^31 nonzeros: even the 64-bit ('_l') entry points take int* ptr/ind arrays

**Vs siblings:** Rarely: RSLAB is an open-source alternative that reports faster solves than PARDISO, CKTSO covers circuit matrices against KLU with a PARDISO comparison, and BaSpaCho or PanguLU give GPU-accelerated sparse Cholesky/LU on current CUDA with source. Pick GSS only if you already hold a commercial licence and run on Windows.

**Gotchas:**
- The bundled trial licence file gss_spd.lic contains the string 'Thu Dec 31 10:11:11 2015', which looks like a trial expiry date; whether the DLL still runs today is not documented
- GPU hybrid mode is off by default (setting[20]=0 is CPU only, 5 is hybrid), yet the guide says its benchmark used 'default parameters' while running hybrid; the exact settings behind Table 1 are therefore unclear
- The header is still stamped v2.3.0 (2012) and its float solve prototypes differ (GSS_solve_is takes a double rhs, GSS_solve_ls a float rhs); the trial DLL list only has the double-precision real build
- After a failed GSS_numeric call the samples set the handle to NULL ('must set hSolver to NULL') and skip GSS_clear; follow that pattern, because the handle's state after an error is not documented

**Status:** Abandoned: the benchmarked release is from 2014, the repo's last commit is from October 2021, and it is a closed-source trial with no licence grant, so treat it as reference only.

[repo](https://github.com/closest-git/GSS) · [benchmark](https://github.com/closest-git/GSS/blob/master/GSS%202.4.1%20x64%20TRIAL/doc/GSS%202.4%20quick%20start%20user%20guide.pdf)

##### HP-SpMM-SDDMM (fast GPU SpMM for GNN graphs)  `C++`  `Apache-2.0 via per-file headers on the HP-SpMM sources (spmm/mm/spmm_kernel.cu, spmm/mm/spmm_common.cpp, include/spmm/mm/*, test/*.cpp). The repo has no LICENSE file. The bundled starml framework headers (e.g. include/starml/basic/matrix.h, allocator.h) and include/spmm/utils/timer_cuda.h carry no license. The integrated GE-SpMM baseline code is MIT upstream.`  `stale`  `Tier C`

FP32 GPU SpMM kernel for GNN graphs (IPDPS'23 HP-SpMM); tops cuSPARSE 12.2 and GE-SpMM on 17 graphs on an H800.

**Beats:** cuSPARSE 12.2 SpMM (CSR ALG2, CSR ALG3, CSR default, COO) and GE-SpMM — First-party README chart on an NVIDIA H800 (host CPU and exact CUDA version not stated beyond cuSPARSE 12.2, NVCC 11.8+, -O3, sm_80/sm_90): FP32 SpMM GFLOPS averaged over K = 32, 64 and 128 on 17 GNN graphs, with HP-SpMM above every cuSPARSE variant and GE-SpMM on all of them, for example about 1730 vs 1050 GFLOPS on Yelp and 3000 vs 1920 on reddit (values read off the chart). HP-SpMM alone runs on the precomputed clustering reorder, whose cost is not counted.

**Known shortcoming:** Not like-for-like: only HP-SpMM gets a precomputed cuGraph row reorder (untimed, no generator script); CHECK_RES off by default; kernel sources carry Apache-2.0 headers but bundled starml is unlicensed and there is no LICENSE file (mixed); HPMLL/HP-SpMM is an identical copy.

**Known shortcoming:** Kernels have no column bounds check, so K not a multiple of 32 reads and writes out of bounds. No SDDMM code despite the name. Only HP-SpMM gets the clustering reorder, and that cost and output zeroing are excluded from its timing; HP-SpMM and GE-SpMM get no warm-up while cuSPARSE gets 20 runs. 32-bit index maths (rows*K and cols*K < 2^31); atomicAdd output makes results non-deterministic. HPMLL/HP-SpMM is an identical copy.

**Independent measurement:** enrichment

**How:** Edge-parallel, load-balanced COO SpMM: each warp takes a fixed slice of 32 (or 128 for dense, large graphs) nonzeros, so skewed degree distributions do not leave idle warps, and partial row sums are flushed to C with atomicAdd when the row changes. The paper calls this a hybrid node/edge-parallel strategy with Dynamic Task Partition and Hierarchical Vectorized Memory Access: the 128-nonzero path loads indices and values with float4/int4 cp.async into double-buffered shared memory (Ampere+). A graph-clustering row reordering (precomputed .cugraph_reorder files) groups rows with similar neighbourhoods so the rows of B they read stay in cache.

**Use it when:**
- Full-graph GNN aggregation (GCN-style A*X) in FP32 on A100/A800/H100/H800 with feature widths K = 32, 64 or 128
- Power-law graphs with skewed degrees (Reddit, ogbn-products, Yelp) where row-per-warp CSR kernels suffer load imbalance; the README chart shows roughly 1.5-1.7x over the best cuSPARSE variant on Yelp, arxiv and reddit
- The graph is static across many epochs, so a one-off clustering reorder and COO conversion are amortized
- As a reference implementation of edge-balanced, vectorized SpMM to port into your own GNN framework

**Skip it when:**
- K not a multiple of 32: the kernels have no column bounds check (cid < k) and read B and write C past the end
- FP16/BF16, FP64 or weighted SpMM with non-default semirings: FP32 only, and the benchmark uses all-ones values
- Pre-Ampere GPUs: the build targets sm_80/sm_90 and the large-graph path uses cp.async
- If you need SDDMM, a maintained library or a PyTorch/DGL binding: none is provided, and there are 6 commits with the last in December 2023
- Graphs that change every step (sampled mini-batches): you cannot reproduce the reorder step from this repo, and without it the speedup is not documented

**Vs siblings:** Pick it over Sputnik when the workload is GNN-style A*X on power-law graphs on Ampere/Hopper and FP32 is enough; Sputnik is the more general deep-learning SpMM/SDDMM library and includes SDDMM. merge-spmv and CSR5 balance load in the same spirit but only for SpMV (one dense column).

**Gotchas:**
- Output is accumulated with atomicAdd: LBSpMM does not zero C, and the timed loop runs 200 launches into the same buffer, so after benchmarking C holds 200x the product (the disabled CHECK_RES compares with a 'div' mode); FP32 atomics also make results non-deterministic in summation order
- Only HP-SpMM gets the clustering reorder; cuSPARSE and GE-SpMM run on the original order, and the reorder cost and C zeroing are excluded from its time. Neither HP-SpMM nor GE-SpMM gets the 20 warm-up runs the cuSPARSE paths get
- Index arithmetic is 32-bit int (colind*k, row*k), so rows*K and cols*K must stay below 2^31; nonzero arrays must be padded to a multiple of 32 as the loader does
- Input is a custom .smtx text format (header line 'rows,cols,nnz', then row offsets and column indices), not Matrix Market

**Status:** Stale research code (last commit December 2023, also mirrored at HPMLL/HP-SpMM); kernel files carry Apache-2.0 headers but there is no LICENSE file and the starml framework is unlicensed, so copy the kernel rather than depend on the repo.

[repo](https://github.com/fan1997/HP-SpMM-SDDMM) · [benchmark](https://github.com/fan1997/HP-SpMM-SDDMM)

##### HYLU  `C (C API header with extern "C", closed-source prebuilt library)`  `None stated: no LICENSE file, and the README, include/hylu.h and doc/ug_en.pdf give no terms; prebuilt binaries only (unlike CKTSO, no license key file is required)`  `active`  `Tier C`

Closed-source multicore sparse LU/Cholesky solver for general large matrices; first-party 1.70x geomean over MKL PARDISO one-time solve.

**Beats:** Intel MKL PARDISO — Author's results.pdf: HYLU 20260331 vs Intel MKL PARDISO 2025.3, 16 threads on one Xeon Gold 6130, 37 SuiteSparse matrices (n 525,825 to 5,558,326): one-time solve 1.70x geomean total (factorization 2.36x, preprocessing 1.48x, substitution 18% slower); repeated solve 2.90x factorization and 2.53x factor+solve, substitution 20% slower; residuals about an order of magnitude lower on geomean. PARDISO settings and compiler flags are not stated, no benchmark harness is public, and the earlier arXiv preprint (34 matrices) reported 1.95x and 2.40x factorization speedups with near-parity on relatively dense matrices.

**Known shortcoming:** Binary-only (no licence text); numbers in doc/results.pdf (Xeon Gold 6130, gcc 13.3.0/8.5.0, no flags, no harness); no paper PDF in the repo. The residual chart shows relative residual about 1 or higher on CurlCurl_2, CurlCurl_4 and dgreen (PARDISO worse), yet those timings count toward the means; the geomean is lifted by 4 PARDISO fill-in outliers; HYLU is slower in total time on af_shell10 (~0.8x). Read from charts, approximate.

**Known shortcoming:** The forward-backward solve is 18-20% slower than PARDISO; the symmetric-indefinite LDL^H does no pivoting, and pivoting is limited to the diagonal supernode, so some unsymmetric systems come back inaccurate; MKL-BLAS builds leak memory (user guide); no license terms anywhere. The arXiv 2509.07690 snippet says near parity with PARDISO on relatively dense matrices; the paper was blocked.

**Independent measurement:** verifier

**Independent measurement:** enricher

**How:** The core is a parallel up-looking (row-by-row) LU and Cholesky factorization that switches between hybrid numerical kernels according to local sparsity, so very sparse regions avoid dense supernode overhead while denser regions run as supernodes (minimum 32 columns by default); the arXiv abstract, seen only as a search snippet, says this is why it is much faster than PARDISO on highly sparse matrices and about even on relatively dense ones. Preprocessing combines static pivoting and scaling with a choice of four fill-reducing orderings (two approximate-minimum-degree and two parallel nested-dissection variants, auto-selected, or best-of-all when repeat=true). Stability comes from static pivoting plus dynamic pivoting restricted to the diagonal supernode, pivot perturbation and automatic iterative refinement, which keeps the factorization's data structures static and parallel; threads are native OS threads (no OpenMP), and the builds link either MKL BLAS or OpenBLAS.

**Use it when:**
- One-time or repeated solves of large general sparse systems (the benchmark set is n = 525,825 to 5,558,326) on a 16-core-class x86-64 server where MKL PARDISO's factorization time dominates.
- Repeated factorization with a fixed sparsity pattern (Newton loops, transient simulation, time stepping): call Analyze once with repeat=true and the first-party results show 2.90x geomean in factorization and faster factor+solve than PARDISO on all 37 test matrices.
- Very sparse, circuit-like or KKT-like matrices where PARDISO's METIS-based fill-in blows up (results.pdf names ASIC_680k, ASIC_680ks, circuit5M and nlpkkt80 as PARDISO's worst cases).
- Projects that can take a binary-only dependency and want a simple C API with 64-bit index variants, complex Hermitian support and condition-number/determinant output without OpenMP.

**Skip it when:**
- Anything that must be open source, audited, rebuilt or redistributed under clear terms: there is no source and no license file or terms anywhere in the repo, only x86-64 Linux .so and Windows .dll binaries.
- ARM, Apple Silicon, 32-bit or CPUs without AVX2 and FMA; only x64 Windows 7/10/11 and Linux (CentOS 7/8 named) are supported.
- Solve-dominated workloads (one factorization, many right-hand sides): forward-backward substitution is 18-20% slower than PARDISO on geometric mean, partly from iterative refinement.
- Symmetric indefinite systems that need pivoting: the LDL^H path does no pivoting at all, and the user guide's fallback is to solve them as unsymmetric with the full matrix.
- Shared or oversubscribed machines and small problems: the guide says performance degrades severely if worker threads exceed idle cores, and no results exist below n = 525,825 or for sequential runs.

**Vs siblings:** Pick HYLU over CKTSO or NICSLU (same author, tuned for circuit matrices and KLU-style refactorization) when the matrices are general FEM/CFD/KKT systems or symmetric/SPD, and over GSS (binary-only, compared with a 2013 PARDISO) or RSLAB (Rust, factorization slower than PARDISO) when you want the fastest PARDISO replacement on x86 multicore; choose Basker (open source in Trilinos) or PanguLU (distributed multi-GPU) when you need source or scale beyond one node.

**Gotchas:**
- Pivoting is limited to the diagonal supernode, so some unsymmetric systems come back inaccurate; the user guide's fix is parm[23]=0, a larger parm[6] and sequential factorization, which costs speed. Check parm[11] (perturbed pivots) and the residual yourself.
- Passing ax=NULL to HYLU_Analyze disables static pivoting and scaling for unsymmetric matrices; the guide strongly recommends passing values.
- Builds linked with Intel MKL BLAS leak memory (the user guide blames MKL BLAS itself); use the OpenBLAS build for long-running processes if that matters.
- With parm[23]=0 and several threads, the parallel nested-dissection ordering is non-deterministic; even with the default setting, sequential and parallel numerical results may differ slightly.

**Status:** Actively developed (version 20260930, last commit 2026-09-30, 39 commits since 2025) but binary-only with no license terms, so it is a reference to call, not code to copy or ship without asking the author.

[repo](https://github.com/chenxm1986/hylu) · [benchmark](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/chenxm1986/hylu/HEAD/doc/results.pdf)

##### ISpMV  `C++`  `MIT (interfaces, examples, benchmarks) plus proprietary ISpMV Binary License for compiled core`  `active`  `Tier C`

Closed-binary GPU SpMV SDK with per-matrix plans; 1.3-2.2x faster than cuSPARSE SpMV on H100 (fp64).

**Beats:** cuSPARSE SpMV (CUDA 13 / cuSPARSE 12.8.6.72) — First-party benchmark on one H100 PCIe (CUDA 13.4.2, cuSPARSE 12.8.6.72), fp64, 100 matrices x 2 orientations x 2 scalar modes, preprocessing excluded. Geometric-mean steady-state time vs cusparseSpMV ALG2 is 2.17x lower on Mittelmann, 1.64x on large MIPLIB and 1.31x on large SuiteSparse; vs cusparseSpMVOp ALG1/ALG2 it is 1.38-1.69x lower. Host compiler, flags and CPU are not stated.

**Known shortcoming:** Core is a closed binary; speedups exclude 37-110 ms preprocessing per direction; 1 star, one commit; no host compiler, flags or CPU.

**Known shortcoming:** LICENSE-BINARY.txt limits the core to internal evaluation and non-commercial research, no redistribution of the .so; validated only on H100 PCIe; fp64 with 32-bit indices only; 24 of 400 cases failed forward-error check (all methods).

**How:** Not documented in technical terms: the core source is private. The docs say plan preparation analyses the matrix on the GPU and picks a representation and kernel from the matrix structure and the device's reported resources (SM count, cache, launch limits). The work is classic inspector-executor: you pay 37-110 ms of matrix-specific preprocessing up front so each later SpMV runs faster.

**Use it when:**
- Iterative fp64 solvers (PDLP-style LP/QP, Krylov methods) on an NVIDIA GPU that apply the same sparsity pattern thousands of times
- LP/MIP constraint matrices like those in Mittelmann and MIPLIB, where the published gain over cuSPARSE ALG2 is largest (1.6-2.2x)
- Non-commercial research or internal evaluation: that is all the binary license allows without written permission
- A100, H100/H200, B200, RTX 4090 or RTX 5090 (sm_80-sm_120) on Linux x86-64 with CUDA 13

**Skip it when:**
- Commercial or production use without a separate agreement: the ISpMV Binary License limits the core to internal evaluation and non-commercial research, and you may not redistribute the .so
- One-off or few SpMVs per matrix: 37-110 ms of preprocessing (geometric mean) wipes out a gain of tens to hundreds of microseconds per call
- FP32, complex, 64-bit indices, device-pointer scalars or CPU execution: all unsupported
- Anything that needs auditable or patchable source: the core is closed, and runtime validation covers only H100 PCIe
- Risk-averse deployments: v0.1.0 is a single-commit repo from late September 2026 with one star

**Vs siblings:** Pick it over merge-spmv or CSR5 when you are on a current NVIDIA GPU, reuse one matrix many times, and can accept a closed non-commercial binary. merge-spmv and CSR5 are open, copyable source but target 2015-16 hardware. Ginkgo or AMGCL fit better when you need a full open solver stack rather than a faster SpMV kernel.

**Gotchas:**
- With copy_device_matrix=0 the plan borrows your CSR arrays, so they must stay immutable and allocated until the plan is released. Plan destruction does not synchronize.
- Changing sparsity, dimensions or device requires a new plan. Changing only values per call is possible via apply_with_values, which bypasses value-dependent representations.
- deterministic=1 (the default) gives bitwise-reproducible results only for the same plan, GPU and build. In the published benchmark, 24 of 400 cases (six SuiteSparse matrices) failed the forward-error criterion; all four methods failed those same cases.
- Plan preparation cannot be captured in a CUDA graph, and graph-captured pointers and scalars are fixed. ispmv_version() returns the ABI major, not the SDK version.

**Status:** Actively released (v0.1.0, single public commit) but reference-only: the core is a proprietary binary licensed for evaluation and non-commercial research, and only the interfaces, examples and benchmark client are MIT.

[repo](https://github.com/PolyU-IOR/ISpMV) · [benchmark](https://github.com/PolyU-IOR/ISpMV/blob/main/benchmarks/README.md)

##### NICSLU  `C (prebuilt libraries only)`  `Proprietary prebuilt binaries with no source: use is gated by a license key file (nicslu202110/license/nicslu.lic), and license/readme.txt says 'License for research/trial purpose only. Long-term license key file is now provided.' The README says the license has been extended to 9999-99-99.`  `finished`  `Tier C`

Retired binary-only parallel sparse LU for SPICE circuit matrices; first-party 1.87x over KLU, 2.15x over MKL PARDISO.

**Beats:** KLU (SuiteSparse) and Intel MKL PARDISO — The author's 2019 results.pdf compares NICSLU 201905B with KLU and Intel MKL PARDISO on an Intel Xeon Gold 6132, using refactorization plus solve time on 182 circuit matrices (136 unpublished real circuits, 46 SuiteSparse) with 'best configurations'; thread counts, versions and compilers are not stated. It reports geomean speedups of 1.87x over KLU (faster on 149 of 182) and 2.15x over PARDISO (faster on 134). The chart shows many matrices near 1x and a few huge outliers (one KLU case at 15691x) lifting the mean; the peer-reviewed TCAD 2013 paper (2.08x to 8.57x over KLU with 1-12 threads, per a search snippet) was not opened.

**Known shortcoming:** Tier C: results.pdf numbers (geomean 2.15x vs MKL PARDISO, 1.87x vs KLU over 182 matrices) are first-party; the license is a proprietary research/trial key file (nicslu202110/license/nicslu.lic). The TCAD 2013 paper (2.08x-8.57x vs KLU, 1-12 threads) was blocked and seen only as a snippet; retier candidate to B.

**Known shortcoming:** Unmaintained; the author points to CKTSO. Serial solve only; the pivoting factorization scales only about 2x at 8-16 threads (CKTSO TCAD paper); the results.pdf geomean is lifted by a few huge KLU outliers (one at 15691x); thread counts and versions unstated; 136 of 182 matrices are private; patent-covered, academic use only. wibraun/NICSLU (LGPL-2.1, NICSLU 3.0.1 from 2011-2013) is the only copyable source, which the author's FAQ calls old and buggy with the closed version up to 3x faster.

**Known shortcoming:** An LGPL-2.1-or-later source of NICSLU 3.0.1 (2011-2013) exists at wibraun/NICSLU (folded here as a duplicate); it bundles restricted HSL MC64 files and the author's FAQ calls it old and buggy, with the closed version up to 3x faster.

**Independent measurement:** verifier

**Independent measurement:** same author's CKTSO doc/tcad.pdf: CKTSO 5.9x over NICSLU at 16 threads, 1.21x-4.69x with the same ordering, implying NICSLU about 2x over PARDISO there (derived from page data)

**How:** It is a Gilbert-Peierls left-looking LU in the KLU lineage with several additions: static pivoting and scaling at analysis (Duff-Koster style permutation of large entries to the diagonal) to cut off-diagonal pivots, and six fill-reducing orderings (AMD, approximate minimum Markowitz, three approximate-minimum-operation variants and approximate minimum deficiency) run in parallel, keeping the one with the fewest predicted flops. Factorization adaptively picks a row-row, partial-supernode or full-supernode kernel by sparsity, and parallelizes over an elimination-tree dependency graph, running wide levels in parallel and narrow levels in a pipelined schedule; it also decides automatically whether a matrix is worth factorizing in parallel at all. Repeated Factorize calls use a pivoting-reduction technique, and ReFactorize reuses the previous pivot order with no pivoting, which is the fast path in converging Newton iterations.

**Use it when:**
- An existing SPICE-style simulator that already integrates NICSLU, for example Dolphin Design SMASH (the README gives a special build for SMASH 7.5.x and nicslu202110 for 7.6.0, enabled with .OPTION SOLVER=NICSLU).
- Highly sparse circuit matrices refactorized thousands of times with a fixed pattern, where KLU occasionally blows up: the results chart shows KLU more than 10x slower on roughly 15 of 182 matrices (read off the chart), mostly where its fill-in is far larger.
- Older x86-64 CPUs without FMA or AVX2: NICSLU ships non-FMA builds, while its successor CKTSO refuses to run without AVX2 and FMA.
- Academic work that needs a frozen solver with a non-expiring key: the README says the license now runs to 9999-99-99, and use is free for academic purposes.
- Studying the algorithm: an older NICSLU 3.0.1 source tree (2011-2013, LGPL-2.1) is mirrored at github.com/wibraun/NICSLU, though the author's FAQ calls that version old and buggy.

**Skip it when:**
- New projects: the author says NICSLU is no longer updated or maintained and points to CKTSO, whose IEEE TCAD 2025 paper reports it 5.9x faster than NICSLU at 16 threads in the no-re-pivot best case (1.21x to 4.69x when both use CKTSO's ordering).
- Commercial products without a deal with the authors: it is copyrighted by NICS Lab (Tsinghua) and Xiaoming Chen, covered by three Chinese patents, free only for academic use, and needs a research/trial license key file to run.
- Solve-dominated or many-right-hand-side workloads: the user guide says only serial forward/backward solving is supported.
- Scaling to many cores: the CKTSO paper says NICSLU's factorization with pivoting gets only about 2x on 8-16 threads, and the auto-selector may run small or very sparse matrices on one thread regardless of the thread count.
- Non-circuit matrices (FEM, CFD) or non-x86 targets: orderings are minimum-degree family only (ColAMD and METIS were removed in 201905A), pre-analysis takes about 2.6x KLU's time, and the macOS/PowerPC request (issue #2, 2023) has no reply.

**Vs siblings:** Pick NICSLU over CKTSO only when you are tied to an existing NICSLU integration, need non-FMA x86-64 builds, or want the non-expiring key; otherwise CKTSO (same author, same API style) is faster and maintained. Choose Basker (open source in Trilinos, measured against KLU and PARDISO) when you need source, and GLU or CKTSO-GPU for GPU refactorization.

**Gotchas:**
- NICSLU expects CSR; passing KLU-style CSC without MATRIX_COLUMN_* gives wrong answers (the FAQ's 'completely wrong for any test case'), and duplicate entries are rejected with -7.
- The __NICS_INT64 macro must match the int32 or int64 library you link, or the integer argument types silently disagree.
- NicsLU_ReFactorize does no pivoting and can go unstable when values change a lot; call NicsLU_Factorize until Newton is converging. The FactorizeMatrix heuristic can misjudge extreme cases, and the guide recommends the low-level calls for DC analysis.
- Passing ax=NULL to NicsLU_Analyze disables static pivoting. The first factorization or refactorization carries one-time setup, so benchmark the second call, as the FAQ advises.

**Status:** Finished: the 'Final update' commit is dated 2026-03-22, the code is unmaintained and replaced by CKTSO, and it is a proprietary, patent-covered, license-keyed binary, so treat it as a reference to call, not code to copy.

[repo](https://github.com/chenxm1986/nicslu) · [benchmark](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/chenxm1986/nicslu/HEAD/results.pdf)

##### Ocean SpGEMM (CornellHPC)  `CUDA/C++`  `no license`  `active`  `Tier C`

GPU SpGEMM (C = A*B, FP64 CSR) that sizes output rows with HyperLogLog estimates; reported 1.4x over spECK on A100.

**Beats:** spECK (primary) and OpSparse; also TileSpGEMM and HSMU-SpGEMM — Per WebSearch snippets of the ICS '26 paper (arXiv 2604.19004, not opened because arXiv, alphaxiv and doi.org are egress-blocked), Ocean averages 1.4x, 2.6x, 3.5x and 2.0x over spECK, OpSparse, TileSpGEMM and HSMU-SpGEMM on 337 square SuiteSparse matrices on an A100, with 1.4x to 2.8x across A100, H100 and rectangular matrices. Whether these are geometric or arithmetic means, the host CPU, and whether cuSPARSE was compared could not be checked.

**Known shortcoming:** Downgraded B to C: the ICS 2026 paper (arXiv 2604.19004) could not be opened, so the 1.4x over spECK and 2.6x over OpSparse figures are snippet-only; no LICENSE file, so usability reference. Retier to B when the paper is reachable.

**Known shortcoming:** run() throws std::runtime_error when the HyperLogLog estimate undershoots the output size beyond the spare buffer (hll_numeric_malloc_expansion_coe 1.3); NUM_SM and SHARED_MEMORY_KB are compile-time hand edits; index_t is uint32 by default; built with -use_fast_math. Whether the snippet speedups are geometric or arithmetic means, and any cuSPARSE comparison, are unknown.

**Independent measurement:** verifier

**Independent measurement:** enricher

**How:** Most GPU SpGEMM codes (spECK, OpSparse, nsparse) run an exact symbolic pass to count each output row's nonzeros before the numeric pass; Ocean replaces it, where profitable, with per-row HyperLogLog cardinality estimates (HLL sketches of B's rows built with MurmurHash3, merged per row of A) and over-allocates by a configurable factor. An analysis stage uses input statistics and sampling to pick among an ultra-sparse path, an estimation path, an exact symbolic path and a 'fat' path, and the numeric phase uses hybrid dense, hash and ESC accumulators binned by row size, with rows that overflow their estimate recomputed by a dense fallback kernel. Code is compiled for compute_61 PTX on purpose to avoid Independent Thread Scheduling, which the Makefile says slows some kernels.

**Use it when:**
- Repeated FP64 SpGEMM (A*A, A*B, AMG Galerkin products, graph contraction) on A100 or H100 where spECK or OpSparse is the current tool.
- Workloads where the symbolic pass dominates; the paper's abstract says it is about 28% of spECK's runtime.
- Benchmarking or research on estimation-based SpGEMM, since the repo ships the 337-square and 64-rectangular SuiteSparse matrix lists and a download script.

**Skip it when:**
- Anything you need to ship: the repository has no license, so it can be read but not legally copied or redistributed.
- GPUs other than A100/H100 or older than compute capability 8.0; the README warns that untested hardware will likely hit compile, configuration or runtime errors.
- FP32, complex or integer values, or matrices you cannot convert to its custom CSR file format without writing glue code (data_t is hard-coded to double).
- Pipelines that cannot tolerate a hard failure: if HLL underestimates output size beyond the spare buffer, run() throws std::runtime_error and asks you to raise hll_numeric_malloc_expansion_coe.
- Memory-tight runs: estimation over-allocates the output (default factor 1.3) and the memory pool is set never to release memory.

**Vs siblings:** Pick Ocean over spECK or OpSparse when you are on A100/H100 and only need to study or benchmark (no license); for code you will ship, use spECK, OpSparse or TileSpGEMM, or Kokkos Kernels SpGEMM where portability and a maintained API matter more than the reported 1.4x to 3.5x.

**Gotchas:**
- Hardware constants are compile-time: a wrong NUM_SM (108 for A100, 114 or 132 for H100) or SHARED_MEMORY_KB (must be 128, 96 or 80) silently changes scheduling or breaks launches.
- index_t defaults to uint32_t, so row offsets and the output's nonzero count must stay below about 4.29 billion unless you rebuild with uint64_t.
- The README says correctness checks against spECK output 'may fail' on some matrices from floating-point differences (relative tolerance 1e-6, auto-fail 1e-4); builds also use -use_fast_math.
- Timed iterations include allocation through cudaMallocAsync from a pool whose release threshold is set to UINT64_MAX, so warm runs reuse memory and cold first-call cost is excluded by the default 10 warmup iterations.

**Status:** Recently published (10 commits, last 2026-04-21, 7 stars, no issues) and buildable with CUDA 12.4+, but with no license it is reference-only; read it for the HyperLogLog-estimation idea rather than vendoring it.

[repo](https://github.com/CornellHPC/Ocean-SpGEMM) · [benchmark](https://arxiv.org/abs/2604.19004)

### parsing-and-text

#### text-search-and-indexing

##### trigrep  `Rust`  `no license`  `active`  `Tier C`

Rust CLI that pre-builds a disk-backed trigram index of a repo, then searches only candidate files, beating ripgrep in a first-party benchmark.

**Beats:** ripgrep — First-party README benchmark on a clone of git/git (4 patterns, 5 timed runs + 1 warmup each, index pre-built) reports mean query time 0.0405s for trigrep vs 0.0640s for ripgrep and 0.5990s for grep, i.e. ~1.58x and ~14.79x; medians for trigrep and ripgrep are tied at 0.0500s. Timed with `/usr/bin/time -p` (10ms resolution) over 20 samples; no CPU model or rustc version given, and index build time is excluded.

**How:** Indexing extracts every overlapping 3-byte trigram per file and writes a sorted, mmap'd lookup table (`lookup.bin`) plus posting lists (`postings.bin`), enabling binary search instead of a byte scan. At query time the regex is parsed into a `regex-syntax` HIR and decomposed into an AND/OR tree of literal trigrams; posting lists are intersected/unioned (smallest-first) to shrink the file set before the real regex engine ever runs. An 8-bit `loc_mask` (byte-offset adjacency) and an 8-bit `next_mask` Bloom filter on the following byte further prune false-positive candidates pre-verification. Indexing itself is parallelized with rayon.

**Use it when:**
- Large, mostly-static trees (git.git-scale or bigger) searched repeatedly, so index-build cost amortizes
- AI coding agents or scripted workflows issuing many regex searches per checkout, as the README targets
- Patterns with real literal content (e.g. TODO|FIXME, ^#include) that decompose into selective trigrams
- Need for grep-compatible text output or structured JSON output in the same tool
- Prebuilt-binary install wanted on Linux/macOS (x86_64/aarch64) or Windows (x86_64) without a Rust toolchain

**Skip it when:**
- One-off or rarely-repeated searches on a tree: index-build time is excluded from the published benchmark and isn't amortized
- Anything requiring code reuse or redistribution rights: no LICENSE file and no license field in either Cargo.toml, so it is reference-only
- Patterns with no extractable literal (bare character classes, anchors, `.`) fall back to a MatchAll node, losing index selectivity
- Decisions resting on the headline 1.58x: trigrep and ripgrep have the same 0.0500s median, so the gap is mean-only and close to the 10ms timer resolution used
- Concurrent or long-lived multi-process use where index staleness/locking matters: thread/process safety around the on-disk index is not documented

**Vs siblings:** Pick trigrep over ngi or ugrep-indexer mainly for its Cursor-derived on-disk format (mmap'd trigram lookup + loc/next-mask filtering) rather than for the strength of the evidence: ngi reports 1.7x-5.9x and ugrep-indexer 10x-21x with clearer separation, while trigrep's own numbers show tied medians and only a mean-based 1.58x over ripgrep.

**Gotchas:**
- Search auto-builds the index if missing, so a cold first query pays full index-build cost that the published benchmark excludes
- No LICENSE file and no license field in Cargo.toml: code can be read but not legally reused or redistributed
- The next_mask adjacency filter is a Bloom filter (false positives possible, no false negatives); correctness depends on the final real-regex verification pass, not the index alone
- `trigrep status` checks staleness against git HEAD but the index is not auto-refreshed on file edits without rerunning `trigrep index`

**Status:** Actively maintained (last commit 2026-04-30, 46 stars) but ships with no license, so usability is reference-only rather than reusable/redistributable.

[repo](https://github.com/PythonicNinja/trigrep) · [benchmark](https://github.com/PythonicNinja/trigrep#benchmark)

#### unicode-utf8

##### Parabix (bitstream UTF-16 validation kernel)  `C++`  `OSL-3.0`  `abandoned`  `Tier C`

Bitstream-parallel text-processing framework whose LLVM-JIT'd SIMD kernel beat a simdutf CLI wrapper on UTF-16 validation.

**Beats:** simdutf — On valid UTF-16LE corpora (128/256 MiB, single thread, Apple M1, median of 7 runs), a third-party benchmark measured Parabix's SIMD kernel at 2900-3760 MiB/s raw (5075-5205 MiB/s overhead-adjusted) against a simdutf v9.0.0 CLI wrapper (clang -O3 -std=c++17) at 1824-2532 MiB/s raw (1883-2600 MiB/s adjusted) -- about 1.18-2.0x raw and 2.0-2.7x adjusted -- but the simdutf wrapper reads the whole file into memory before validating while Parabix streams it, so part of the gap reflects I/O handling rather than the validation kernels.

**Known shortcoming:** The benchmarked UTF-16 validator is not in this mirror: it is a patch in an unlicensed 0-star student repo (dakshkashyap/cmpt479-project-group8), and its timings are whole-process runs dominated by file I/O rather than validation.

**How:** Core technique is Cameron et al.'s parallel bit-stream method: input is transposed (s2p) into 8/16 bitstreams, each holding one bit-position across the whole buffer, turning per-character branching into bitwise AND/OR/shift ops across a full register width, plus optional multicore pipeline parallelism (--thread-num). On this specific benchmark part of the apparent win is a process/I-O gap rather than kernel speed: Parabix streams the file through ReadSourceKernel while the simdutf wrapper CLI reads the whole file into a std::vector via ifstream before validating; the benchmark authors' own methodology doc says I/O is not equalized between the two.

**Use it when:**
- Building a new streaming text pipeline (regex search, XML parsing, transcoding) where adopting the whole Parabix framework is acceptable, not just linking a validator
- Multi-stage text transforms where replacing many per-character branches with bitwise ops across a full register/vector width is the goal (icgrep-style regex matching)
- Research or teaching on bit-parallel SIMD algorithms and LLVM JIT code generation
- Environments that can carry an LLVM 5+/Boost 1.61+/Z3/CMake toolchain at both build and run time
- Workloads that also want multicore pipeline parallelism (thread-num > 1) inside the same kernel model

**Skip it when:**
- You need a small, embeddable UTF-8/UTF-16 validator with a stable C/C++ API — no such component exists in this mirror; use simdutf directly
- Startup latency matters: Parabix's LLVM JIT pipeline load adds ~0.019s fixed overhead per process vs ~0.002s for simdutf, dominating small-input timings
- You need permissive licensing — Parabix/icgrep is OSL-3.0 (strong copyleft), unlike simdutf's permissive license
- You need an actively maintained project — no commits on this mirror since 2021-08-10
- You need UTF-8 rather than UTF-16 — this benchmark and the validator it measures are UTF-16LE only

**Vs siblings:** None of the catalogued UTF-8 siblings (ada-url/idna, simdutf8, xutf, SimdUnicode, utf8_range) target UTF-16, so there's no direct sibling for this workload; pick Parabix over building your own UTF-16 path only if you're already adopting its whole bit-parallel framework for other text processing, not for a standalone validator.

**Gotchas:**
- The benchmarked tools/utf16validate isn't in this GitHub mirror; it's added by a third-party patch to Parabix commit f0369dd pulled from the SFU GitLab, and that commit postdates this mirror's last sync (2021-08-10)
- Fixed per-process overhead (~0.019s, mostly LLVM JIT pipeline load) is roughly 9x simdutf's (~0.002s) — raw wall-clock throughput on small inputs is dominated by this, use the benchmark's overhead-adjusted numbers instead
- GitHub reports this repo's license as NOASSERTION even though the README and OSL3.0.txt/LLVM-LICENSE.txt in the tree declare OSL-3.0 for Parabix code and the LLVM Release License for vendored LLVM files
- This is a read-only mirror: it does not accept GitHub pull requests; patches go to an SFU GitLab research repo instead

**Status:** Abandoned on this mirror since 2021-08-10 (no evidence in this session of active development elsewhere) and usability is mixed: it's a research framework with no stable API, requiring a full LLVM/Boost/Z3 build toolchain rather than a library you can drop in.

[repo](https://github.com/parabix/parabix-devel-mirror) · [benchmark](https://github.com/dakshkashyap/cmpt479-project-group8/blob/main/results/utf16_benchmark_apple_arm64_summary.md)

### runtime-and-systems

#### allocators-gcs

##### LWMalloc  `C`  `no license`  `active`  `Tier C`

618-line single-file C malloc for embedded Linux, injected via LD_PRELOAD; paper claims up to 53% faster than glibc ptmalloc.

**Beats:** glibc ptmalloc — Only press-release and news snippets were reachable: up to 53% shorter execution time and 23% lower memory use than glibc ptmalloc on real applications on Raspberry Pi Zero W, Raspberry Pi 4 and Jetson Orin Nano, with 530 lines and 20 KB vs ptmalloc's 4838 lines and 116 KB. The IEEE paper, its workloads, compiler flags and glibc version could not be read, and the repo has no benchmark code, so none of this could be checked.

**Known shortcoming:** No locks (unsafe in multi-threaded programs), 8-byte alignment, no posix_memalign or aligned_alloc, WSIZE hard-coded to 8. Issue 2: the test segfaults on 32-bit ARM, yet the paper lists a Pi Zero W (32-bit), so the published code may not be what was measured. calloc reads the header before the NULL check and has no overflow check; the sbrk failure check is wrong; test.c double-frees after a discarded realloc; likely fails under GCC 14 default errors. Still no license (issue 1). The 53% and 23% figures are snippet only.

**Independent measurement:** snippet only

**How:** Small requests (up to 120 bytes) go to per-size singly linked bins carved from 4 KiB sbrk chunks, so they allocate and free in O(1) with an 8-byte header. Larger blocks use boundary tags (header plus footer) and 62 segregated free lists searched first-fit. Frees next to a free neighbour are parked on a buffer list and merged lazily on the next large malloc or realloc (deferred coalescing), which skips work that ptmalloc does on every free. There are no locks, arenas, tcache or per-thread state, which is where both the small footprint and the single-threaded speed come from.

**Use it when:**
- Single-threaded C programs on 64-bit embedded Linux boards (the paper names Raspberry Pi 4 and Jetson Orin Nano) where glibc malloc's code size or overhead matters.
- Experiments comparing allocator policies (deferred coalescing, small-chunk pools) against ptmalloc on small devices.
- Reading material: the whole allocator fits in one 618-line file built on the classic CS:APP implicit/segregated-list design.

**Skip it when:**
- Any multi-threaded process: all free lists and the heap pointer are unsynchronized globals with no locks, so concurrent malloc/free will corrupt the heap.
- 32-bit targets: word sizes are hard-coded (WSIZE 8, DSIZE 16) instead of sizeof(size_t)/sizeof(void*), and issue #2 (open, no reply) reports a segfault of the bundled test on a 32-bit Allwinner ARM SoC, even though the paper lists a Raspberry Pi Zero W.
- Code that needs 16-byte alignment (SSE/NEON vectors, long double, max_align_t): ALIGNMENT is 8.
- Programs that call posix_memalign, aligned_alloc or memalign (common in C++ runtimes and media libraries): those still go to glibc, and passing such pointers to the preloaded free() is undefined behaviour.
- Anything shipped: there is no license (issue #1, open since 2025-09-04, unanswered), so the code cannot legally be reused.

**Vs siblings:** Pick LWMalloc over rlsf or Talc only for single-threaded 64-bit Linux processes you can LD_PRELOAD and only for study, since it has no license; for a licensed small-footprint allocator with real-time bounds rlsf (TLSF, 260-320 cycles vs dlmalloc 450-750) is the safer choice, and for general multi-threaded use any of the jemalloc/mimalloc-class siblings apply.

**Gotchas:**
- Memory is never returned to the OS: the heap only grows via sbrk, and small-object chunks are never merged back into the large-block pool.
- Error handling is broken in places: lw_mem_init and lw_sbrk compare sbrk's result to NULL instead of (void *)-1, lw_sbrk ignores sbrk failure, and lw_calloc reads the header of the returned pointer before its NULL check and does not check nmemb*size for overflow.
- The Makefile builds liblwmalloc.so while the README tells you to preload lwmalloc.so.
- The bundled test.c discards realloc's return value and then frees the old pointer, which is a double free under LWMalloc (a 4-to-8-byte realloc moves the block); in lw_realloc the branch that merges both neighbours is unreachable because the preceding 'if (!next_alloc)' already catches that case.

**Status:** 10 commits, 93 stars, last commit 2026-07-07, three open issues (license, 32-bit segfault, mallinfo) with no maintainer replies; unlicensed and not thread-safe, so reference only.

[repo](https://github.com/taehyeon-masu/lwmalloc) · [benchmark](https://ieeexplore.ieee.org/iel8/6488907/6702522/10883044.pdf)

##### mem++ (memplusplus)  `C++`  `no license`  `stale`  `Tier C`

Experimental single-threaded C++ arena allocator with GC smart pointers and heap compaction; beats jemalloc in its own charts, not glibc malloc.

**Beats:** jemalloc, mimalloc, rpmalloc, ptmalloc2/3 (glibc malloc), gcpp — First-party Google Benchmark runs (clang-15, Release, CPU unknown, results only as box-plot images): 4096 random-size allocations take about 590 us for mem++ vs about 1160 us for jemalloc and 960 us for mimalloc, but about 220 us for glibc 2.31 malloc and 150-200 us for rpmalloc; the 1M-op mixed benchmark is about 1010 ms vs jemalloc about 2000 ms and rpmalloc about 1340 ms, but slower than mimalloc (about 670 ms) and glibc malloc (about 700 ms). The 4-8x figure compares iterating a linked list after compaction with the same list randomized in mem++'s own heap.

**Known shortcoming:** Not faster than glibc malloc: its own charts show ptmalloc2 ahead on both timing benchmarks; it beats only jemalloc and rpmalloc. No LICENSE file.

**Known shortcoming:** Bench build is clang-15 Release with Google Benchmark, 5 repetitions, CPU unknown. The alloc benches call the deprecated raw mpp::Allocate/Deallocate, not the GC path; the 'ptmalloc2' column is system glibc 2.31 malloc. Allocate/Deallocate scan the arena list linearly. Still no LICENSE (404), stale since 2023-11-22, single-thread only.

**Independent measurement:** first-party charts

**Independent measurement:** code reading by enricher

**How:** Allocation is a bump of the arena's top chunk when it has room; otherwise it does a best-fit lookup in a per-arena treap of freed chunks (ChunkTreap, GetFirstGreaterOrEqualToChunk) and splits the result. Free coalesces with neighbouring chunks and the top chunk, ptmalloc-style, using 16-byte headers and 32-byte minimum chunks. During GC it splits the object graph into connected components, places each component contiguously in one arena, and for singly-linked-list-shaped components lays nodes out in traversal order, which is where the 4-8x iteration speedup over a randomized list comes from.

**Use it when:**
- Research or teaching on compacting GC and locality-improving heap layout in C++.
- Single-threaded programs built around pointer-chasing structures (linked lists) whose nodes end up scattered in memory, where a manual compaction pass can pay off.
- Experiments comparing bump/treap allocators against jemalloc, which its own complex benchmark shows about 2x slower than mem++ (chart-read values).

**Skip it when:**
- As a faster general allocator: in its own charts glibc malloc (ptmalloc2, glibc 2.31) and rpmalloc beat it on the 4096-allocation test, and mimalloc and glibc malloc beat it on the 1M-op complex test.
- Any multithreaded program: the README says it supports only single-threaded applications, and multithreading is an open low-priority issue (#21).
- Production code: the README says it is not recommended for production, the API is unstable (0.3.5), and the last commit was 2023-11-22.
- Code that keeps references or raw pointers into GC-managed objects across CollectGarbage(), since compaction invalidates them.
- Windows, or projects needing a clear license: Windows support is an open issue (#27) and the repo has no LICENSE file.

**Vs siblings:** Pick mem++ over SGCL only if you want compaction and locality-driven relocation rather than a concurrent tracing collector; for plain allocation speed, fast-alloc pools or IsoAlloc beat glibc malloc where mem++ does not.

**Gotchas:**
- The allocator benchmarks call the deprecated raw mpp::Allocate/Deallocate, not the GC path, so they do not measure MakeShared or CollectGarbage cost.
- Allocate and Deallocate scan the arena list linearly (GetSuitableChunk loops over every arena; Deallocate finds the owning arena by range check), so cost grows with the number of 32 MB arenas.
- The 'ptmalloc2' column in the benchmarks is the build machine's system malloc (glibc 2.31); the benchmark build uses clang-15 Release with Google Benchmark, 5 repetitions, CPU not stated.
- Garbage collection is manual only; automatic collection is an open issue (#45). Compaction moves objects and invalidates raw pointers and references.

**Status:** Stale since 2023-11-22 with 22 open issues, no LICENSE file and an author warning against production use, so it is reference material only.

[repo](https://github.com/m4drat/memplusplus) · [benchmark](https://github.com/m4drat/memplusplus-benchmarks)

##### SpeedMalloc  `other`  `no license`  `unknown`  `Tier C`

Hardware proposal: a small in-order support core runs malloc/free for all cores; simulated 1.15x over mimalloc and 1.75x over jemalloc at 16 threads.

**Beats:** mimalloc, jemalloc, TCMalloc — In full-system gem5 simulation of AArch64 cores (with McPAT power/area modelling), the paper reports 16-thread speedups of 1.75x over jemalloc, 1.18x over TCMalloc, 1.15x over mimalloc, 1.23x over Mallacc and 1.18x over Memento+, with equal or lower energy; allocator versions, workloads and core configuration could not be checked because the paper was blocked and only search snippets were read.

**Known shortcoming:** A hardware proposal, not a software allocator: a support core plus four new ISA instructions (mallocstart, freestart, mallocend, freeend), a modified compiler, an assumed 8-cycle invocation, evaluated only in gem5 AArch64 plus McPAT. The figures are for 16 threads. No code; snippet only.

**Independent measurement:** snippet only

**How:** All allocator metadata lives in the support core's own L1 caches (for example a 16 KB L1-D), so it no longer pollutes the main cores' L1/L2 and evicts user data. Because one core serializes every metadata update, the allocator needs no atomics and no cross-core metadata synchronization. Hardware message queues with a dispatch queue, a priority scheduler and round-robin fairness absorb bursts; the invocation path is assumed to take 8 cycles.

**Use it when:**
- Architecture research on allocator offload, metadata cache pollution or heterogeneous helper cores
- Citing a simulated upper bound for what removing allocator synchronization could buy multi-threaded, allocation-heavy code
- Comparing against hardware allocator accelerators such as Mallacc and Memento

**Skip it when:**
- Any real software project: no existing CPU has the support core or the ISA extensions
- As evidence that mimalloc or jemalloc can be beaten on current hardware: every number comes from gem5 simulation
- When you need reproducible numbers: no code, gem5 configuration or modified compiler release was found
- Single-threaded programs: the claimed benefit comes from removing cross-core synchronization

**Vs siblings:** Never as a library. Every sibling (v8malloc, Mesh, LLFree, fast-alloc) runs on today's CPUs; cite SpeedMalloc only when the question is hardware offload. Exgen-Malloc, from the same group, is the software single-thread counterpart.

**Gotchas:**
- The 1.75x/1.18x/1.15x figures are for 16-thread workloads, not an average over thread counts
- Energy and area figures come from McPAT models, not silicon
- One support core serves all main cores; the paper says it is not a bottleneck at the core counts simulated, but scaling beyond them is not documented here
- The 8-cycle invocation latency is an assumption of the model

**Status:** Simulation-only research proposal with no code release; reference only and not usable on existing hardware.

[benchmark](https://arxiv.org/abs/2508.20253)

##### fc_malloc  `C++`  `no license`  `abandoned`  `Tier D`

2013 proof-of-concept thread-caching allocator with a dedicated free-recycling thread; README claims about 2x faster than glibc and jemalloc.

**Beats:** glibc malloc and jemalloc — First-party wall times from one random producer-consumer run on unstated hardware, compiler and jemalloc version: 2.6 s vs 5.8 s glibc and 4.5 s jemalloc on 1 thread, and 6.8 s vs 18.2 s and 13.6 s on 10 threads; a second table shows 4.8-12.9 s vs jemalloc's 9.7-27.9 s at 1-10 threads with about 14% more RAM. The benchmarked allocator (malloc2.cpp at 39e4d67) serves one fixed 60-byte size, uses a spinning extra thread, and its unbounded-overwrite rings can drop or double-issue blocks under exactly this cross-thread free load, so the numbers do not describe a general-purpose, correct malloc.

**Known shortcoming:** The benchmarked code is malloc2.cpp at commit 39e4d67, not fc_malloc. Its get_bin() ignores size so all sizes share one bin (heap overflow on mixed sizes); the garbage ring (16K) and recycle ring (1M) have no backpressure, so blocks can be dropped or handed out twice under the 10-thread cross-free load; the recycler thread busy-spins on an extra core; the bench used 60 B, not the README's 128 B. HEAD fc_malloc.cpp/.h do not compile.

**Independent measurement:** code reading by enricher

**How:** It borrows the LMAX Disruptor single-writer idea. Each thread bump-allocates from its own 8 MB mmap page and pushes freed pointers into a private, non-atomic ring buffer (16K slots). One garbage-collector thread busy-polls every thread's ring and moves the pointers into a shared 1M-slot recycle ring. Allocating threads then claim 16 recycled blocks at a time with a single relaxed fetch_add, so the fast path is a thread-local cache pop with no locks or CAS.

**Use it when:**
- As reading material on Disruptor-style allocator design: single-producer free queues per thread plus a dedicated recycler thread.
- To reproduce a 2013-era producer-consumer microbenchmark with fixed-size blocks, cross-thread frees and a spare core for the recycler.
- As a starting point for a fixed-size-class pool inside your own code, after you rewrite the synchronization with proper atomics and backpressure.

**Skip it when:**
- Anything in production: no license (issue #1 closed without one), abandoned since 2013-05-07, and the last commit message says the fixed_pool design 'still has multi-threaded' bugs.
- Mixed allocation sizes: in the benchmarked malloc2.cpp, get_bin() ignores the size and returns the same bin for every request, so a recycled small block can be handed out for a larger request (heap overflow).
- Programs that free in bursts faster than the single recycler thread can drain them: the per-thread garbage ring and the shared recycle ring have no backpressure, so the writer can lap the reader and pointers get dropped (leak) or recycled twice (double handout).
- Machines without a spare core: the recycler thread busy-spins (its usleep is commented out) even when idle.
- Programs that need memory returned to the OS: pages are never unmapped.

**Vs siblings:** Effectively never for use: IsoAlloc, Spaces or micromalloc are licensed, maintained, size-class-correct malloc replacements with real benchmarks. Read fc_malloc only for the Disruptor-style recycler-thread idea, which none of the catalogued siblings use.

**Gotchas:**
- The README says 128-byte allocations, but the benchmark at the commit that added the tables (39e4d67, malloc2.cpp) allocates 60 bytes (rounded to 64 plus a 16-byte header) and never touches the memory; HEAD bench.cpp instead allocates 10000 bytes into 32K-slot arrays with memset, a configuration that matches neither table.
- free2() publishes its ring position only after more than 10 frees, so up to 10 frees per thread stay invisible to the recycler.
- mmap_alloc checks `if(!limit)` instead of MAP_FAILED, so a failed mmap returns (char*)-1; on Linux it opens /dev/zero for every page and never closes the fd. The HEAD fixed_pool maps at address hints that encode the size class ((ItemSize<<32) + pos*PageSize) and only asserts that the hint was honoured; on macOS it passes MAP_FIXED to that address, which can clobber existing mappings.
- Open issues #3-#5 (2020) report double allocation after block merging and duplicate ring-buffer claims in malloc3.cpp; none were answered.

**Status:** Abandoned since 2013-05-07 with no license (all rights reserved) and HEAD sources that do not compile as a library; reference only.

[repo](https://github.com/bytemaster/fc_malloc) · [benchmark](https://github.com/bytemaster/fc_malloc/blob/master/README.md)

#### filesystems-and-io

##### copy-fast  `C`  `no license`  `active`  `Tier C`

Student C11 Linux file-copy tool with threaded pipeline and io_uring backends, compared only against its own naive read/write loop.

**Beats:** project's own naive sequential read/write backend (backend_naive.c); 1-worker run for the multi-file test — The README's single-run table, produced by bench/benchmark.c and bench/run_benchmarks.sh, shows a 100 MB page-cache-resident file copied in 0.0376 s by the threaded pipeline vs 0.0869 s by the project's own sequential read/write loop (2.31x) and 0.0487 s by io_uring, on Linux 6.18 x86_64 with -O3 and an unstated CPU and compiler; GNU cp was never measured. The 1,000-file 10.49x figure compares 4 workers on the naive path against 1 worker on the heavier per-file pipeline path, so it is not a clean parallelism measurement.

**Known shortcoming:** Harness flaw behind the numbers: copy_file_dispatch (src/backends.c) sends files under 512 KB to the naive backend only when jobs > 1, so the -j 1 baseline runs the pipeline backend per 32 KB file (2 pthread_create plus 8x1 MB posix_memalign each) while -j 4 and -j 8 run naive; the 10.49x mixes a backend change with parallelism, which explains the super-linear 4-worker result and the slower 8 workers. The io_uring backend ignores short writes (silent truncation risk); the bench is a single run on a page-cache-resident /tmp file with no destination fsync; fadvise SEQUENTIAL|WILLNEED ORs enum values. No license; GNU cp never measured.

**Independent measurement:** code reading by enricher

**How:** The pipeline backend runs a reader pthread (pread) and a writer pthread (pwrite) over a bounded pool of 4 KB-aligned 1 MB slots, so reads and writes overlap. The io_uring backend submits up to queue_depth reads via liburing and chains a write SQE on each read completion. Directory copies use a bounded work queue drained by -j N worker threads. Sparse files are walked with lseek(SEEK_HOLE/SEEK_DATA) and holes are skipped. It does not use copy_file_range, sendfile or reflinks (FICLONE), which are what make modern cp fast.

**Use it when:**
- Reading a compact, readable example of a reader/writer bounded-buffer copy pipeline in C11 with pthreads
- Studying a minimal liburing read-then-write copy loop with fixed slot buffers
- Teaching SEEK_HOLE/SEEK_DATA sparse copying and a resume journal design
- Linux-only experiments on page-cache-resident files where you want to compare overlap strategies yourself

**Skip it when:**
- As a production replacement for GNU cp, rsync, fcp or wcp: no license, 7 commits, 0 stars, and it was never benchmarked against cp
- On filesystems where cp would reflink or use copy_file_range (Btrfs, XFS, NFS server-side copy): copyfast always moves bytes through user space
- When you need durability: no backend fsyncs the destination unless -v or an interrupt triggers fdatasync, so timings and 'done' mean data is only in the page cache
- Non-Linux platforms: requires liburing and Linux syscalls
- Trees of many small files with -j 1: each file takes the pipeline path, which spawns two threads and allocates 8 x 1 MB buffers per file

**Vs siblings:** Only for reading the code: for real copies prefer fcp or wcp (both measured against GNU cp, the latter with an io_uring design) or uring-sync for many small files, all of which beat cp itself rather than a self-written naive loop.

**Gotchas:**
- Multi-file benchmark confound: copy_file_dispatch sends files under 512 KB to the naive backend only when jobs > 1, so the -j 1 'baseline' copies each 32 KB file via the pipeline backend (two pthread_create calls plus 8 MB of posix_memalign per file) while -j 4/-j 8 use the naive loop. The 10.49x 4-worker figure therefore mixes a backend change with parallelism, which also explains why it is super-linear and why 8 workers (3.45x) is slower than 4.
- The io_uring backend ignores short writes (a completion with res smaller than the requested length is counted and the slot freed with no resubmission), and its SQ-full fallback discards the pwrite return value, so a partial write could silently truncate data; none of this affects the published numbers on a local filesystem but it is a correctness gap.
- bench/benchmark.c times one run per backend, in a fixed order, on a 100 MB file just written to /tmp and still page-cache resident, with no destination fsync; results measure memory-to-page-cache copy, not NVMe throughput (and /tmp may be tmpfs). The dense test also runs with sparse_aware=true.
- posix_fadvise is called with POSIX_FADV_SEQUENTIAL | POSIX_FADV_WILLNEED; these are enum values, not flags, so the OR evaluates to WILLNEED only.

**Status:** Seven-commit OS-course project (Week 12 viva checklist, syllabus matrix) last updated 2026-10-04 with no license file, so it is reference-only and cannot legally be copied.

[repo](https://github.com/rushmanthnalluri/copy-fast) · [benchmark](https://github.com/rushmanthnalluri/copy-fast)

##### couring  `C++`  `MIT`  `abandoned`  `Tier C`

Single-file C++20 teaching demo comparing blocking reads, a thread pool, raw io_uring and io_uring coroutines for loading OBJ files.

**Beats:** single-threaded blocking file reads — One run of run_all on unspecified hardware and compiler (CMake Release, GCC gets -fcoroutines), loading 512 OBJ files. Wall times: blocking single-thread 0.419 s, thread pool 0.177 s (2.4x), io_uring 0.368 s (1.14x), coroutines 0.339 s (1.24x), coroutines plus thread pool 0.230 s (1.8x, all derived from page data). Multithreaded parsing, not io_uring, gives the biggest gain.

**Known shortcoming:** Correctness bug: Task::promise_type::return_value does result = std::move(result), assigning the parameter to itself (it shadows the member), so --coroutines and --coro-pool throw their parse results away; parsing still runs so timings roughly hold, but nothing is checked (the only assert is compiled out in Release and read() return values are ignored). --coro-pool also busy-spins the main thread and calls done() across threads without synchronization. Abandoned demo: 4 commits, last 2022-11-30. Not faster: a plain thread pool beats every io_uring variant.

**Independent measurement:** code reading by enricher

**How:** The io_uring variants queue one IORING_OP_READ per file into a 512-entry ring with liburing and collect completions with io_uring_submit_and_wait / io_uring_peek_cqe. The coroutine variants wrap each read in a C++20 awaitable whose completion entry carries the coroutine handle, so a completion resumes parsing. --coro-pool then hops onto a BS::thread_pool (v3.3.0) to parse on many threads. The thread-pool variant simply runs blocking read() plus parse across hardware threads, and since parsing dominates, that is where the gain comes from.

**Use it when:**
- Learning how to bridge io_uring completions to C++20 coroutine handles (awaitable + user_data = coroutine_handle pattern)
- As a starting skeleton for batching many small whole-file reads through one ring on Linux 5.1+
- Teaching that CPU-bound parsing, not I/O, often dominates 'load many files' workloads

**Skip it when:**
- As a production I/O library: no API, no error handling for short reads, no tests, abandoned since 2022-11-30
- When files are page-cache hot and parsing dominates: the README's own run has the plain thread pool (0.177 s) beat every io_uring variant (0.230-0.368 s)
- On non-Linux platforms or kernels older than 5.1; liburing is required
- When you need more than 512 files: openFiles stops at MAX_FILES = 512

**Vs siblings:** Pick it only to learn the coroutine-over-io_uring pattern. For real io_uring work use liburing directly (it is the dependency here). For a measured multi-file copy or read pipeline, copy-fast or uring-sync are closer to usable tools.

**Gotchas:**
- Coroutine results are thrown away: promise_type::return_value(Result result) does `result = std::move(result);`, which assigns the parameter to itself (it shadows the member). So --coroutines and --coro-pool return empty ObjReaders. Parsing still runs, so the timings reflect the work, but the output is never checked.
- Nothing validates the output: the only check is an assert (compiled out in Release) that each mesh has 1024 faces, and 'Processed N files' counts every result, good or not. Short or failed read() calls are ignored in the trivial and thread-pool paths.
- --coro-pool busy-spins the main thread on io_uring_peek_cqe, which inflates user time (0.732 s against 0.371 s for trivial).
- Timings come from bash `time` on one run of the whole process, including directory walk and opening all 512 fds. The README's data prep copies one OBJ file hundreds of times, so reads are almost certainly page-cache hot.

**Status:** Abandoned demo (4 commits, last 2022-11-30, no issues), MIT-licensed; worth reading for the coroutine/io_uring glue, not for vendoring.

[repo](https://github.com/pabloariasal/couring) · [benchmark](https://github.com/pabloariasal/couring)

##### file_io_benchmark (Windows unbuffered multi-threaded loading)  `C++`  `no license`  `active`  `Tier C`

Windows benchmark showing multi-threaded FILE_FLAG_NO_BUFFERING reads reach 11.3 GB/s on NVMe versus fread and memory mapping.

**Beats:** fread / memory-mapped file reads — On an AMD Ryzen 9 7950X with a Samsung SSD 9100 PRO 4TB, loading 1,000 x 1 MiB chunks over 5 repetitions with the file evicted from cache, unbuffered multi-threaded reads reached 11.3-11.4 GB/s versus 6.8-7.3 GB/s for multi-threaded memory mapping and 4.2-6.3 GB/s for fread; compiler and flags are not stated (CMake project, MSVC implied). The fread rows read sequentially rather than in the shuffled order, so the comparison is not like-for-like, though the bias favors fread.

**Known shortcoming:** Harness flaw in the fread rows: no fseek, so they read the file sequentially instead of the shuffled range.offset order, and the shared FILE* lock serializes fread in the parallel case. The reference-value check still passes and the bias favours fread, so the unbuffered win holds, but the rows are not like for like. No LICENSE file; Windows and MSVC C++23 only.

**Independent measurement:** code reading by enricher

**How:** Unbuffered (direct) I/O skips the Windows file cache, so data goes from the SSD by DMA straight into a sector-aligned user buffer with no extra copy and no cache bookkeeping. Throughput comes from parallelism: std::for_each(std::execution::par) runs many threads, each issuing one blocking 1 MiB overlapped ReadFile and waiting on GetOverlappedResult, which keeps enough requests in flight to approach the drive's rated 14.8 GB/s. Single-threaded, the same path reaches only 4.7-4.9 GB/s.

**Use it when:**
- Windows apps that read large files once (point clouds, assets, model weights) and do not benefit from the OS cache.
- Chunked loads of 1 MiB-scale, sector-aligned blocks that can be issued from many threads at once to saturate a PCIe 4/5 NVMe drive.
- As a reference for writing your own Windows direct-I/O loader before reaching for IoRing or DirectStorage.
- When memory mapping tops out (about 7 GB/s here with many threads, 1.2 GB/s with one) and you need the remaining drive bandwidth.

**Skip it when:**
- Linux or macOS: the code is Windows-only (MappedFile.h has a literal TODO for Linux and will not compile there); use liburing or O_DIRECT instead.
- Single-threaded readers: unbuffered at one thread (4.7-4.9 GB/s) did not beat fread (4.4-6.3 GB/s) in the author's table.
- Data read repeatedly or small/unaligned reads: bypassing the cache throws away reuse, and offsets, sizes and buffer addresses must be multiples of the physical sector size.
- Anything you need to ship as a dependency: no LICENSE file, 2 commits, no tests, error handling is exit() with a stack trace.

**Vs siblings:** Pick it when you are on Windows and want the simplest pattern for saturating NVMe; on Linux, liburing (io_uring) or SPDK are the catalogued choices, and LLFIO is the cross-platform library that wraps direct I/O properly.

**Gotchas:**
- Harness flaw: the fread benchmarks never call fseek, so every fread reads the next sequential 1 MiB of the file instead of the shuffled range.offset; the reference-value check still passes because the same first 1,000 MiB are read in some order. fread therefore got sequential reads with OS read-ahead while the other methods read in random order, and in the 'auto' case all threads share one FILE* whose CRT lock serializes them (which explains the author's puzzle that fread par is slower than fread seq).
